Demographic details for allotment and communication are fetched from the depositories using the DP ID, client ID and PAN given in the bid, which is why investors must keep demat records updated.
Which category of bidder is allowed to bid at the 'cut-off' price in a book-built IPO?
Qualified institutional buyers
Retail individual investors
Non-institutional investors bidding above ₹2 lakh
Anchor investors

Only retail individual investors (and eligible employees and shareholders in reserved portions within the limit) may bid at cut-off. QIBs and NIIs must bid at a specific price and cannot use the cut-off option.
Anchor investors in a book-built IPO submit their bids:
On the last day of the bid period
One working day before the issue opens to the public
On the day of listing
After the basis of allotment is finalised by the registrar
The anchor investor bid/issue period is one working day before the issue opening date. Allocation to anchors is disclosed before the public issue opens, which signals institutional interest.
An ASBA bidder in an IPO is not allotted any shares. What happens to the application money?
The blocked amount is unblocked in the bidder's bank account
A refund cheque is posted to the bidder's address
The amount is adjusted against the next IPO
It is transferred to the issuer and refunded later by cheque
Under ASBA, money never leaves the bidder's account until allotment. For unsuccessful bids, the bank simply releases the block on instruction, so no refund cheque or transfer is needed.

Roles and Responsibilities in a Public I.overview: A public issue involves many intermediaries: the issuer, lead managers, registrar to the issue, bankers, sponsor bank, SCSBs, syndicate members, registered brokers, collecting depository participants, underwriters, monitoring agency and the stock exchanges. This chapter covers what each does and the requirements SEBI places on them. Learners should know who monitors the use of issue proceeds, where investors can submit ASBA forms, the account into which funds of successful bidders move, the role of the designated stock exchange and the special market-making requirement for SME issues.
questions: Monitoring the use of issue proceeds in a large IPO is done by a monitoring agency, which must be a:
Statutory auditor of the issuer company
Credit rating agency registered with SEBI
Registrar to the issue for that IPO
Scheduled commercial bank acting as banker to the issue
Since 2022, ICDR requires the monitoring agency for issues above the threshold to be a SEBI-registered credit rating agency. It reports on utilisation of proceeds against the stated objects.
In a public issue, the intermediary that agrees to subscribe to any shares left unsubscribed by the public is the:
Underwriter
Registrar to the issue
Sponsor bank
Debenture trustee

An underwriter commits to take up the shortfall in subscription, for a commission. The registrar processes applications, the sponsor bank handles UPI mandates and a debenture trustee serves debenture holders.
Apart from the branches of SCSBs, an investor can submit a physical ASBA bid form at:
Designated locations of syndicate members, registered brokers, RTAs and CDPs
Any office of the Registrar of Companies in the issuer's state
The issuer's registered office only
Any branch of SEBI

SEBI widened bid collection to syndicate members, registered stock brokers, registrars and collecting DPs at designated centres. They upload bids to the exchange platform and forward forms for blocking of funds.
When an issue is to be listed on more than one exchange, the issuer chooses one of them, for allotment and related purposes, as the:
Principal clearing exchange
Designated stock exchange
Lead stock exchange
Primary listing authority
The issuer names a designated stock exchange in the offer document. The basis of allotment is finalised in consultation with it, and its representative is involved in allotment-related processes.
Once allotment is finalised, the blocked amounts of successful ASBA bidders are transferred to the:
Investor Education and Protection Fund
Depository's settlement account
Public issue account
Lead manager's current account

On instructions from the registrar, SCSBs and the sponsor bank debit the blocked funds for successful bids and transfer them to the public issue account opened by the issuer with the banker to the issue.
Under ICDR, the issuer must appoint as Registrar to the issue an entity that:
Is a subsidiary of the lead manager
Holds at least 1% of the issuer's paid-up equity shares
Is also the issuer's statutory auditor
Has electronic connectivity with both depositories

Since allotment is made only in demat form, ICDR requires the issuer to appoint a registrar with connectivity to both NSDL and CDSL. Shareholding in the issuer or links with the auditor are not requirements.
A successful IPO applicant finds that allotted shares have not been credited to his demat account. Whom should he contact first?
The registrar to the issue
The stock exchange's trading desk
The Reserve Bank of India
His mutual fund distributor
The registrar handles post-issue matters such as allotment, demat credit and unblocking, and must redress such complaints. If not resolved, the investor can escalate through SEBI's grievance system.
For IPOs on the SME platform, the lead manager must ensure compulsory market making for a minimum of:
Six months from listing
One year from listing
Ten years from listing or until migration to the main board
Three years from listing
ICDR requires market making for SME issues for at least three years from listing so that the shares have liquidity. The market maker gives two-way quotes for a minimum portion of the trading day.

Depository Services.overview: This chapter explains the depository system in India: the two depositories, depository participants, beneficial owners, issuers and RTAs, and the services available to account holders. Learners should know what a Basic Services Demat Account is, how the Demat Debit and Pledge Instruction replaced broad powers of attorney, limits on joint holders, who can nominate, how freezing works, and why demat securities are fungible. Focus on the rights of the beneficial owner and how the depository's records drive dividends, voting and other corporate benefits.
questions: An investor who wants to hold shares in electronic form opens an account with a:
Registrar to the issue
Depository participant
Credit rating agency
Clearing corporation
Investors cannot open accounts directly with NSDL or CDSL; they open a demat account through a SEBI-registered depository participant such as a bank or broker that is an agent of the depository.
A Basic Services Demat Account (BSDA) is meant for:
Foreign portfolio investors who trade actively in equity derivatives
Companies that hold treasury shares
Brokers who hold clients' securities in a pool
Individuals with a single demat account and small holdings, at reduced charges
The BSDA is designed for small individual investors who have only one demat account and holdings below a value set by SEBI. Annual maintenance charges are nil or low, depending on holding value.
To let a stock broker debit shares from a client's demat account for sales and pledges, SEBI now requires the client to give a:
Demat Debit and Pledge Instruction (DDPI)
General power of attorney for all purposes
Delivery instruction slip for every trade
Letter of confirmation from the RTA

The DDPI replaced the broad power of attorney and limits the broker's authority to specific purposes such as settlement of trades and margin pledges. It reduces the risk of misuse of client securities.
What is the maximum number of holders allowed in a single demat account?
Three
Two
Four, if all are resident individuals
Five
A demat account may be held by one person singly or by up to three joint holders. The order of names in the account must match the order on securities for demat requests to be accepted.
Which demat account holder cannot make a nomination for the account?
A body corporate
A sole individual holder
Individual joint holders
A resident individual holding shares singly
Nomination is available to individuals holding singly or jointly. Non-individuals such as companies, trusts and HUFs cannot nominate, since succession rules on death do not apply to them.
A demat account holder going abroad for a long period wants to prevent any debit from her account. She can ask her DP to:
Close the account and reopen it later
Rematerialise all her holdings
Transfer holdings to her broker's pool account
Freeze her account for debits
Depositories let account holders freeze their accounts for debits, credits or both. Freezing debits protects holdings from unauthorised transfers while still allowing credits such as bonus shares.
Shares held in demat form do not carry distinctive numbers because they are:
Held only by the issuer company and not by individual investors
Fungible, so any share of that ISIN is identical to any other
Not entitled to corporate benefits
Converted into debentures on credit to the account

Demat securities of the same ISIN are fungible; ownership is recorded as a quantity rather than as specific numbered certificates. This makes transfer and settlement fast and avoids certificate-level tracking.
For dematerialised shares, who is entitled to receive dividends and to vote at general meetings?
The depository, since it is the registered owner
The beneficial owner as shown in the depository's records
The depository participant that maintains the beneficial owner's account
The RTA of the issuer company

Although the depository is the registered owner, the Depositories Act gives all rights and benefits, including dividend and voting, to the beneficial owner. The depository has no voting rights on such shares.

Processes related to Depositories.overview: This chapter describes how depository processes work end to end: dematerialisation and rematerialisation, pledge, off-market transfers, transmission on death and corporate actions. The RTA plays a key role in confirming demat and remat requests, cancelling certificates, updating the register of members and reconciling capital. Learners should know the sequence of steps and who initiates each request, common reasons for rejection of demat requests, and the quarterly reconciliation of share capital audit. Pay attention to what the RTA does with physical certificates and how records are kept consistent between depositories and the issuer.
questions: After an investor submits a demat request, the shares are credited to her demat account only when:
The DP receives the original certificates by post from the investor
The issuer's RTA confirms the request electronically to the depository
The stock exchange approves the request
The investor sells the shares in the market
The DP forwards the request electronically and sends certificates to the RTA. Only after the RTA verifies and confirms does the depository credit the beneficial owner's account.
Which of these is a common reason for an RTA to reject a demat request?
The investor's depository participant is a private sector bank
The signature on the request does not match the specimen in the RTA's records
The shares have a face value of ₹1 each
The investor already holds other shares in demat
RTAs verify certificates, names and signatures against their records. A signature mismatch, a name mismatch or certificates not matching the folio are typical reasons for rejection.
After confirming a demat request, what does the RTA do with the physical certificates?
Returns them to the investor for safe keeping
Sends them to the stock exchange for storage
Keeps them active in case the investor later wants to sell in physical form
Cancels and mutilates them and records the depository as the holder of those shares
Once confirmed, the certificates are cancelled and mutilated so they cannot be reused, and the register of members is updated to show the depository as the registered owner.
In rematerialisation of shares, the physical certificates are printed and dispatched to the investor by:
The depository participant
The issuer's RTA
The depository
The clearing corporation

The investor submits a remat request through the DP. The depository blocks the holding and informs the RTA, which prints and dispatches certificates and confirms, after which the demat balance is debited.
In a pledge of dematerialised shares, the pledge creation request is initiated by the:
Pledgee, without any involvement or consent of the pledgor
RTA of the issuer company
Stock exchange
Pledgor, through its depository participant
The pledgor (the borrower who owns the shares) initiates the pledge through its DP. The pledgee confirms the request through its own DP, after which the shares are marked as pledged.
Anil wants to gift 50 shares from his demat account to his sister's demat account. He instructs his DP using:
A demat request form
A remat request form
A transmission request form signed by both of them
An off-market delivery instruction

Gifts and other non-exchange transfers are made as off-market transfers using a delivery instruction slip or its online equivalent, giving the reason for transfer. Demat, remat and transmission forms have other uses.
The reconciliation of share capital audit, which ties total issued capital to holdings in NSDL, CDSL and physical form, is carried out:
Once in five years by the statutory auditor
Every quarter by a practising chartered accountant or company secretary
Only at the time of an IPO by the lead manager
Every month by the stock exchange
The Depositories and Participants Regulations require issuers to get this audit done every quarter by a qualified practising CA or CS and to submit the report to the stock exchanges.
A sole demat account holder dies, leaving a registered nominee. How are the shares transmitted?
The RTA issues physical certificates in the nominee's name
The nominee must buy the shares on the exchange
The shares are cancelled and the company pays their face value
The DP transfers them to the nominee's demat account on receiving the required documents

The nominee submits a transmission request form and death certificate to the deceased's DP. After verification, the securities are transmitted to the nominee's demat account; the nominee needs a demat account.

Investor Interface with the R&T Agent.overview: This chapter covers the service requests an RTA handles directly for investors, especially holders of physical securities: KYC updation, nomination, transmission, signature updation, duplicate securities and dividend payment. Learners should know the purpose of the common ISR and SH forms, how deletion of a deceased joint holder is treated, why demat holders must update details through their DP, and how unclaimed dividends and shares move to the Investor Education and Protection Fund. Focus on matching each request with the correct process and documents.
questions: A holder of physical shares wants to register his PAN, mobile number and email address with the RTA. Which form should he submit?
Form ISR-4
Form SH-13
Form ISR-1
Form ISR-5
SEBI's common forms use ISR-1 for registering or updating PAN, KYC and contact details. ISR-4 is for service requests like duplicate securities, SH-13 for nomination and ISR-5 for transmission.
A holder of physical shares wishes to register a nominee for the first time. Which form is used?
Form SH-14
Form SH-13
Form ISR-3
Form ISR-2
SH-13 under the Companies Act rules is used to make a nomination. SH-14 is for cancelling or varying a nomination, ISR-3 for opting out of nomination and ISR-2 for banker's attestation of signature.
Shares are held jointly by Suresh and Kavita. Suresh dies, and Kavita asks the RTA to delete his name. This request is processed as:
Transmission in favour of the surviving holder
Transposition of names
Transfer by way of gift
Rematerialisation of shares
On the death of a joint holder, the deceased's name is deleted by transmission to the surviving holder, on submission of the death certificate. Transposition only changes the order of living holders.
An investor's signature on a request does not match the specimen in the RTA's records. The RTA should ask for:
A fresh demat account opening form
Form ISR-2 with the signature attested by the investor's banker
A copy of the company's annual report
A transmission request supported by a death certificate
SEBI norms allow the RTA to update a signature using Form ISR-2, in which the investor's banker attests the signature and confirms bank details. This prevents fraudulent requests.
A holder of physical shares has not registered bank account details with the RTA. Under current SEBI norms, how will his dividend be paid?
By a physical dividend warrant posted to his address
In cash at the RTA's investor service centre
By crediting it to his broker's client account
Only electronically, after he furnishes the required KYC and bank details
SEBI requires dividends and other payments to physical holders to be made only electronically once PAN, contact, bank details and specimen signature are registered. Payment is held until then.
To issue duplicate securities in place of lost share certificates, an RTA typically requires:
Only a phone call from the registered mobile number
A no-objection letter from the stock exchange
Form ISR-4 along with an affidavit and an indemnity from the holder
A letter from any other shareholder of the company

Because duplicates replace lost certificates, the holder must protect the company against misuse through an affidavit and indemnity, with other documents depending on value. The RTA then issues a letter of confirmation.
A shareholder holding only demat shares writes to the company's RTA to change her address. What should the RTA advise?
Submit Form ISR-1 to the RTA so that it can change the depository records
Update the address through her DP, since the RTA uses depository records for demat holdings
Convert the shares into physical form first
Write to SEBI, which updates addresses for all investors

For demat holdings, the RTA relies on beneficial owner details downloaded from the depositories. Address and bank changes must therefore be made through the DP, after which they flow to the company's records.
Shares on which dividend has been unclaimed for seven consecutive years were transferred to the IEPF. How can the shareholder claim them back?
By filing Form IEPF-5 online with the IEPF Authority
By submitting Form ISR-1 to the company's RTA
By asking the DP to reverse the transfer
The shares cannot be claimed once transferred
Shares and unclaimed amounts transferred to the IEPF can be claimed by filing Form IEPF-5, with documents verified by the company. Neither the RTA nor the DP can reverse the transfer directly.

Secondary Market Transactions.overview: This chapter explains how trades in listed securities are executed and settled: trading members, contract notes, the clearing corporation, pay-in and pay-out, auctions for short delivery, bulk deal disclosures and the link between ex-date and record date under T+1 settlement. Learners should understand how securities reach the buyer's demat account under current direct pay-out rules and what happens when a seller fails to deliver. Since RTAs depend on depository data as on the record date, knowing the trading and settlement cycle helps in getting corporate action entitlements right.
questions: Who can place orders directly in a stock exchange's trading system?
Any investor with a PAN
The company's RTA
Trading members registered with SEBI
Depository participants that are banks
Only trading members (stock brokers) registered with SEBI and admitted by the exchange can enter orders. Investors trade through these brokers, while RTAs and DPs have no trading access.
A stock broker must issue a contract note to a client for trades executed on an exchange within:
Seven days of the trade
One month of the trade
The next quarterly statement
24 hours of the trade
SEBI requires brokers to issue contract notes, physically or electronically, within 24 hours of execution. The note records price, quantity, brokerage and charges, and is evidence of the trade.
In the settlement of exchange trades, 'pay-in' refers to:
The clearing corporation releasing funds and securities to members
Investors paying dividends to the company
The company paying listing fees to the exchange
Clearing members delivering funds and securities to the clearing corporation

Pay-in is when members deliver their obligations of funds and securities to the clearing corporation. Pay-out is the reverse, when the clearing corporation releases funds and securities to receiving members.
A selling broker fails to deliver shares on the settlement day. To meet the buyer's entitlement, the clearing corporation normally:
Cancels the buyer's trade and refunds the brokerage only
Conducts an auction to buy the shares, or closes out if the auction fails
Asks the issuer to print new shares for the buyer
Waits until the seller delivers, however long it takes

Short deliveries are handled through an auction in which shares are bought for the buyer, with the cost recovered from the defaulting seller. If the auction fails, the trade is closed out at a prescribed price.
Under current SEBI norms, securities bought by a client in the cash segment are paid out:
First to the broker's pool account and later to the client
To the RTA, which then credits the client
To the depository's suspense account for seven days
Directly to the client's demat account by the clearing corporation
To protect client securities, SEBI mandated direct pay-out of securities by the clearing corporation to clients' demat accounts, instead of routing them through brokers' pool accounts.
A deal in a single scrip in which the total quantity bought or sold by a client exceeds 0.5% of the company's listed equity shares is called a:
Block deal
Spot deal
Bulk deal
Odd-lot deal
Trades by a client in a day totalling more than 0.5% of listed equity shares are bulk deals and must be disclosed by the exchanges. Block deals are large trades executed in a separate window.
Under the T+1 rolling settlement cycle, the ex-date for a corporate action such as a dividend is:
One working day before the record date
The same day as the record date
Two working days after the record date
The date of the board meeting
Since a buyer on T receives shares on T+1, a buyer on the record date would not be on the record. So with T+1, the ex-date and record date fall on the same day.
An investor buys shares on the exchange and wants to check that delivery has been completed. Which record should she verify?
Her demat account statement or holding balance with the DP
The company's register of members for physical holders
The lead manager's allotment list
The RTA's list of unclaimed dividends

Exchange-traded purchases are delivered by credit to the buyer's demat account, so the DP holding statement confirms receipt. The company's physical register and IPO allotment lists are not relevant here.

Client Servicing.overview: This chapter deals with how RTAs serve investors and resolve grievances: the difference between queries and complaints, SEBI's SCORES platform and its timelines, online dispute resolution, unpaid dividend accounts, investor charters, data confidentiality and good service practices. Learners should know the time allowed to resolve a SCORES complaint, the next step if an investor is still dissatisfied, where unclaimed dividends go and how to handle incomplete requests efficiently. Focus on practical scenarios, because client servicing questions often test the right response rather than a definition.
questions: Under SEBI's SCORES system, an entity receiving an investor complaint must resolve it and file an action taken report within:
7 calendar days of receipt
21 calendar days of receipt
45 calendar days of receipt
90 calendar days of receipt

SEBI's revised SCORES framework requires the entity to redress the complaint and upload an action taken report within 21 calendar days. Delays are escalated and monitored by the designated body and SEBI.
An investor remains dissatisfied after the RTA's response and the SCORES process. Which mechanism can he use next for conciliation or arbitration?
The online dispute resolution portal (SMART ODR)
The Registrar of Companies
The consumer helpline of the RBI
The company's AGM
SEBI's online dispute resolution framework lets investors start online conciliation and, if needed, arbitration against market participants, including RTAs, through the common ODR portal.
A company's dividend warrant remains unpaid or unclaimed 30 days after declaration. The unpaid amount must be transferred to:
The company's general reserve
The Investor Education and Protection Fund immediately
The RTA's own current account
A special unpaid dividend account of the company with a scheduled bank
Section 124 of the Companies Act requires unpaid dividends to be moved to an Unpaid Dividend Account within seven days after the 30-day period. Only amounts unclaimed for seven years go to the IEPF.
SEBI requires RTAs to display an 'investor charter' on their websites. Its main purpose is to:
Publish the RTA's annual profit and loss account
List all shares held by the RTA's employees
Advertise new IPOs managed by the RTA
Tell investors about services, timelines, their rights and the grievance process

The investor charter sets out services offered, expected timelines, investors' rights and duties, and how to escalate grievances. It aims to make service standards transparent, not to publish financials or adverts.
An investor phones the RTA to ask about the record date for an upcoming dividend. How should this be treated?
As a complaint, to be reported on SCORES
As a transmission request needing documents
As a query, to be answered promptly with accurate information
As a request to be referred to SEBI
A request for information with no allegation of deficiency is a query. Only grievances about service failure, such as non-receipt of dividend, are complaints recorded and redressed as such.
A marketing firm asks an RTA for a list of shareholders' mobile numbers and email addresses for a promotion. The RTA should:
Share it for a fee, since the data belongs to the RTA
Share it if the firm promises to use it carefully
Share only email addresses, since they are not sensitive
Decline, since investor data must be kept confidential and used only for authorised purposes
RTAs hold investor data on behalf of issuers and must protect it. Sharing it with third parties for marketing would breach confidentiality obligations under SEBI norms and data protection law.
An RTA finds three deficiencies in a transmission request. What is the best practice?
Reject the request without giving any reasons
Raise one deficiency at a time as each is fixed
Inform the claimant of all the deficiencies together in a single communication
Process it anyway and seek documents after transfer
Listing all deficiencies at once avoids repeated rounds and delays. Processing without the required documents could cause wrongful transmission, and rejection without reasons is poor service.
Which of the following is an example of a complaint rather than a query?
An investor asks for the RTA's office address
An investor reports that a declared dividend was not credited to his bank account
An investor asks when the AGM will be held
An investor asks for a copy of the nomination form
A complaint alleges a service failure needing redressal, such as non-receipt of a dividend. Requests for addresses, dates or forms are queries and can be answered directly.

Introduction to Securities.overview: This chapter introduces securities and the structure of the Indian securities market. It covers the difference between the primary market, where issuers raise fresh capital, and the secondary market, where existing securities change hands. Learners should know the main intermediaries such as stock exchanges, clearing corporations, depositories and depository participants, the difference between money market and capital market instruments, and how government securities are issued. Revise the settlement process, the role of dematerialisation and how each intermediary protects investors, since RTA work depends on understanding these basic market linkages.
questions: A company sells new shares to the public for the first time through an IPO. In which market does this transaction take place?
Secondary market
Money market
Over-the-counter debt market
Primary market

An IPO is a fresh issue of securities by the issuer to investors, so money flows to the company. That is a primary market transaction. Later trading of these shares between investors happens in the secondary market.
A company wants to raise funds for ten years to build a new plant. Which instrument suits this need?
A 91-day treasury bill
A 10-year corporate bond
A 3-month commercial paper
A 6-month certificate of deposit

Long-term needs are met through capital market instruments, which usually have maturities above one year. A 10-year bond qualifies, while treasury bills, commercial paper and certificates of deposit are short-term money market instruments maturing within a year.
Shares held in dematerialised form by investors in India are held in electronic accounts with:
NSDL or CDSL, through a depository participant
The stock exchange where the shares are listed
The registrar of companies of the issuer's state
The company's own bankers as safe custody

India has two depositories, NSDL and CDSL, which hold securities in electronic form. Investors access them through depository participants such as banks and brokers. Stock exchanges provide trading platforms but do not hold investors' securities.
An investor opens a demat account through her bank to hold shares electronically. In this arrangement, the bank acts as a:
Clearing member
Registrar to an issue
Depository participant
Custodian of the depository

A depository participant is the agent of a depository through which investors open and operate demat accounts. Many banks and brokers are registered DPs. A clearing member settles trades on an exchange, which is a different role.
What is the main role of a clearing corporation in the stock market?
Listing new companies after scrutiny of their offer documents
Acting as counterparty to trades and guaranteeing settlement
Holding shareholders' securities in electronic form
Setting the price band of each listed share

A clearing corporation clears and settles trades, often becoming the counterparty to both buyer and seller through novation. This guarantees settlement and removes counterparty risk. Holding securities electronically is the depository's job.
What is the standard rolling settlement cycle for trades in the equity cash segment in India?
India moved fully to a T+1 rolling settlement cycle for the equity cash segment in January 2023, so trades settle one working day after the trade date. T+2 was the earlier cycle and is now outdated.
Commercial paper is best described as:
A long-term secured bond issued by the central government for infrastructure
A deposit receipt issued by banks against fixed deposits
A share certificate issued by a company in physical form
An unsecured short-term promissory note issued by companies

Commercial paper is an unsecured money market instrument issued by highly rated companies to meet short-term funding needs, usually at a discount. Certificates of deposit are issued by banks, and government bonds are long-term instruments.
Dated government securities of the Government of India are issued in the primary market through auctions conducted by:
The Reserve Bank of India
SEBI
The National Stock Exchange
The Ministry of Corporate Affairs

The RBI manages the public debt of the Government of India and conducts auctions for dated securities and treasury bills. SEBI regulates the securities market but does not issue or auction government securities.

Characteristics of Equity Shares.overview: This chapter explains what an equity share represents and the rights and risks that come with it. Focus on ownership, limited liability, voting, residual claim on profits and assets, and the absence of any guaranteed return. Revise corporate actions that change a shareholder's holding, such as bonus issues, rights issues, stock splits and buybacks, and be able to work out their effect on the number of shares and face value. Basic valuation ratios such as earnings per share and price-to-earnings are also useful. These concepts matter because RTAs process such corporate actions for shareholders.
questions: A shareholder holds 100 shares of a company. The company announces a 1:1 bonus issue. After the bonus, the shareholder will hold:
150 shares, after paying the face value
200 shares, without paying any money
200 shares, after paying the market price
100 shares with double the face value

In a 1:1 bonus, one free share is given for every share held, so 100 shares become 200. Bonus shares are issued by capitalising reserves, so the shareholder pays nothing. Total value of the holding does not change on its own.
A company splits its shares of face value ₹10 into shares of face value ₹2. An investor holding 100 shares before the split will hold:
500 shares of ₹2 each
100 shares of ₹2 each
20 shares of ₹10 each
200 shares of ₹5 each

A stock split divides each share into smaller units. Splitting ₹10 into ₹2 gives five shares for each share held, so 100 shares become 500 shares of ₹2 each. The total face value of the holding stays at ₹1,000.
In a rights issue, new shares are offered:
Free of cost to all existing shareholders
Only to qualified institutional investors at a discount to the market price
To employees as part of their compensation
To existing shareholders in proportion to their holdings

A rights issue gives existing shareholders the right to buy additional shares, usually at a price below market, in proportion to what they already hold. Shares given free are bonus shares, and shares for employees come under ESOP schemes.
If a company is wound up, equity shareholders are paid:
Before secured lenders, since equity shareholders are the owners of the company
Along with debenture holders, in equal priority
Only after creditors and preference shareholders are paid
Before preference shareholders but after banks

Equity shareholders have a residual claim. On liquidation, secured and unsecured creditors are paid first, then preference shareholders, and only what remains goes to equity shareholders. This is why equity carries higher risk than debt.
What does 'limited liability' mean for an equity shareholder of a company limited by shares?
Dividend is limited to a fixed rate each year
Voting rights are limited to special resolutions
The shares can be sold only to limited buyers
Loss is limited to the amount invested or unpaid on the shares

Limited liability means a shareholder cannot be asked to pay the company's debts beyond the amount unpaid on their shares. Once shares are fully paid, the maximum loss is the investment itself. It has nothing to do with dividend rate or voting.
A share trades at ₹150 and the company's earnings per share is ₹5. What is its price-to-earnings (P/E) ratio?

The P/E ratio is market price divided by earnings per share. Here ₹150 ÷ ₹5 = 30, meaning investors pay ₹30 for every rupee of annual earnings. Multiplying the two, or dividing the other way round, gives the wrong figures.
When a company buys back its own shares from shareholders, the usual effect is that:
The number of shares outstanding is reduced
The face value of each share is increased
New shares are issued to existing shareholders
The company's debt is converted into equity

In a buyback, the company uses its funds to purchase its own shares, which are then extinguished. This reduces the number of shares outstanding and can raise earnings per share. It does not change face value or issue new shares.
Which statement about returns on equity shares is correct?
Dividends are fixed at the time of issue and paid every year
Returns come from dividends and price changes, neither of which is guaranteed
Capital appreciation is assured if the shares are held for at least five continuous years
Returns are protected by the depository against market losses

Equity returns consist of dividends, which are paid at the board's discretion, and capital gains or losses from price movements. Neither is assured, which makes equity a risk investment. Depositories hold shares but do not protect their value.

Characteristics of Debt Securities.overview: This chapter covers debt securities such as bonds, debentures and money market instruments. Key ideas are face value, coupon, maturity, yield and the inverse relationship between interest rates and bond prices. Learners should understand the main risks in debt, including interest rate risk, credit or default risk, reinvestment risk and liquidity risk, and how credit ratings signal safety. Revise special features such as zero coupon bonds, secured and unsecured debentures, and call and put options. Practise simple yield calculations, since current yield and price sensitivity are common application questions.
questions: If market interest rates rise, what generally happens to the prices of existing fixed-coupon bonds?
They rise
They remain unchanged until maturity
They fall
They rise only for long-term bonds

Bond prices move inversely to interest rates. When rates rise, new bonds offer higher coupons, so older bonds with lower coupons become less attractive and their prices fall until their yield matches the market.
A zero coupon bond is one that:
Is issued at a discount and pays face value at maturity
Pays interest monthly at a floating rate
Carries no credit risk at all, as such bonds are issued only by the government
Is repaid in equal instalments over its life

A zero coupon bond pays no periodic interest. It is issued at a discount to its face value and the investor earns the difference when it is redeemed at face value on maturity. Its issuer can be any borrower, so credit risk may exist.
A bond with a face value of ₹100 carries an 8% annual coupon and is currently trading at ₹80. What is its current yield?
Current yield is annual coupon divided by market price. The coupon is ₹8 (8% of ₹100), and ₹8 ÷ ₹80 = 10%. The coupon rate of 8% is based on face value, not on the price the investor actually pays.
A secured debenture differs from an unsecured debenture because a secured debenture:
Is guaranteed by SEBI against default
Always carries a higher coupon rate
Can be converted into equity shares
Is backed by a charge on specified assets of the issuer

A secured debenture has a charge created on the issuer's assets, which holders can enforce if the issuer defaults. SEBI does not guarantee any security. Convertibility is a separate feature, and secured debt usually pays a lower coupon.
Among the following long-term credit ratings, which one indicates the highest degree of safety for timely servicing of debt?
AA+
A
AAA
BBB-

Rating agencies use AAA for the highest safety and lowest credit risk. AA and A indicate high and adequate safety respectively, while BBB- is the lowest investment-grade rating. Ratings below BBB- are speculative grade.
Two bonds have the same coupon and credit rating, but one matures in 2 years and the other in 15 years. If interest rates change, which statement is correct?
The 2-year bond's price will change more
Both prices will change by the same amount
Neither price will change as the coupons are fixed
The 15-year bond's price will change more

Longer maturity bonds have higher duration, so their prices are more sensitive to interest rate changes. The 15-year bond will therefore show a larger price movement than the 2-year bond for the same change in rates.
A bond with a call option allows:
The issuer to redeem the bond before its maturity date
The investor to sell the bond back to the issuer early
The investor to convert the bond into equity shares
The issuer to stop paying interest for one year

A call option gives the issuer the right to repay the bond early, usually when interest rates fall. The investor's right to demand early repayment is a put option. Conversion into shares is a feature of convertible bonds.
An investor receives half-yearly coupons from a bond but interest rates in the market have fallen, so the coupons can only be invested at lower rates. This is an example of:
Credit risk
Reinvestment risk
Liquidity risk
Market liquidity risk

Reinvestment risk is the risk that interim cash flows such as coupons must be reinvested at lower rates than expected. It is highest when rates fall. Credit risk relates to default by the issuer, and liquidity risk to difficulty in selling.

Characteristics of Other Securities.overview: Apart from plain equity and debt, the securities market offers several other instruments. This chapter covers preference shares and their types, warrants, depository receipts, hybrid securities, units of REITs and InvITs, and derivatives such as futures and options. Learners should understand who has a right and who has an obligation in each contract, how preference shares rank against equity, and how instruments like warrants and convertibles may lead to new equity. Focus on comparing features and on applying them to short scenarios, for example identifying whether an option buyer gains when prices rise or fall.
questions: Preference shareholders have priority over equity shareholders in:
Voting on all company resolutions
Payment of dividend and repayment of capital
Receiving bonus shares and rights issues
Appointing the company's directors

Preference shares get preference over equity in receiving dividends, usually at a fixed rate, and in repayment of capital on winding up. They normally do not carry voting rights on all matters, so equity holders control the company.
A company could not pay the dividend on its cumulative preference shares for two years. What happens to this unpaid dividend?
It lapses and is not payable in later years
It is converted into additional equity shares
It is paid to the shareholders out of the Investor Education and Protection Fund
It accumulates and must be paid before any equity dividend

For cumulative preference shares, unpaid dividends accumulate as arrears. The company must clear these arrears before it can declare any dividend to equity shareholders. For non-cumulative preference shares, a missed dividend lapses.
A warrant issued by a company gives the holder:
An obligation to sell shares to the company at maturity
A fixed interest income for the life of the warrant
The right to buy the company's shares at a set price in future
Ownership of shares from the date of issue itself

A warrant entitles the holder to subscribe to the issuer's shares at a predetermined price within a specified period. The holder is not obliged to exercise it and does not own the shares until exercise. Warrants carry no interest.
An investor buys a call option on a stock. Which statement correctly describes her position?
She has the right, but not the obligation, to buy the stock
She is obliged to buy the stock on the expiry date
She has the right to sell the stock to the option writer at the strike price
She receives the premium from the option seller

A call option buyer pays a premium for the right, but not the obligation, to buy the underlying at the strike price. The seller receives the premium and has the obligation. The right to sell belongs to a put option buyer.
In a futures contract on a stock, which of the following is true?
Only the buyer has an obligation, the seller has a right
The buyer pays a non-refundable premium to the seller
Neither party has any obligation until the contract expires
Both buyer and seller are obliged to complete the contract

A futures contract is a binding agreement in which both parties are obliged to buy or sell the underlying at the agreed price on expiry. There is no premium as in options; instead both parties deposit margins with the exchange.
An Indian company issues shares abroad in the form of instruments listed on a US stock exchange. These instruments are called:
American Depository Receipts
Indian Depository Receipts
Foreign Currency Convertible Bonds
Global Treasury Receipts

Depository receipts represent shares of a company held with a custodian and are listed abroad. When listed in the US they are called American Depository Receipts. Indian Depository Receipts are issued in India by foreign companies.
A Real Estate Investment Trust (REIT) in India mainly invests in:
Housing loans given to individual home buyers
Shares of listed real estate developers only
Completed, income-generating real estate such as office parks
Undeveloped agricultural land, to be sold later when land prices have risen

REITs pool money from investors to own completed, rent-yielding properties, mainly commercial office space, and distribute most of their income. They are regulated by SEBI. They do not lend to home buyers or mainly hold developer shares.
An investor buys a put option on an index with a strike price of 22,000. In which situation will the option be profitable on expiry, ignoring the premium?
If the index closes above 22,000
If the index closes below 22,000
If the index closes exactly at 22,000
Whatever the level at which the index closes

A put option gives the right to sell at the strike price. It has value on expiry only if the index is below the strike, because the holder can sell at 22,000 something worth less. Above the strike, the put expires worthless.

SEBI – Role and Regulations.overview: This chapter deals with the Securities and Exchange Board of India, the regulator of the securities market including mutual funds and RTAs. Learners should know how SEBI was set up, its objectives of protecting investors, developing the market and regulating intermediaries, and the powers it has to register, inspect, investigate and penalise. Revise the appellate route through the Securities Appellate Tribunal, the investor grievance mechanisms such as SCORES and the online dispute resolution platform, and the role of industry bodies like AMFI, which are not regulators. Questions often ask which body handles which function.
questions: SEBI was first set up in 1988 and was given statutory powers through:
The Companies Act, 1956
The SEBI Act, 1992
The Securities Contracts (Regulation) Act, 1956
The Depositories Act, 1996

SEBI started as a non-statutory body in 1988 and became a statutory regulator when the SEBI Act was passed in 1992. The Act sets out its powers and functions. The other Acts deal with companies, contracts and depositories.
The preamble of the SEBI Act states SEBI's purpose as:
Fixing interest rates and controlling money supply in the economy
Collecting taxes on capital gains from securities transactions
Protecting investors and developing and regulating the securities market
Guaranteeing returns to investors in listed securities

SEBI's three core objectives are to protect the interests of investors in securities, to promote the development of the securities market and to regulate it. Monetary policy is the RBI's job, and taxation belongs to the income tax department.
A mutual fund distributor is aggrieved by a penalty order passed by SEBI. To which body can the distributor appeal?
Securities Appellate Tribunal
National Company Law Tribunal
AMFI's disciplinary committee
The Reserve Bank of India

Appeals against orders of SEBI lie with the Securities Appellate Tribunal (SAT). NCLT deals with company law matters, AMFI is an industry association and the RBI is the banking regulator; none of them hears appeals against SEBI.
A party wants to challenge a decision of the Securities Appellate Tribunal. The next appeal lies with:
SEBI's whole-time members
The Ministry of Finance
The relevant stock exchange
The Supreme Court of India

Under the SEBI Act, an appeal against an order of the Securities Appellate Tribunal lies with the Supreme Court. SEBI itself cannot review SAT orders, and neither the Ministry of Finance nor stock exchanges have appellate powers here.
Which of the following best describes the Association of Mutual Funds in India (AMFI)?
The statutory regulator of mutual funds under the SEBI Act
An industry body of SEBI-registered AMCs that promotes ethical practices
A government department under the Finance Ministry that approves new mutual fund schemes
A depository that holds mutual fund units in electronic form

AMFI is an association of SEBI-registered asset management companies. It promotes professional and ethical standards, registers distributors through ARN and runs investor awareness programmes. SEBI, not AMFI, is the regulator that approves and regulates schemes.
An investor's complaint against an RTA was closed on SCORES, but she is still not satisfied. Under SEBI's framework, she can next:
File a case directly with the Securities Appellate Tribunal
Ask the stock exchange to cancel the RTA's registration
Complain to the RBI banking ombudsman
Take the dispute to the online dispute resolution platform

SEBI's framework lets investors who are not satisfied with the resolution through the intermediary or SCORES take the dispute to the online dispute resolution (ODR) platform, which uses conciliation and online arbitration. SAT hears appeals against SEBI orders, not such disputes.
Which of these is a power available to SEBI under the SEBI Act?
Granting banking licences to new private banks
Fixing the face value of shares of every company
Conducting inspections and investigations of intermediaries
Deciding the income tax rate on dividends

SEBI can call for information, inspect books, investigate intermediaries such as RTAs and AMCs, and impose penalties. Banking licences are issued by the RBI, face value is decided by companies within the law, and tax rates are set by Parliament.
SEBI regulations aimed at preventing persons from dealing in securities on the basis of unpublished price-sensitive information relate to:
Insider trading
Takeovers
Delisting
Buyback of securities

The SEBI (Prohibition of Insider Trading) Regulations prohibit trading while in possession of unpublished price-sensitive information. Takeover, delisting and buyback regulations deal with acquisitions, removing shares from exchanges and companies purchasing their own shares.

Basics of Registrars and Transfer Agents.overview: This chapter explains who registrars and transfer agents are and what they do for mutual funds. An RTA is appointed by the AMC to handle investor-facing operations: processing transactions, maintaining the unitholder register, computing distributor commissions, reconciling collections, sending statements and handling service requests. Learners should understand the folio structure, the meaning of an official point of acceptance and time-stamping, and the fact that the AMC remains responsible to investors for outsourced work. Know the large RTAs in the Indian mutual fund industry and shared platforms such as MF Central, and focus on how RTA functions link to investor service.
questions: MF Central, a common platform where investors can carry out service requests across mutual fund houses, has been developed jointly by:
SEBI and the Reserve Bank of India
NSDL and CDSL
AMFI and the stock exchanges
The two large mutual fund RTAs, CAMS and KFintech

MF Central was developed by the RTAs CAMS and KFin Technologies, under SEBI's direction, as a single platform for investors to view holdings and submit financial and non-financial transactions across AMCs they service.
An AMC outsources its investor servicing to an RTA. If an investor faces deficient service, who remains ultimately responsible to the investor?
The AMC
The RTA alone
The investor's distributor
AMFI

An AMC can outsource operations to an RTA, but it cannot outsource its responsibility. The AMC remains accountable to investors for the RTA's work and must monitor service standards. The RTA is answerable to the AMC under their agreement.
Applications received at an official point of acceptance are time-stamped mainly to:
Calculate the trail commission payable to the distributor each month
Determine the applicable NAV for the transaction
Fix the date for the next IDCW payout
Decide the investor's risk profile

Time-stamping records the exact date and time an application is received. Since the applicable NAV depends on cut-off times, this record decides which day's NAV applies. It also provides an audit trail that protects investors from backdating.
Which of these tasks is typically carried out by a mutual fund RTA on behalf of the AMC?
Selecting securities for the scheme's portfolio
Approving the scheme information document
Calculating commission payable to distributors
Fixing the scheme's benchmark index

RTAs compute the upfront and trail commission due to distributors based on transaction and holding data, which the AMC then pays. Portfolio selection is done by the fund manager, and approval of scheme documents involves the AMC, trustees and SEBI.
A scheme declares an IDCW with a fixed record date. Which RTA function decides who is entitled to it?
Valuing the scheme's securities at market prices
Placing orders with brokers for the scheme
Preparing the scheme's annual financial statements
Maintaining the register of unitholders as on the record date

IDCW is paid to unitholders whose names appear in the register on the record date. The RTA maintains this register, so it identifies eligible investors and their holdings. Valuation, trading and annual accounts are AMC or fund accounting functions.
An investor already has a folio with an AMC and wants to invest in another scheme of the same AMC. Which statement is correct?
A new folio must be opened with fresh KYC
The new investment can be made under the same folio
The investor must close the existing folio first
Folios are linked to schemes, so one per scheme is required

A folio is an investor account with an AMC and can hold units of several schemes of that AMC. Investing under the existing folio keeps holdings consolidated and avoids repeating documentation, though a new folio is also allowed if the investor wishes.
Which RTA activity matches money received in the scheme's collection bank account with the transactions submitted by investors?
Portfolio rebalancing
NAV computation
Funds reconciliation
Risk-o-meter updation

Funds reconciliation compares credits in the collection account with application data so that units are allotted only against realised money. Mismatches are investigated. Rebalancing, NAV computation and risk labelling are not reconciliation activities.
After an RTA processes a purchase, the investor receives an SMS and email with details of units allotted. This communication is sent:
By the RTA on behalf of the AMC
By SEBI after approving the allotment
By the stock exchange where units trade
By the investor's bank after the debit

RTAs send transaction confirmations and account statements to investors on behalf of the AMC, using the contact details in the folio. SEBI does not approve individual allotments, and the bank only confirms the debit of money.

Registrar and Transfer Agents Regulation.overview: This chapter covers the regulatory framework for RTAs. Registrars to an issue and share transfer agents must be registered with SEBI and follow the regulations that govern them along with the common provisions for intermediaries. Learners should understand the categories of registration, eligibility and fit-and-proper criteria, the code of conduct, the duties to maintain records and redress grievances, the role of the compliance officer, and the consequences of default such as suspension or cancellation. Also revise obligations under anti-money laundering law and the enhanced requirements placed on large, systemically important RTAs. Concepts matter more than numerical limits here.
questions: Under the RTA regulations, a Category II registrant may act as:
Both a registrar to an issue and a share transfer agent, for listed and unlisted companies
A registrar only for government securities
A share transfer agent only for its group companies
Either a registrar to an issue or a share transfer agent, but not both

Category I permits an entity to act as both registrar to an issue and share transfer agent. Category II permits it to act in only one of the two capacities. There is no category limited to government securities or group companies.
Before an entity can act as a registrar or share transfer agent for securities, it must:
Obtain a licence from the RBI
Become a member of a stock exchange
Obtain a certificate of registration from SEBI
Register as a distributor with AMFI

Acting as a registrar to an issue or share transfer agent requires a certificate of registration from SEBI under the relevant regulations. RBI licences, exchange membership and AMFI registration apply to other activities.
Common requirements for registration and the 'fit and proper person' criteria applicable to RTAs are laid down in:
SEBI (Intermediaries) Regulations, 2008
SEBI (Mutual Funds) Regulations, 1996
SEBI (Depositories and Participants) Regulations, 2018
Indian Trusts Act, 1882

The SEBI (Intermediaries) Regulations, 2008 contain common provisions for all intermediaries, including RTAs, such as the fit and proper criteria and the procedure for action in case of default. The other laws govern mutual funds, depositories and trusts.
An RTA appoints a compliance officer. This officer is mainly responsible for:
Managing the investment portfolio of the mutual fund schemes serviced by the RTA
Monitoring compliance with SEBI rules and redressal of investor grievances
Approving the RTA's annual budget and salaries
Marketing the RTA's services to new AMC clients

The compliance officer monitors the RTA's compliance with the SEBI Act, regulations and circulars, reports any non-compliance and oversees the redressal of investor grievances. Portfolio management belongs to the AMC, and budgets and marketing are business functions.
As an intermediary, an RTA has obligations under the Prevention of Money Laundering Act. Which of these is one of them?
Fixing the minimum investment amount for schemes
Reporting suspicious transactions to FIU-IND
Approving the KYC of foreign portfolio investors for SEBI
Collecting income tax on capital gains from investors

Under the PMLA and SEBI's AML guidelines, intermediaries including RTAs must monitor transactions, maintain records and report suspicious transactions to the Financial Intelligence Unit-India. They do not set scheme minimums or collect capital gains tax.
An RTA repeatedly fails to resolve investor complaints and ignores SEBI's directions. What action can SEBI take under the regulations?
Transfer the RTA's shares to AMFI
Order the AMCs to merge with the RTA
Only issue an advisory without any penalty
Suspend or cancel the RTA's registration after due process

SEBI can take action against an RTA that violates regulations, including monetary penalties, suspension or cancellation of its certificate of registration, after following the procedure in the Intermediaries Regulations. It cannot transfer ownership to AMFI.
Which of the following is expected of an RTA under its code of conduct?
Exercising due diligence and not misrepresenting facts to investors or clients
Giving preference to large investors when processing requests
Recommending schemes of AMCs that pay the RTA higher fees
Sharing investor data with group companies so that they can cross-sell other products

The code of conduct requires an RTA to act with integrity, due diligence and fairness, treat all investors equally and keep information confidential. Favouring large investors, product pushing or sharing data for marketing would breach the code.
SEBI has designated certain RTAs as Qualified RTAs (QRTAs). Such RTAs are identified on the basis of:
Being owned by a public sector bank
Being listed on a stock exchange for three years
The large number of folios they service, making them systemically important
Having only one AMC as a client

QRTAs are RTAs that service a very large number of folios and are therefore systemically important. SEBI places enhanced obligations on them, covering governance, risk management, systems audit and business continuity. Ownership or listing is not the criterion.

Basics of Mutual Funds.overview: This chapter introduces the mutual fund as a pooled investment vehicle. Learners should understand how investors' money is pooled and managed by professionals, how net asset value is computed, and how NAV changes with market prices, expenses and income distributions. Revise the difference between open-ended, close-ended and interval schemes, direct and regular plans, and the main benefits and limitations of mutual funds such as diversification, liquidity, transparency, costs and absence of guaranteed returns. Practise NAV and simple return calculations, and be clear about why an IDCW payout reduces the NAV.
questions: On a given day a debt fund reports net assets of ₹245 crore, calculated after deducting ₹5 crore of payables from its ₹250 crore holdings. If 10 crore units are in issue, the NAV works out to:

NAV per unit equals net assets divided by units outstanding. Net assets are ₹250 crore minus ₹5 crore, which is ₹245 crore, and ₹245 crore ÷ 10 crore units gives ₹24.50. Ignoring or adding the liabilities gives the wrong values.
An investor bought units at an NAV of ₹10 and the NAV is now ₹12.50. Ignoring loads and IDCW, what is her absolute return?

Absolute return is (current NAV minus purchase NAV) divided by purchase NAV. Here (12.50 − 10) ÷ 10 = 0.25, or 25%. The 20% figure wrongly divides the gain by the current NAV instead of the purchase NAV.
In an open-ended scheme, investors can:
Buy units only during the new fund offer
Redeem units only on the scheme's maturity date
Buy and redeem units from the fund on an ongoing basis
Trade units only with other investors on stock exchanges during market hours

Open-ended schemes issue and redeem units on a continuous basis at NAV-based prices, so there is no fixed maturity. Close-ended schemes accept money only during the NFO and are listed for liquidity until maturity.
An interval scheme is one that:
Is open for purchase and redemption only during specified intervals
Pays IDCW at fixed intervals of one month
Invests only in securities with fixed maturity intervals
Switches automatically between equity and debt

An interval scheme combines features of open and close-ended schemes. It is open for purchases and redemptions only during specified transaction periods and is otherwise closed. It must also be listed on an exchange.
A scheme's NAV is ₹20 just before it pays an IDCW of ₹1 per unit. Assuming no other change, the NAV immediately after the payout will be about:

An IDCW is paid out of the scheme's assets, so the NAV falls by the amount distributed. ₹20 minus ₹1 leaves about ₹19. The investor's total wealth is unchanged before tax, as the payout simply moves value from the NAV to her bank account.
Two plans of the same scheme hold the same portfolio. Why does the direct plan usually have a higher NAV than the regular plan over time?
It invests in higher-return securities that the regular plan is not permitted to hold
It has a lower expense ratio as no distributor commission is paid
It is exempt from tax on capital gains and dividends
It is managed by a more experienced fund manager

Direct and regular plans share one portfolio and one fund manager. The direct plan carries no distribution commission, so its expense ratio is lower and less is deducted from its NAV, which therefore grows faster over time.
Which of the following is a limitation of investing through mutual funds?
Investors cannot redeem units from open-ended schemes
Investors cannot see the scheme's portfolio holdings
Investors cannot choose the individual securities held in the portfolio
Investors cannot invest small amounts through SIPs

In a mutual fund, the fund manager decides the portfolio within the scheme's objective, so investors cannot customise holdings. Open-ended schemes are liquid, portfolios are disclosed regularly, and SIPs allow small investments.
The total expense ratio (TER) of a scheme refers to:
The exit load as a percentage of redemption value
The stamp duty as a percentage of purchase amount
The fund manager's salary expressed as a share of the AMC's annual profit after tax
Annual scheme expenses as a percentage of its average net assets

TER expresses the scheme's recurring expenses, such as management fees and distribution costs, as an annual percentage of average net assets. It is accrued daily in the NAV. Exit load and stamp duty are transaction charges, not part of TER.

Mutual Fund Structure and Constituents.overview: This chapter explains the legal structure of a mutual fund in India and the roles of its constituents. A mutual fund is set up as a trust by a sponsor, with trustees overseeing it and an asset management company managing the schemes. Learners should know the documents linking them, such as the trust deed and the investment management agreement, key SEBI requirements on AMC net worth and independent directors and trustees, and the roles of service providers such as custodians, RTAs, auditors and distributors. Revise who is responsible for what, and newer measures aligning AMC employees' interests with unitholders.
questions: The structure of a mutual fund in India is commonly described as three-tier. The three tiers are:
Sponsor, trustees and asset management company
SEBI, AMFI and the asset management company
Custodian, RTA and distributor
Sponsor, stock exchange and depository

The sponsor establishes the mutual fund trust, the trustees hold its property for the benefit of unitholders and supervise, and the AMC manages the schemes. SEBI and AMFI are regulator and industry body, and custodians and RTAs are service providers.
The trust deed of a mutual fund is executed:
By the AMC in favour of SEBI
By the custodian in favour of the AMC
By unitholders in favour of the sponsor
By the sponsor in favour of the trustees

The sponsor creates the mutual fund trust by executing a trust deed in favour of the trustees, who then hold the trust property for unitholders. The trust deed is registered and must be approved under SEBI's regulations.
The agreement under which the trustees appoint the AMC to manage the mutual fund's schemes is called the:
Custodial services agreement
Investment management agreement
Memorandum of association
Distribution agreement

Trustees enter into an investment management agreement with the AMC, which sets out the AMC's duties in managing the schemes. Custodial and distribution agreements cover other service providers, and the memorandum relates to company incorporation.
Under SEBI's regulations, what is the minimum net worth an AMC must maintain?
₹10 crore
₹25 crore
₹50 crore
₹100 crore

SEBI requires an AMC to have and maintain a net worth of at least ₹50 crore. This was raised from the earlier ₹10 crore requirement to ensure that AMCs have adequate financial strength to run their business.
What proportion of the directors on an AMC's board must be independent, as per SEBI's requirements?
At least one-third
At least two-thirds
At least 25%
At least 50%

SEBI requires that at least half of the AMC's board consist of independent directors, that is, persons not associated with the sponsor. For the board of the trustee company, the requirement is stricter at two-thirds independent trustees.
Which of these is a function of the AMC rather than the trustees?
Making day-to-day investment decisions for the schemes
Ensuring that the AMC acts in unitholders' interests
Reviewing whether the AMC complies with SEBI regulations and the trust deed
Approving the investment management agreement

The AMC manages money, so investment decisions for the schemes are its job. The trustees play a supervisory role: they appoint the AMC, approve key agreements and check that the AMC complies with regulations and protects unitholders.
SEBI requires a portion of the salary of key employees of an AMC to be paid in units of the schemes they manage or oversee. The main aim is to:
Increase the assets under management of newly launched schemes of the AMC
Align the interests of these employees with those of unitholders
Reduce the tax liability of the AMC's employees
Replace the sponsor's contribution to the AMC

Under the 'skin in the game' rules, a part of the compensation of designated employees is paid in scheme units with a lock-in. They gain or lose along with investors, encouraging responsible decisions. It is not aimed at raising AUM or saving tax.
A mutual fund wants an independent entity to verify that its scheme accounts are fairly stated. It must appoint:
The same auditor as the sponsor company
The custodian to certify the accounts
An auditor independent of the auditor of the AMC
The RTA's internal audit team

Scheme accounts must be audited by an independent auditor, who cannot be the auditor of the AMC. This separation strengthens objectivity. Custodians and RTAs are service providers and cannot act as statutory auditors of the schemes.

Mutual Fund Products.overview: This chapter describes the categories of mutual fund schemes defined by SEBI's scheme categorisation framework. Learners should know the main equity categories such as large cap, mid cap, small cap, multi cap, flexi cap, focused and ELSS, the debt categories defined by maturity or credit quality such as overnight, liquid and gilt funds, and hybrid, solution-oriented and other schemes such as index funds, ETFs and funds of funds. Focus on the defining feature of each category, minimum allocations, lock-ins and the definition of large, mid and small cap companies. Application questions usually ask which category fits an investor's need.
questions: According to SEBI's definition, large cap companies are:
The 1st to 50th companies by full market capitalisation
Companies with a market cap above ₹10,000 crore
The 1st to 250th companies by full market capitalisation
The 1st to 100th companies by full market capitalisation

SEBI defines large cap companies as the top 100 companies by full market capitalisation, mid caps as the 101st to 250th, and small caps as the 251st onwards. AMFI publishes the list periodically so that schemes follow a uniform definition.
A multi cap fund must invest a minimum of 25% of its total assets in each of:
Large cap, mid cap and small cap stocks
Equity, debt and gold
Indian equity, foreign equity and debt
Large cap and mid cap stocks only

SEBI's rules require multi cap funds to invest at least 75% in equity, with at least 25% each in large, mid and small cap stocks. This differs from flexi cap funds, which can allocate freely across market capitalisations.
A liquid fund can invest in debt and money market securities with a maturity of up to:
1 day
1 year
91 days
3 years

Liquid funds invest in debt and money market instruments maturing within 91 days. Overnight funds are limited to one-day maturity, and ultra short or low duration funds hold longer maturities. This short maturity keeps interest rate risk low.
An investor wants to benefit from price differences between the cash and futures markets with low risk. Which category suits this strategy?
Small cap fund
Arbitrage fund
Credit risk fund
Sectoral fund

Arbitrage funds buy a stock in the cash market and sell its futures at a higher price, earning the spread with limited market risk. Small cap, credit risk and sectoral funds take higher equity or credit risk and do not follow this strategy.
A focused fund is an equity scheme that invests in:
Only one sector of the economy
Only stocks outside India
Stocks that pay high dividends
A maximum of 30 stocks

SEBI defines a focused fund as one that holds a concentrated portfolio of at most 30 stocks. A single-sector scheme is a sectoral fund, overseas exposure belongs to international funds, and high-dividend stocks define dividend yield funds.
A gilt fund must invest at least 80% of its total assets in:
AAA-rated corporate bonds
Government securities across maturities
Bank certificates of deposit
Treasury bills only

Gilt funds invest a minimum of 80% in government securities across maturities. They have negligible credit risk but can face significant interest rate risk. Corporate bonds and CDs belong to other debt categories.
A parent invests in a children's fund, which is a solution-oriented scheme. What lock-in applies to such investments?
3 years from the date of each investment
Till the child attains majority, with no other minimum lock-in period applying
5 years or till the child attains majority, whichever is earlier
No lock-in, as it is an open-ended scheme

SEBI requires children's funds to have a lock-in of at least five years or until the child attains majority, whichever is earlier. Retirement funds have a similar rule linked to retirement age. A three-year lock-in applies to ELSS.
A scheme that invests mainly in units of other mutual fund schemes is called a:
Fund of funds
Balanced advantage fund
Exchange traded fund
Multi asset allocation fund

A fund of funds invests in the units of other mutual fund schemes, domestic or overseas, rather than directly in securities. Investors bear expenses of both layers. ETFs and balanced advantage or multi asset funds invest directly in securities.

Operational Concepts of Mutual Funds.overview: This chapter covers the operational rules that decide how transactions are priced and processed. Learners should know the cut-off timings for different scheme types, how the applicable NAV is fixed for purchases and redemptions, and the special rules for liquid and overnight funds. Revise loads, including the abolition of entry load and the crediting of exit load to the scheme, stamp duty on purchases, the computation of units allotted, NFO pricing and the daily accrual of expenses in the NAV. Practise unit and amount calculations with stamp duty and exit load, as these are common numerical questions.
questions: For a purchase in an equity scheme, where the funds are available for use before the cut-off, what is the cut-off time to get the same day's NAV?
12:00 noon

For equity and most debt schemes other than liquid and overnight funds, the cut-off is 3:00 p.m. If the application is received and funds are realised before then, the same day's NAV applies. The 1:30 p.m. cut-off applies to liquid and overnight funds.
An investor submits a redemption request for an equity scheme at 2:30 p.m. on a business day. Which NAV applies?
The NAV of the previous business day
The NAV of the next business day
The NAV of the same business day
The average NAV of the week

For redemptions in equity schemes, requests received before the 3:00 p.m. cut-off get the same day's closing NAV. Unlike purchases, redemption does not depend on realisation of funds, so time of receipt alone decides the NAV.
An investor's SIP of ₹20,000 goes into a scheme with an NAV of ₹40. After stamp duty of 0.005%, how many units are allotted?
Stamp duty is 0.005% of ₹20,000, which is ₹1, so ₹19,999 is invested. Dividing by the NAV of ₹40 gives 499.975 units. Ignoring stamp duty would wrongly give 500 units.
The exit load collected by a scheme when investors redeem units is:
Kept by the AMC as its income
Paid to the distributor as commission
Transferred to SEBI's investor protection fund
Credited back to the scheme, net of GST

SEBI requires exit load, net of GST, to be credited to the scheme rather than kept by the AMC. This benefits the remaining investors who bear the cost of redemptions. Distributor commission comes from scheme expenses, not exit load.
Which statement about entry load in Indian mutual funds is correct?
Entry load of up to 2.25% is allowed on equity schemes
SEBI has abolished entry load on all schemes
Entry load is charged only on regular plans
Entry load applies only to SIP instalments

SEBI abolished entry loads in 2009, so no load can be charged at the time of purchase. Distributors are paid commission by the AMC out of scheme expenses in regular plans, and investors in direct plans pay no commission.
A purchase request for a liquid fund, with funds credited in time, is received at 2:00 p.m. on a Wednesday that is a business day. Which NAV applies?
Wednesday's NAV
Thursday's NAV
Tuesday's NAV
Friday's NAV

For liquid funds, applications received after the 1:30 p.m. cut-off get the closing NAV of the day immediately preceding the next business day. As Thursday is the next business day, the NAV of Wednesday, the preceding day, applies.
How are the recurring expenses of a scheme reflected for investors?
They are billed to investors separately every quarter
They are deducted only from redemption proceeds
They are charged once a year on the anniversary of investment
They are accrued daily and deducted while computing the NAV

Recurring expenses within the TER limit are charged to the scheme and accrued every day in the NAV. Investors therefore do not receive separate bills; the published NAV is already net of expenses. Exit load, if any, is deducted on redemption.
During a new fund offer, units of an open-ended scheme are usually allotted at:
The NAV of an existing scheme of the same AMC
A price decided by bidding among investors
The face value of the units, commonly ₹10
A premium of 10% to the face value

In an NFO, units are generally offered at face value, typically ₹10, because the scheme has no portfolio yet. After the scheme reopens for continuous transactions, purchases and redemptions take place at the prevailing NAV.

Investors in Mutual Funds.overview: This chapter covers the types of investors who can invest in mutual funds and the documents and rules that apply to each. Learners should know the eligibility of resident individuals, minors through guardians, HUFs, non-individuals such as companies, trusts and societies, and NRIs and other foreign investors, with the difference between repatriable and non-repatriable investment. Revise modes of holding, KYC through KYC registration agencies, PAN-exempt KYC for small investments, and FATCA/CRS self-certification. Focus on the documents an RTA must check before accepting an application and on what changes when a minor or NRI's status changes.
questions: A Hindu Undivided Family wishes to invest in a mutual fund. The investment is made:
In the name of each coparcener separately
Only through a registered trust of the family
In the name of the eldest son as guardian
In the name of the HUF, through its Karta

An HUF can invest in mutual funds, with the Karta signing and operating the investment on its behalf. KYC is done for the HUF and the Karta. There is no need to form a trust or invest separately for each coparcener.
Who can act as guardian for a minor's mutual fund folio?
Any adult relative nominated by the minor
A natural guardian (parent) or a court-appointed legal guardian
The distributor who sources the investment
Any person who funds the investment

SEBI's norms allow either a natural guardian, that is, a parent, or a court-appointed legal guardian to operate a minor's folio. Proof of the relationship or the court order must be provided. Relatives or distributors cannot act as guardian merely by funding the investment.
An NRI invests in a mutual fund using money from her NRO account. How is this investment treated?
On a fully repatriable basis
As a foreign portfolio investment
On a non-repatriable basis
As a deposit under FEMA
