Money from an NRO account represents income earned in India, so investments from it are generally non-repatriable, with limited repatriation allowed under RBI rules. Investments from NRE or FCNR accounts are repatriable.
A folio is held jointly by two investors with the mode of holding 'joint'. What is required to redeem units?
Signatures of both holders
Signature of the first holder only
Signature of either holder
Signature of the nominee
In 'joint' mode, all holders must sign for transactions such as redemption. In 'anyone or survivor' mode, any one holder can transact. Nominees have no rights while the holders are alive.
A private limited company wants to invest its surplus funds in a liquid fund. Which document is typically required along with KYC?
A no-objection certificate from SEBI
An approval letter from the company's bankers
A board resolution authorising the investment and signatories
A certificate from the registrar of companies for each investment

Non-individual investors such as companies must submit a board resolution authorising the investment and naming authorised signatories, along with entity KYC. No SEBI, bank or ROC approval is needed for each investment.
An investor completed KYC through one AMC. When she invests with a different AMC, what happens?
Her KYC record with the KRA can be used, so full KYC need not be repeated
She must complete fresh in-person verification with the new AMC before her first investment
She must obtain a KYC transfer letter from SEBI
She can invest only in the same category of schemes

KYC details are uploaded to a KYC registration agency, and other SEBI-registered intermediaries can access and rely on that record. This avoids repeating KYC. Her KYC should be in a validated status for smooth processing.
FATCA and CRS self-certification is collected from mutual fund investors mainly to:
Verify their income for suitability of schemes
Check whether they hold a demat account
Calculate stamp duty on their purchases
Identify their tax residency for reporting accounts of foreign tax residents

Under FATCA and the Common Reporting Standard, financial institutions in India must identify accounts of foreign tax residents and report them to tax authorities. Investors therefore declare their country of tax residence, citizenship and related details.
Small investors who do not have a PAN, such as for micro SIPs within a specified annual limit, can invest after completing:
Exemption granted by SEBI on a case-by-case basis
PAN-exempt KYC, with an alternate identity document
A declaration from the distributor about their income
No KYC at all, as the amounts are small

Investments within the specified limit, such as micro SIPs, are exempt from the PAN requirement but not from KYC. Investors complete PAN-exempt KYC using another officially valid identity document, and receive a reference number.

Banking Operations in Mutual Funds.overview: This chapter covers the banking side of mutual fund transactions. Learners should understand bank mandates and why redemption and IDCW proceeds are paid only to registered bank accounts, registration of multiple bank accounts, bank account validation, and electronic payment modes such as NEFT, RTGS, IMPS, UPI and NACH. Revise the rules on third-party payments and their permitted exceptions, SEBI's ban on pooling of investor funds by intermediaries, and how SIP mandates are registered and cancelled. Focus on the RTA's controls against fraud and the actions to be taken when payments fail.
questions: Redemption proceeds of a mutual fund folio are paid to:
Any bank account mentioned in the redemption form
The distributor's account for onward transfer
The bank account registered in the folio
The account of the nominee by default

To prevent fraud, redemption and IDCW proceeds are paid only to a bank account registered in the folio. A new account must first be registered through a proper change of bank mandate process. Distributors and nominees cannot receive proceeds.
An individual investor may register more than one bank account in a folio. Up to how many accounts are allowed?

Individuals and HUFs can register up to five bank accounts in a folio, while non-individual investors can register up to ten. One account is marked as default for payouts, and the others can be used for payments or chosen for redemption.
Which of these is a permitted exception to the ban on third-party payments for mutual fund purchases?
A close friend paying for an investor's lump sum purchase through his own cheque
An employer paying for an employee's SIP through payroll deductions
A distributor paying on behalf of a client
A neighbour paying through an online transfer

Third-party payments are generally not accepted. Exceptions include payment by an employer for employees through payroll deduction, by a parent or grandparent for a minor within a limit, and by a custodian for an FPI, with required declarations.
Before registering a new bank account, many RTAs credit a small amount to the account to check the name and account number. This is known as:
Cheque truncation
Reverse mortgage
Standing instruction
Penny drop validation

In penny drop validation, a small amount such as ₹1 is credited to the account, and the bank's response confirms that the account is active and gives the holder's name. This is matched with the investor's name before registration.
Under SEBI's rules for mutual fund transactions, investment platforms and distributors may NOT:
Help investors place mutual fund orders through stock exchange platforms like BSE StAR MF
Collect transaction orders from investors electronically
Earn commission on investments in regular plans
Pool investors' money in their own accounts before paying the AMC

SEBI has prohibited pooling of investor funds by intermediaries in mutual fund transactions. Money must flow directly from the investor's bank account to the mutual fund's account, and redemptions directly back, reducing the risk of misuse.
An investor wants SIP instalments to be debited automatically from her bank account each month. What should be registered?
A demand draft for each instalment
A NACH mandate with her bank
A standing order with the RTA's bank
A power of attorney in favour of the AMC

A NACH mandate authorises the mutual fund to debit the investor's bank account for SIP instalments up to the approved amount. It is registered with the investor's bank. Demand drafts or powers of attorney are not needed for SIPs.
Large redemption payouts to investors are usually credited directly through:
Cash payments at the RTA's service centre
Demand drafts sent by ordinary post
Electronic modes such as NEFT, RTGS or IMPS
Postal money orders to the registered address

Mutual funds credit redemption and IDCW proceeds electronically to the registered bank account through NEFT, RTGS or IMPS, which is faster and safer. Cheques or drafts are used only where electronic credit is not possible, and cash is never paid.
An investor wants to stop her SIP permanently and also cancel the auto-debit. What should she do?
Submit an SIP cancellation request and cancel the NACH mandate
Keep the account balance low so that debits fail
Redeem all units, as this cancels the SIP automatically
Write to SEBI to stop the debits

SIPs should be cancelled through a formal request to the AMC or RTA, along with cancellation of the mandate. Letting debits fail is not correct practice, as banks may charge penalties. Redeeming units does not necessarily stop future SIP instalments.

Financial Transactions.overview: This chapter covers the financial transactions an RTA processes, such as purchases, redemptions, switches, systematic plans and IDCW payouts or reinvestment. Learners should be able to compute units allotted, redemption amounts after exit load, and units allotted on IDCW reinvestment. Revise the first-in-first-out principle for loads and holding periods, the treatment of switches, payment timelines and the interest payable for delays, and SIP modifications such as pausing or top-ups. Questions are often numerical or scenario-based, so practise working through each step and check how loads and timelines affect the final amount.
questions: An investor redeems 300 units at an NAV of ₹45. A 1% exit load applies. What amount will she receive, ignoring taxes?
Redemption value is 300 × ₹45 = ₹13,500. A 1% exit load is ₹135, so the investor receives ₹13,365. Adding the load instead of deducting it, or ignoring it altogether, gives the incorrect values.
An investor wants to redeem ₹10,000 from a scheme whose NAV is ₹25, with no exit load. How many units will be redeemed?

For an amount-based redemption, units redeemed equal the amount divided by NAV. ₹10,000 ÷ ₹25 = 400 units. The RTA reduces the folio balance by 400 units and pays ₹10,000 to the registered bank account.
An investor holds 1,000 units under the IDCW reinvestment option. The scheme declares ₹2 per unit and the ex-IDCW NAV is ₹20. Ignoring tax deduction, how many additional units will be allotted?

IDCW payable is 1,000 × ₹2 = ₹2,000. Under the reinvestment option this is used to buy units at the ex-IDCW NAV of ₹20, giving ₹2,000 ÷ ₹20 = 100 units. In practice, TDS may reduce the amount reinvested.
An investor bought units in a scheme on several dates and now redeems part of her holding. For computing exit load, units are generally treated as redeemed:
On a last-in-first-out basis
In the order chosen by the distributor
On a first-in-first-out basis
At the average purchase date of all units

Mutual funds apply the first-in-first-out (FIFO) method, so the oldest units are redeemed first. Exit load applies only to those redeemed units that fall within the load period. The same principle is used for capital gains holding periods.
An investor switches units from an equity scheme into a debt scheme of the same AMC within the exit load period of the equity scheme. Which statement is correct?
Exit load of the equity scheme may apply on the switch-out
No load applies because the AMC is the same
Load is charged on the switch-in to the debt scheme instead of on the switch-out
The switch is not allowed during the load period

A switch is a redemption from one scheme and a purchase in another. So the exit load of the source scheme can apply to units switched out within its load period, unless the scheme documents waive it. There is no entry load on the switch-in.
If an AMC fails to transfer redemption proceeds within the time allowed by SEBI, it must pay the investor interest at the rate of:
6% per annum for the delay
15% per annum for the delay
The bank's savings account rate
No interest, only an apology letter

SEBI regulations require the AMC to pay interest at 15% per annum for the period of delay beyond the stipulated time for transfer of redemption or repurchase proceeds. This interest is borne by the AMC, not the scheme.
An investor facing a temporary cash crunch wants to skip a few SIP instalments without cancelling the SIP. Which facility can she use, where the AMC offers it?
Systematic transfer plan
Switch to IDCW option
SIP pause
Change of nominee

Many AMCs offer an SIP pause facility, allowing investors to suspend instalments for a specified number of months, after which the SIP resumes automatically. STP and IDCW options serve different purposes, and nomination has no effect on SIP debits.
An investor sets up an SIP with a 'top-up' feature. This means:
Additional units are allotted free when NAV falls
The SIP continues even after the bank mandate expires
Units are bought only when the market is rising
The SIP amount increases periodically by a specified amount or percentage

An SIP top-up, also called step-up, increases the instalment amount at chosen intervals, usually yearly, by a fixed amount or percentage. It helps investments keep pace with rising income. It does not give free units or depend on market direction.

Non-Financial Transactions.overview: Non-financial transactions change folio details without moving money, and they are a large part of an RTA's workload. This chapter covers nomination, transmission, changes in name, address, contact details and bank mandate, minor to major conversion, consolidation of folios, and marking of lien or pledge on units. Learners should know the documents and checks required for each request, including how RTAs guard against fraud in high-risk changes. Revise the rules on who can nominate, how transmission works with and without a nominee or surviving joint holder, and the role of KYC in updating investor details.
questions: Which of the following investors cannot make a nomination in a mutual fund folio?
A resident individual holding singly
A joint holder in an individual folio
A private limited company
A parent investing in their own name

Nomination is available only to individuals holding units on their own behalf, singly or jointly. Non-individuals such as companies, trusts, societies and the Karta of an HUF cannot nominate, as the entity's holding passes as per its own legal arrangements.
A folio is held jointly by two persons. One of them dies. The units will normally be:
Transferred to the nominee of the deceased
Transmitted to the surviving joint holder
Redeemed and paid to the legal heirs
Frozen until a court order is received

In a joint folio, on the death of one holder, the units go to the surviving holder or holders, who submit the death certificate and updated KYC. Nominees come into the picture only when all holders have died.
A sole unitholder has died without registering a nominee. Who can claim the units?
The distributor who sold the scheme
The AMC, which redeems and keeps the money
Anyone who holds the original account statement and the deceased's PAN card copy
The legal heirs, after submitting the required succession documents

Without a nominee or joint holder, units are transmitted to the legal heirs. The RTA asks for documents such as the death certificate, proof of legal heirship and indemnity, or a succession certificate or probate where the value is high.
An investor takes a loan against her mutual fund units. What does the RTA record in her folio?
A lien or pledge in favour of the lender
A transfer of the units to the lender's folio
A redemption of the units in favour of the lender
A change of the investor's name to the lender's name

When units are pledged, the RTA marks a lien in favour of the lender. The investor remains the owner, but cannot redeem or switch the pledged units until the lender releases the lien. If she defaults, the lender may invoke the pledge.
An investor has three different folios with the same AMC with identical holders and details. She wants a single folio. This request is called:
Transmission of folio units
Consolidation of folios
Switch of units
Change of status

Consolidation merges multiple folios with the same holders in the same order and the same mode of holding into one folio, making records easier to manage. Transmission relates to death of a holder, and switches move money between schemes.
A woman investor changes her surname after marriage and wants it updated in her folio. What is normally required?
A request with proof of name change, such as a marriage certificate, and updated KYC
Only a phone call to the RTA's call centre
A new PAN card in the name of her spouse
Redemption of units and fresh purchase in the new name

Change of name requires a written request with supporting proof such as a marriage certificate or gazette notification, and the KYC record must also be updated. A phone call is not enough, and there is no need to redeem and reinvest.
Why do RTAs verify a new email address or mobile number before updating it in a folio?
Because SEBI charges a fee for each update
Because distributors earn an extra commission whenever an investor's contact details change
Because transaction alerts go there, and fraudulent changes could hide misuse
Because the NAV depends on the investor's location

Contact details receive OTPs, alerts and statements. If a fraudster changes them, the real investor may not learn of unauthorised transactions. Validation ensures the details belong to the investor. Fees, commissions and NAV are unrelated.
After the death of a sole unitholder, the AMC transmits the units to the registered nominee. What is the effect for the AMC?
It must hold the units until all legal heirs give consent
It must pay the units' value to the legal heirs as well
It must redeem the units and deposit the money in court until the heirs settle their claims
It is discharged of its liability for those units towards the legal heirs

Transmission to a valid registered nominee gives the AMC a valid discharge. Any claim that the legal heirs may have is a matter between them and the nominee under succession law, and does not require the AMC to pay twice or hold the units.

Introduction to the Financial System.overview: This chapter introduces the building blocks of a financial system: financial institutions, markets, instruments and services, and how they move savings from households to businesses and government. Learners should be clear on the difference between primary and secondary markets, money and capital markets, direct and intermediated finance, and the roles played by banks, NBFCs, mutual funds, insurers and market intermediaries. When revising, focus on classifying instruments by maturity and market, understanding why intermediaries reduce transaction costs and information gaps, and how a well-functioning system supports price discovery, liquidity and economic growth.
questions: A company raises fresh capital by issuing shares to investors for the first time. In which segment does this transaction take place?
Primary market
Money market
Secondary market
Over-the-counter derivatives market

Fresh issue of securities by an issuer, where money flows to the company, happens in the primary market. In the secondary market, existing securities change hands between investors and the issuer receives nothing.
Which of the following is the best example of a capital market instrument?
A ten-year corporate bond
A three-month commercial paper
An overnight call money loan
A 91-day treasury bill
Capital market instruments have maturities above one year and fund long-term needs. Treasury bills, commercial paper and call money are short-term money market instruments.
The main benefit of secondary market trading for an investor who bought shares in an IPO is that it:
Allows the investor to return the shares to the issuer for a refund
Guarantees that the shares will always trade above the issue price once they are listed
Converts the equity shares into fixed-income instruments over time
Provides liquidity, allowing the investor to exit by selling to another investor
The secondary market gives investors an exit route and continuous price discovery. It does not guarantee returns, and shares are not normally returned to the issuer for a refund.
When a household deposits money in a bank and the bank lends it to a business, the process is called:
Securitisation
Financial intermediation
Disintermediation
Dematerialisation

The bank stands between savers and borrowers, pooling deposits and lending them on, which is financial intermediation. Disintermediation is the opposite, where borrowers raise funds directly from investors.
A large company stops borrowing from banks and instead raises funds by issuing commercial paper directly to investors. This trend is known as:
Monetisation of debt
Financial repression
Credit rationing
Disintermediation
Disintermediation means bypassing intermediaries such as banks and tapping savers directly through market instruments like commercial paper or bonds. It reduces the role of banks as intermediaries.
Which of the following is a function of a financial system rather than of a single intermediary?
Issuing a contract note to one trading client
Collecting the premium on one insurance policy
Price discovery through the interaction of many buyers and sellers
Maintaining a particular client's demat account
Price discovery emerges from the collective interaction of market participants. The other options are specific services provided by individual intermediaries.
Which pair correctly matches the market with the typical maturity of its instruments?
Money market - more than five years; capital market - up to one year
Money market - exactly one year; capital market - exactly ten years
Money market - up to one year; capital market - more than one year
Money market and capital market - no difference in maturity
The money market deals in short-term funds with maturity up to one year, while the capital market deals in long-term instruments such as equity and bonds.
Why are market intermediaries such as brokers, depositories and registrars regulated more strictly than ordinary businesses?
They are exempt from company law and need a separate legal framework
They are not allowed to make profits from their services
They are owned by the government and must therefore follow all public sector rules on pay and hiring
They hold client money or securities and their failure can harm investors and market integrity
Intermediaries handle investor assets and information, so lapses can cause wide losses and erode trust. That is why registration, capital, conduct and compliance requirements apply to them.

Regulatory Framework – General View.overview: This chapter maps out who regulates what in Indian finance. It covers SEBI for the securities market, RBI for banks, NBFCs, money, foreign exchange and government securities markets, IRDAI for insurance, PFRDA for pensions, IFSCA for GIFT IFSC, and the Ministry of Finance and Ministry of Corporate Affairs. It also explains co-ordination bodies such as the Financial Stability and Development Council and the key laws behind each regulator. While revising, learn to match an activity to its regulator and statute, and note areas of shared jurisdiction, such as listed company matters under the Companies Act.
questions: A company wants to set up a finance business in GIFT City's International Financial Services Centre. Which regulator will primarily supervise it?
Securities and Exchange Board of India
International Financial Services Centres Authority (IFSCA)
Pension Fund Regulatory and Development Authority
Insurance Regulatory and Development Authority of India
IFSCA is the unified regulator for financial products, services and institutions in an IFSC such as GIFT City. It took over the powers that SEBI, RBI, IRDAI and PFRDA would otherwise exercise there.
Which regulator issues directions on foreign exchange transactions under FEMA, 1999?
Competition Commission of India
Reserve Bank of India
SEBI
Ministry of Corporate Affairs
FEMA is administered mainly by the RBI, which frames regulations and issues directions on foreign exchange transactions, in consultation with the Central Government.
The Financial Stability and Development Council (FSDC) is chaired by the:
Prime Minister of India
Chairman of SEBI
Governor of the Reserve Bank of India
Union Finance Minister
The FSDC is an apex co-ordination body for financial sector regulators. It is chaired by the Union Finance Minister and includes heads of RBI, SEBI, IRDAI, PFRDA and IFSCA.
Which regulator supervises the government securities market and the call money market?
Reserve Bank of India
SEBI
Pension Fund Regulatory and Development Authority
Ministry of Corporate Affairs
The RBI regulates the money market, the government securities market and the forex market. SEBI regulates trading in listed securities on stock exchanges.
For listed companies, provisions of the Companies Act, 2013 relating to issue and transfer of securities and non-payment of dividend are administered by:
SEBI
The Reserve Bank of India
The Insurance Regulatory and Development Authority of India
The Registrar of Companies alone
Section 24 of the Companies Act, 2013 gives SEBI power to administer provisions on issue and transfer of securities and non-payment of dividend for listed companies and those intending to list.
An NBFC that is also registered as a stock broker would be supervised by:
RBI alone, since it is primarily a finance company
The Ministry of Corporate Affairs, since it supervises all companies registered in India
SEBI alone, since securities activities override other licences
RBI for its NBFC activities and SEBI for its stock broking activities
India follows activity-based regulation, so an entity with multiple activities answers to each relevant regulator for that activity. Each regulator inspects the activity under its law.
Insurance companies and insurance intermediaries in India are regulated by:
IFSCA
PFRDA
IRDAI
SEBI
The Insurance Regulatory and Development Authority of India, set up under the IRDA Act, 1999, regulates insurers, insurance brokers, agents and other insurance intermediaries.
Which body under the Ministry of Finance is responsible for capital market policy matters and legislation such as the SEBI Act and the SCRA?
Department of Economic Affairs
Department of Revenue
Department of Expenditure
Department of Financial Services
The Department of Economic Affairs, through its capital markets division, handles policy and legislation relating to the securities market, while SEBI is the market regulator.

Introduction to Compliance.overview: This chapter explains what compliance means for a SEBI-registered intermediary and why it matters. It covers compliance risk, the role of the board and senior management, the position and duties of the compliance officer, compliance policies and manuals, monitoring and testing, regulatory reporting and record keeping. It also contrasts compliance with internal audit and risk management, and discusses building a compliance culture. Focus on the independence and responsibilities of the compliance officer, the consequences of non-compliance such as penalties and reputational loss, and practical tools like checklists, maker-checker controls and escalation of breaches.
questions: Compliance risk for an intermediary is best described as the risk of:
Legal or regulatory sanctions, financial loss or reputational damage from failing to follow laws, rules and codes
A breakdown of computer systems at the stock exchange
Losing money because market prices move against the firm's own positions
A counterparty failing to pay what it owes on settlement day
Compliance risk arises from not complying with laws, regulations, codes of conduct and internal standards. Market, credit and operational risk are separate categories.
Who carries ultimate responsibility for an intermediary's compliance with regulations?
The statutory auditor
The compliance officer alone
The stock exchange or depository where it is a member
The board of directors and senior management
The compliance officer advises, monitors and reports, but the board and senior management are ultimately accountable for ensuring the firm complies.
A compliance officer finds a serious breach of client fund rules and senior management asks him to keep it quiet. What should he do?
Wait for the next inspection to see if it is noticed
Escalate it to the board and report to the regulator as required
Resolve it informally with the affected clients and close the matter without recording it
Keep it confidential to protect the firm's reputation
Compliance officers must report non-compliance to the board and to the regulator where rules require it. Hiding a breach exposes the firm and the officer to action.
How does the compliance function differ from internal audit?
Compliance only deals with tax laws, while internal audit deals with SEBI rules
Compliance monitors regulatory adherence on an ongoing basis, while internal audit gives periodic independent assurance on controls
There is no difference; the two terms mean exactly the same thing
Compliance work is always outsourced to outside consulting firms, while internal audit can be performed only by the board of directors itself
Compliance is an ongoing second-line function, while internal audit provides independent periodic assurance on controls, including on the compliance function itself.
A 'maker-checker' control in an intermediary's back office means:
The same person enters and approves a transaction to save time
Transactions are checked only after the year-end audit
Clients check their own transactions and confirm them online
One person enters a transaction and a different person verifies and approves it
Maker-checker separates entry and approval between two people, reducing errors and fraud. It is a basic preventive control. It is widely used for payments and client fund transfers.
Which document typically sets out an intermediary's compliance responsibilities, procedures and escalation paths?
The annual income-tax return
A board-approved compliance policy or manual
The memorandum and articles of association of the firm
The client registration form
A compliance policy or manual approved by the board lays out roles, procedures, monitoring and reporting, guiding staff on how to meet regulatory requirements.
An intermediary keeps a regulatory calendar listing every report and filing due date. This mainly helps to:
Increase the firm's brokerage income
Reduce the minimum net worth the firm must maintain
Replace the need for a compliance officer
Avoid missed or delayed regulatory submissions
A compliance calendar tracks due dates for reports, returns and renewals so that filings are made on time, a common area of lapses and penalties.
A firm with an effective compliance culture is most likely to show which feature?
Compliance is discussed only when an inspection is announced
Business targets override compliance checks during busy periods
Breaches are fixed quietly without any record being kept
Staff report concerns freely and senior management acts on them
A healthy compliance culture is driven from the top, encourages escalation of issues without fear and treats compliance as part of everyday business.

SEBI Act, 1992.overview: This chapter covers the SEBI Act, 1992, which created SEBI as a statutory body to protect investors and to develop and regulate the securities market. Key areas are the composition of the SEBI Board, its functions and powers under Section 11, powers of investigation, inspection, search and seizure, interim orders, registration under Section 12, adjudication and monetary penalties, settlement of proceedings, and appeals to the Securities Appellate Tribunal and then the Supreme Court. Focus on which section gives which power, the difference between adjudication and directions, and the offences and penalties provided for violations.
questions: The preamble of the SEBI Act, 1992 states SEBI's objectives as:
Collecting taxes on capital gains made in the securities market
Fixing the prices at which shares are issued to the public
Protecting investors' interests in securities and developing and regulating the securities market
Regulating banks and controlling inflation in the economy
SEBI was set up to protect investors, develop the securities market and regulate it. Monetary policy and banks are RBI's domain, and SEBI does not fix issue prices or collect taxes.
Before the SEBI Act, 1992 was passed, SEBI existed as:
A non-statutory body set up by a government resolution in 1988
A wing of the Ministry of Corporate Affairs
A self-regulatory organisation jointly owned by the major stock exchanges
A department of the Reserve Bank of India
SEBI was first set up in April 1988 through a resolution of the Government of India and was given statutory powers by the SEBI Act, 1992.
A person aggrieved by an order of a SEBI adjudicating officer wants to challenge it. To which forum should he first appeal?
National Company Law Tribunal
Supreme Court of India
Securities Appellate Tribunal
Central Government
Orders of SEBI and its adjudicating officers are appealable to the Securities Appellate Tribunal. Only after a SAT order does an appeal lie to the Supreme Court.
During an investigation, SEBI wants to stop a company from issuing further securities until the matter is decided. Which power is it using?
Power to pass interim orders pending investigation
Power to cancel the company's incorporation
Power to levy a monetary penalty through adjudication
Power to prosecute the company in a criminal court
SEBI can pass interim or ex-parte orders under Sections 11 and 11B, such as restraining an issue, to protect investors while an investigation is pending.
A person facing SEBI proceedings applies to settle them by paying a settlement amount without admitting or denying guilt. This is possible under:
The SCRR, 1957
The Depositories Act, 1996
The settlement mechanism under Section 15JB of the SEBI Act
The compounding provisions of the Income-tax Act, 1961 for tax offences
Section 15JB allows settlement of administrative and civil proceedings on payment of settlement amount and other terms, subject to SEBI's settlement regulations.
Under the SEBI Act, which of these is an investigative power SEBI can use?
Freezing every bank account in the country during an inquiry
Calling for information and records from intermediaries and persons associated with the securities market
Ordering the arrest of any market participant without a court warrant
Changing the tax rate on securities transactions
SEBI can call for information, inspect books, summon persons and examine records. Search and seizure need approval of a designated court, and SEBI has no power to arrest.
A person who knowingly fails to pay a penalty imposed by an adjudicating officer and does not comply with SEBI's directions may face:
Recovery proceedings, including attachment of bank accounts and property, by a SEBI recovery officer
Transfer of the matter to the Reserve Bank for recovery
Only a warning letter, since penalties imposed by an adjudicating officer cannot be enforced against assets
Automatic waiver of the penalty after one year
Section 28A empowers SEBI's recovery officers to recover unpaid penalties and amounts through attachment and sale of assets and bank accounts, and arrest in some cases.
An appeal against a SEBI order must normally be filed with the Securities Appellate Tribunal within:
Any time, as there is no time limit
Seven days from the date the order is received
45 days from the date the order is received
One year from the date of the order
Section 15T allows 45 days for filing an appeal with SAT, which may admit a late appeal if there was sufficient cause for the delay.

SCRA, 1956 and SCRR, 1957.overview: This chapter deals with the Securities Contracts (Regulation) Act, 1956 and the Securities Contracts (Regulation) Rules, 1957, which govern recognition of stock exchanges and clearing corporations, contracts in securities and listing. Learners should know the wide definition of 'securities', recognition and corporatisation and demutualisation of exchanges, the power to regulate contracts and options, conditions for listing, appeals against refusal to list, and penalties. The Rules set norms on minimum public offer and minimum public shareholding. When revising, focus on definitions, the role of recognised exchanges and the separation of ownership from trading rights.
questions: Under the SCRA, 1956, which of the following is included in the definition of 'securities'?
A residential property title deed
A life insurance policy
Units of a mutual fund scheme
A savings bank deposit

Section 2(h) of the SCRA includes shares, bonds, derivatives, government securities, units of mutual funds and collective investment schemes, and security receipts. Bank deposits and insurance policies are not securities.
Corporatisation and demutualisation of a stock exchange means:
The exchange is converted into a government department
The exchange stops trading in equity and moves to derivatives
Ownership and management are separated from the trading rights of members
Only brokers may own shares in the exchange
Demutualisation separates owners from traders so that brokers' trading interests do not control the exchange, improving governance and reducing conflicts of interest.
A stock exchange refuses to list a company's securities. Under the SCRA, the company can appeal against this decision to:
The National Company Law Tribunal
The Registrar of Companies
The Securities Appellate Tribunal
The Reserve Bank of India
Section 22 of the SCRA lets a company appeal to SAT when a recognised stock exchange refuses, omits or fails to list its securities.
A stock exchange in India can operate legally only if it:
Is registered as a non-banking finance company
Is approved by the Ministry of Corporate Affairs
Has at least ten listed companies
Is recognised under the SCRA
Recognition under Section 4 of the SCRA is mandatory for a stock exchange. The Central Government's power to grant recognition is exercised by SEBI.
Under the SCRR, 1957, minimum public shareholding norms require a listed company to:
Bring its public shareholding up to the required level within the time allowed if it falls short
Keep all public shareholders' holdings in physical form
Delist automatically from all stock exchanges as soon as its public shareholding falls below 50% of capital
Ensure promoters always hold at least 75% of the shares
Rule 19A requires listed companies to maintain minimum public shareholding and to restore it within the specified period if it falls below, failing which regulatory action follows.
Derivatives are treated as 'securities' under the SCRA. As a result, trading in derivatives is legal when it is:
Approved in writing by the company whose shares are the underlying of the derivative
Settled only in cash through a bank
Traded on a recognised stock exchange under its rules and bye-laws
Agreed between any two persons, with no further conditions
Section 18A makes derivative contracts legal and valid if traded on a recognised stock exchange and settled on its clearing house as per its rules and bye-laws.
Which body may, under the SCRA, supersede the governing board of a recognised stock exchange in public interest?
The company with the largest market capitalisation on the exchange
The Registrar of Companies
The stock exchange's largest broker
SEBI, exercising powers delegated by the Central Government
Section 11 of the SCRA allows supersession of a stock exchange's governing board in the interest of the trade or the public. This power is exercised by SEBI.
A clearing corporation in the securities market mainly:
Sets interest rates for margin funding
Issues contract notes to retail clients
Clears and settles trades and acts as the central counterparty
Lists securities and approves offer documents
A recognised clearing corporation clears and settles exchange trades, guarantees settlement as central counterparty and manages the settlement guarantee fund.

SEBI (Intermediaries) Regulations, 2008.overview: These regulations set common rules for all SEBI-registered intermediaries, alongside the activity-specific regulations. The chapter covers the application and registration process, the fit and proper person criteria, general obligations such as appointing a compliance officer and redressing investor grievances, the general code of conduct, prior approval for change in control, and the procedure for action against an intermediary, including the role of the designated authority, show cause notices and orders. Revise the types of action SEBI can take, the obligations that continue after registration and the circumstances that trigger prior approval or fresh registration.
questions: An intermediary proposes a change in control. Under the Intermediaries Regulations, it must:
Surrender its existing registration and apply afresh as a new entity in every case
Simply update its website, as no approval is needed
Obtain SEBI's prior approval before the change in control takes effect
Inform SEBI within one year after the change is completed
A change in control of a registered intermediary requires SEBI's prior approval, so that the incoming controllers can be assessed for the fit and proper criteria.
Which of the following would most likely make an applicant NOT 'fit and proper' for registration?
Its promoters have earlier run another registered intermediary without any regulatory action
A pending charge sheet for an economic offence against its director
Its directors hold postgraduate degrees
It has filed audited accounts every year
Criminal complaints or charge sheets for economic offences, debarment orders and similar matters are disqualifications under the fit and proper criteria.
Under the Intermediaries Regulations, every intermediary must appoint a compliance officer who is responsible for:
Fixing the brokerage rates charged to all clients
Monitoring compliance with the Act, rules and regulations and redressing investor grievances
Preparing the firm's income-tax returns
Representing the firm before courts in civil suits
The compliance officer monitors compliance with securities laws, reports non-compliance to SEBI where observed and handles investor grievances. The officer is also the point of contact for SEBI.
When SEBI proposes action against an intermediary, the intermediary receives a show cause notice. Its main purpose is to:
Ask the intermediary to pay the penalty immediately
Inform the public and the stock exchanges that the intermediary has already been found guilty
Give the intermediary an opportunity to respond before an order is passed
Transfer the intermediary's clients to another firm
A show cause notice follows principles of natural justice, letting the intermediary reply to the allegations before the designated authority's recommendation and final order.
Which of the following is NOT one of the actions SEBI may take against an intermediary under these regulations?
Cancellation of the certificate of registration
Imprisonment of the intermediary's directors by SEBI
Suspension of the certificate of registration
Issue of a warning or prohibition from taking new clients
SEBI can suspend or cancel registration, prohibit taking new clients, issue warnings and other directions. Imprisonment can be ordered only by a court in criminal proceedings.
An investor complains against an intermediary on SEBI's SCORES platform. The intermediary is expected to:
Wait until SEBI imposes a penalty before responding
Resolve the complaint and upload an action taken report within the prescribed time
Ignore it, since complaints on SCORES can be lodged only against listed companies and their RTAs
Forward it to the stock exchange and take no further action
Registered intermediaries must redress complaints received through SCORES within the timelines set by SEBI and upload action taken reports, with escalation if unresolved.
After SEBI cancels an intermediary's certificate of registration, the intermediary must generally:
Change its name and resume business without any new approval
Stop the registered activity and protect the interests of existing clients as directed
Continue taking new clients until the appeal is decided
Transfer client funds to its own accounts for safekeeping
On cancellation, the intermediary must cease the activity and allow clients to move, for example transferring records and assets, in line with SEBI's directions.
An intermediary must ensure its key managerial personnel and employees meet the requirements of SEBI. This includes ensuring that:
Persons dealing with clients hold the NISM certifications prescribed for their roles
All employees are relatives of the promoters
Employees trade only through personal accounts held with competing intermediaries, never with the firm
Only employees with ten years' experience deal with clients
SEBI requires associated persons in specified functions, such as compliance, operations and client dealing, to obtain the relevant NISM certification.

SEBI (Prohibition of Insider Trading) Re.overview: The SEBI (Prohibition of Insider Trading) Regulations, 2015 prohibit trading by insiders when in possession of unpublished price sensitive information (UPSI). The chapter covers definitions of insider, connected person and UPSI, the ban on communicating UPSI except for legitimate purposes, trading windows, pre-clearance and contra trade restrictions, trading plans, initial and continual disclosures, the code of fair disclosure, the code of conduct for listed companies and intermediaries, and the structured digital database. Focus on who is an insider, what counts as UPSI, timelines for disclosures and the responsibilities of the compliance officer.
questions: Which of the following would generally be treated as unpublished price sensitive information (UPSI)?
Draft quarterly results of a listed company before they are announced
A press release already posted on the company's website
An audited annual report already filed with the exchange
The company's closing share price as published on the stock exchange website
UPSI is information not generally available that is likely to materially affect the price, such as financial results, dividends or mergers before public disclosure.
A person who was a statutory auditor of a company four months ago, and had access to its UPSI, trades in its shares. Under the regulations he is:
A connected person, since the association was within six months before the act
Not an insider, because his engagement has ended
Exempt, as auditors are outside the scope of these rules
An insider only if he currently holds over 10% of the shares
A connected person includes anyone associated with the company in a way giving access to UPSI during the six months prior to the act concerned.
The trading window for designated persons of a listed company is ordinarily closed from the end of every quarter until:
Seven days before the board meeting that approves the results
The first day of the next quarter
The annual general meeting of the company
48 hours after the declaration of financial results
Trading restriction for designated persons generally runs from the end of the quarter until 48 hours after the financial results are made public.
A company shares UPSI with its bankers for evaluating a loan. Under the regulations, such sharing is:
Allowed only if the bankers first obtain SEBI's specific written approval for each instance of sharing
Allowed as a 'legitimate purpose', provided the recipient is given notice to keep it confidential
Always prohibited, regardless of purpose
Allowed only after the information is published
UPSI may be shared for legitimate purposes, such as with lenders, auditors or advisers, in the ordinary course of business, with confidentiality obligations and database entries.
A listed company must maintain a structured digital database (SDD) to record:
The voting results of all general meetings
The salary details of all employees
The dividend paid to every shareholder in the last ten years
The names and PAN of persons with whom UPSI is shared, with time stamps
The SDD records the nature of UPSI and details of persons sharing and receiving it, with time stamps and audit trails, so that leaks can be traced.
A promoter wants to trade in his company's shares despite regularly holding UPSI. The regulations allow this through:
A trading plan approved by the compliance officer and disclosed to the stock exchanges in advance
Trading through a relative's account
Trading only on days when the market is closed
Verbal permission from the managing director, recorded later in the minutes of the next board meeting
A trading plan is a pre-scheduled, publicly disclosed plan that lets persons who perpetually hold UPSI trade without breaching the prohibition, subject to conditions.
Under the Code of Fair Disclosure, a listed company should designate a senior officer to deal with dissemination of information. This officer is called the:
Chief Risk Officer
Principal Officer
Designated Director
Chief Investor Relations Officer
The code requires a senior officer, the Chief Investor Relations Officer, to oversee uniform and prompt disclosure of UPSI to avoid selective disclosure.
Once a designated person makes a continual disclosure of trades to the company, the company must inform the stock exchanges within:
The next annual general meeting
Two trading days of receiving the disclosure
Thirty days of receiving the disclosure
Seven calendar days after the end of the quarter
The company must notify the stock exchanges of the details within two trading days of receiving the continual disclosure or becoming aware of it.

SEBI (PFUTP) Regulations, 2003.overview: The SEBI (Prohibition of Fraudulent and Unfair Trade Practices relating to Securities Market) Regulations, 2003 prohibit fraud, manipulation and unfair practices in dealing in securities. This chapter explains the wide definition of 'fraud', the general prohibition in Regulation 3, and the illustrative list of manipulative practices in Regulation 4, such as circular and wash trades, price rigging, spreading false information, front running, mis-selling and misuse of client accounts. It also covers SEBI's powers of investigation and action. When revising, learn to recognise the practices from scenarios and note that intermediaries and their employees are specifically covered.
questions: Two connected parties repeatedly buy and sell the same shares between themselves with no real change of ownership. This is called:
Wash or circular trading
Arbitrage trading
Hedging
Block deal trading
Trades with no genuine change in beneficial ownership create a false appearance of activity and are prohibited as manipulative under the PFUTP Regulations.
A person posts false news on social media about a large order win by a small company to push up its share price and then sells his holdings. This is:
A fraudulent practice of spreading false information to manipulate prices
Legitimate investment research
Permitted marketing by an investor
A routine block deal
Disseminating misleading information to influence prices and then profiting, often called pump and dump, is expressly prohibited under PFUTP. SEBI can also order disgorgement of the profits made.
A distributor sells a high-risk product to an elderly client by describing it as 'capital protected'. Under PFUTP this is:
Only a breach of the distributor's internal policy
Permitted if the product is listed on an exchange
Mis-selling, which is a fraudulent and unfair trade practice
Acceptable as long as the client has signed the application form and risk disclosure
Mis-selling, including selling unsuitable products or making false or misleading statements, is specifically listed as an unfair trade practice. A signed form does not cure a misleading sales pitch.
A trader places large buy orders far from the market price and cancels them repeatedly to create a false impression of demand. This practice is known as:
Spoofing or layering
Portfolio rebalancing
Short covering
Market making
Placing orders without intent to execute, to mislead other participants about demand or supply, is a manipulative practice under PFUTP.
Under the PFUTP Regulations, 'fraud' includes:
Only acts committed by listed companies
Only acts that cause a combined loss of more than ₹1 crore to investors and are proved by a court of law
Only acts that are also offences under the Indian Penal Code
Any act or concealment that induces another person to deal in securities, even without wrongful gain
The definition of fraud is deliberately wide and covers acts, omissions and concealment that induce dealing, even without proof of wrongful gain or loss.
A broker executes excessive trades in a client's account mainly to earn more brokerage, without regard to the client's interest. This is called:
Algorithmic trading
Proprietary trading
Margin trading facility
Churning, an unfair trade practice
Excessive trading in a client account to generate commissions harms the client and is treated as an unfair trade practice by an intermediary.
An employee of a mutual fund buys a stock just before the fund places a large order in it, using his knowledge of the order. Under PFUTP this is:
Legitimate personal investment
Front running
Insider trading of UPSI of a listed company
Index rebalancing
Trading ahead of a large non-public order with knowledge of it is front running, which is covered under PFUTP regardless of whether the person is an intermediary.
A company issues a misleading advertisement about its financial performance to attract investors to its share issue. This falls under PFUTP because:
Only stock brokers and their employees can be held liable under PFUTP, not listed companies
PFUTP applies only to derivative trades
Publishing misleading information to induce dealing in securities is a prohibited practice
Advertisements are never regulated by SEBI
Making or publishing false or misleading statements to induce investors to deal in securities is a fraudulent practice under PFUTP.

Prevention of Money Laundering Act, 2002.overview: This chapter covers the Prevention of Money Laundering Act, 2002, the PML Rules and SEBI's AML/CFT guidelines for intermediaries. It explains what money laundering is, its stages of placement, layering and integration, and the obligations of reporting entities: client due diligence, identifying beneficial owners, risk-based categorisation, ongoing monitoring, record keeping and reporting to FIU-IND through cash transaction and suspicious transaction reports. It also covers the Principal Officer and Designated Director, the ban on tipping off and staff training. Focus on reporting timelines, beneficial ownership thresholds and red flags in client behaviour.
questions: Which stage of money laundering involves moving funds through many complex transactions to hide their origin?
Structuring of tax returns
Layering
Placement
Integration
Placement introduces illicit cash into the system, layering disguises the trail through multiple transactions, and integration brings the funds back into the economy as apparently legitimate.
A reporting entity files an STR on a client. A staff member then tells the client about the report. This is:
Tipping off, which is prohibited
Allowed if the client asks directly
Good customer service
Required by law within seven days
Disclosing to the client that an STR has been filed is prohibited, as it may help the client evade investigation.
Under the PML Rules, besides the Principal Officer, a reporting entity must appoint a:
Chief Investment Officer to approve all large transactions of high-value clients
Statutory auditor to file STRs
Designated Director to ensure overall compliance with PMLA obligations
Public relations officer for FIU-IND
The Designated Director, typically the managing director or a whole-time director, is responsible for overall compliance with PMLA obligations. Both officers' details must be shared with FIU-IND.
A client who is a politically exposed person (PEP) opens a trading account. Under SEBI's AML guidelines, the intermediary should:
Refuse the account in all cases
Open the account without any additional checks
Apply simplified due diligence because PEPs are well known
Apply enhanced due diligence and obtain senior management approval for the relationship
PEPs are high-risk clients, so intermediaries must perform enhanced due diligence, verify source of funds and get senior management approval to establish or continue the relationship.
Which of the following is a typical red flag of possible money laundering in a broking account?
A client choosing to receive contract notes electronically
Large funds deposited and withdrawn soon after with little trading activity
A client updating his correspondence address after relocating to another city for work
A salaried client investing a small amount every month
Funds routed through an account with little genuine trading suggest the account is being used to move money, which should be examined for an STR.
FIU-IND, which receives reports from reporting entities, functions under:
SEBI's Integrated Surveillance Department
The Reserve Bank of India
The Ministry of Home Affairs
The Department of Revenue, Ministry of Finance
Financial Intelligence Unit-India is the central agency for receiving, analysing and disseminating financial transaction information and functions under the Department of Revenue.
For a client that is a company, the PML Rules identify a beneficial owner as a natural person who, alone or together, holds a controlling ownership interest of more than:
51% of shares, capital or profits
10% of shares, capital or profits
75% of shares, capital or profits
1% of shares, capital or profits
Following the 2023 amendment to the PML Rules, the threshold for controlling ownership interest in a company is more than 10% of shares, capital or profits.
Under the PMLA, a reporting entity applies a risk-based approach. This means it should:
Apply due diligence checks only to clients who invest more than ₹1 crore in a financial year
Apply due diligence measures in proportion to the money laundering risk each client poses
Treat all clients as high risk and reject most applications
Leave risk assessment to FIU-IND
Clients are categorised as low, medium or high risk, and the depth of due diligence and monitoring is matched to that risk.

SEBI (KYC Registration Agency) Regulatio.overview: This chapter covers the SEBI (KYC Registration Agency) Regulations, 2011, under which KRAs maintain centralised KYC records of investors in the securities market. It explains registration of KRAs, their functions and obligations, the duties of intermediaries in performing initial KYC, in-person verification and uploading records, and the validation of KYC records by KRAs against official databases. It also covers data security, confidentiality and the link with the Central KYC Records Registry. While revising, focus on the division of responsibility between intermediary and KRA, the 'one-time KYC' benefit for investors and the restrictions on how KRAs may use investor data.
questions: An investor completes KYC with a stock broker and later opens an account with a mutual fund distributor. Because of the KRA system, the investor:
Must visit SEBI's office to transfer the KYC
Need not repeat the full KYC process, as the second intermediary can fetch the KYC record from the KRA
Must complete full KYC again with every new intermediary
Can invest only after the broker gives written consent
KRAs hold KYC records centrally so that an investor's KYC done once can be relied upon by other SEBI-registered intermediaries, avoiding duplication.
Under the KRA Regulations, a KRA may use the KYC data it holds:
To recommend suitable investment products to investors based on their income details
To sell investor contact lists to marketing companies
To publish investor details on its website
Only for the purposes permitted under the regulations, keeping it confidential
KRAs must maintain confidentiality and data security and may not use KYC information for any purpose other than what the regulations permit.
Which entity is primarily responsible for carrying out the initial KYC of a client, including obtaining documents and in-person verification where needed?
The client's bank, which has already verified the client while opening the savings account
The KYC Registration Agency
The SEBI-registered intermediary with whom the client first opens an account
SEBI
The intermediary performs initial KYC and uploads it to the KRA. The KRA stores, validates and makes the record available to other intermediaries.
A KRA validates a client's KYC record by checking it against official sources such as the Income Tax Department database. The purpose of this validation is to:
Approve the client's trading limit
Calculate the client's tax liability
Determine the client's eligibility for IPO allotment
Confirm key attributes like PAN, name and address so the record can be relied upon
KRAs independently validate records against official databases so that intermediaries can rely on them, which also supports portability of KYC.
To be registered as a KRA, an applicant must obtain a certificate of registration from:
CERSAI
SEBI
The stock exchanges jointly
The Reserve Bank of India
KRAs are registered and regulated by SEBI under the KRA Regulations, 2011. CERSAI runs the Central KYC Records Registry, which is a different system.
If an intermediary finds that a client's KYC details have changed, such as a new address, it should:
Collect supporting documents and update the record in the KRA system
Report the change only to the stock exchange
Ignore the change until the annual review
Close the existing account and open a fresh account with new KYC documents
Intermediaries must update changes in KYC details with the KRA so that the central record stays accurate for all intermediaries relying on it.
A KRA must have adequate systems to ensure that KYC records are:
Destroyed immediately after an account is opened
Available freely to any member of the public
Stored only in paper form in fireproof cabinets at the head office
Protected against unauthorised access, alteration or loss
KRA Regulations require robust systems for data security, integrity and confidentiality, along with disaster recovery arrangements. Paper-only storage would not meet these standards.
Which of the following is the main benefit of KRAs to intermediaries?
Reduced duplication of KYC work and access to a uniform, verified KYC record
Freedom from having to know their clients at all
Exemption from all anti-money laundering obligations
A guarantee from SEBI against client fraud
KRAs save repeated KYC effort and provide uniform records, but intermediaries still remain responsible for due diligence and AML obligations.

SEBI (Foreign Portfolio Investors) Regul.overview: This chapter covers the SEBI (Foreign Portfolio Investors) Regulations, 2019, which govern portfolio investment by foreign entities in Indian securities. It explains eligibility, the Category I and Category II classification, registration through Designated Depository Participants, permanent registration, investment conditions and limits, investor group rules, the treatment of NRIs and OCIs as constituents, offshore derivative instruments, and the obligations of FPIs, DDPs and custodians. When revising, focus on who may register in which category, the role of DDPs, the consequence of crossing the individual investment limit and the conditions for issuing ODIs.
questions: Under the FPI Regulations, 2019, an applicant applies for FPI registration through:
The Reserve Bank of India directly
The Ministry of External Affairs
Any SEBI-registered stock broker in India with a foreign client desk
A Designated Depository Participant (DDP) approved by SEBI
Registration of FPIs is granted by DDPs on behalf of SEBI. DDPs also carry out KYC and ongoing monitoring of FPIs.
Which of the following is most likely to be classified as a Category I FPI?
A family office
An unregulated corporate body incorporated in a tax haven
An individual resident in a foreign country
A pension fund regulated in a FATF member country
Category I covers government and related investors, pension funds, and appropriately regulated entities from FATF member jurisdictions. Individuals, family offices and corporates fall in Category II.
An FPI's holding in a listed Indian company crosses the individual investment limit. The FPI must:
Seek approval from the company's board to keep it
Convert the shares into debentures
Divest the excess within the prescribed time or have the entire holding treated as FDI
Retain the holding without any further action
If an FPI breaches the limit, it may either sell down the excess within the specified period or have its total investment reclassified as foreign direct investment.
Offshore derivative instruments (ODIs) with Indian securities as underlying may be issued only by:
Category I FPIs, subject to conditions
Indian mutual funds
Any FPI regardless of category
SEBI-registered Indian stock brokers only
Only Category I FPIs, other than those undertaking certain activities, may issue ODIs, and only to eligible persons after KYC, with reporting to SEBI.
Under the FPI Regulations, 2019, an FPI's registration is:
Permanent, unless suspended or cancelled, subject to payment of fees
Temporary until approved by Parliament
Valid only until the FPI makes its first investment in Indian securities
Valid for one year and must be renewed annually
Since 2019, FPI registration is permanent unless suspended or cancelled, provided the FPI pays the applicable fees periodically. Earlier, registration had to be renewed periodically.
Can a non-resident Indian (NRI) be a constituent of an FPI?
Yes, without any limits whatsoever
No, NRIs are completely barred from any link with FPIs
Yes, subject to limits on individual and aggregate contribution and other conditions
Only if the NRI becomes a resident Indian first
NRIs, OCIs and resident Indians may be constituents of FPIs within prescribed contribution limits and conditions, though NRIs cannot register as FPIs themselves.
Which entity typically provides custody services to an FPI investing in India?
A SEBI-registered custodian
The Securities Appellate Tribunal
A KYC Registration Agency
The issuer company itself
FPIs must appoint a SEBI-registered custodian for safekeeping of securities and reporting of transactions to regulators. The custodian also reports the FPI's holdings to regulators.
For applying the investment limit, investments by FPIs with common ownership of more than 50% or common control are:
Counted only if they are in the same country
Treated separately, regardless of common ownership
Clubbed together as one investor group
Exempt from all limits
FPIs having common ownership above 50% or common control are clubbed as an investor group, and the investment limit applies to the group as a whole.

SEBI (Stock Brokers) Regulations.overview: This chapter covers the regulatory framework for stock brokers and clearing members, including registration, eligibility, capital adequacy, the code of conduct, and the obligations of brokers towards clients. Key topics are client registration and KYC, risk disclosure, segregation and upstreaming of client funds and securities, running account settlement, margin collection and pledge, contract notes and statements, authorised persons, internal controls, grievance redressal and inspections. Focus on how client money and securities must be handled, documents given to clients, and conduct obligations, since these are frequent sources of violations and enforcement action.
questions: A broker holds client funds at the end of the trading day. Under current SEBI requirements, these client funds must be:
Kept in the broker's proprietary account for safety
Invested in fixed deposits in the broker's own name to earn interest for the firm
Used to meet the broker's operating expenses
Upstreamed to the clearing corporation, not retained with the broker or its bank
SEBI requires brokers to upstream clients' clear funds to clearing corporations at the end of each day, reducing the risk of misuse of client money.
A client opts for quarterly running account settlement. This means the broker must:
Settle the client's funds by returning unused credit balance as per the settlement schedule
Keep the client's funds indefinitely without any settlement
Transfer the balance to the broker's own account each quarter
Settle the account only when the client closes it, regardless of any credit balance outstanding
Under running account settlement, brokers must periodically pay out clients' unutilised funds on the specified schedule, retaining only what is permitted.
Under the margin pledge mechanism, when a client provides shares as margin, the shares:
Are sold by the broker and the cash is kept as margin
Remain in the client's demat account and are pledged in favour of the broker
Are transferred to the broker's own demat account
Are held in physical form by the broker
Since 2020, securities given as collateral must be pledged and re-pledged rather than transferred to the broker, keeping them in the client's account.
An authorised person (AP) of a stock broker is:
An agent appointed by the broker, with exchange approval, to deal with clients on its behalf
An independent broker with direct exchange membership
A SEBI official who audits stock brokers and their branch offices on behalf of the stock exchanges
A client with power of attorney over other clients
APs act as agents of the broker and are approved by the stock exchange. The broker remains responsible for their acts.
Which document must a broker give a client when the account is opened, explaining the risks of trading in the securities market?
Risk Disclosure Document
Scheme Information Document
Offer Document
Information Memorandum
The Risk Disclosure Document, along with the rights and obligations document, is provided at account opening to inform clients of trading risks.
A broker executes a trade for a client without the client's instructions. This is:
Acceptable during volatile market conditions
Permitted if the trade makes a profit and the client is informed later
Allowed if the client had a debit balance
Unauthorised trading, a violation of the broker's obligations
Brokers must trade only on clients' instructions. Unauthorised trades breach the code of conduct and can lead to disciplinary action.
Instead of a broad power of attorney, a client may now authorise a broker to transfer securities for settlement and pledging through a:
Demat Debit and Pledge Instruction (DDPI)
Letter of indemnity
Delivery Instruction Slip signed in blank
General power of attorney covering all assets
SEBI introduced DDPI to limit the broker's authority to specific purposes such as settlement and margin pledge, replacing broad powers of attorney.
A broker carries out proprietary trades and client trades. Under SEBI rules, the broker must:
Combine proprietary and client trades in one account for efficiency
Use clients' securities as margin for its own trades
Keep proprietary and client accounts separate and disclose proprietary trading to clients
Never trade on its own account under any circumstances
Brokers must segregate proprietary and client accounts and inform clients whether they undertake proprietary trading, avoiding misuse of client assets.

SEBI (Merchant Bankers) Regulations etc..overview: This chapter covers merchant bankers and related issue intermediaries such as bankers to an issue and underwriters. It explains registration, categories and capital requirements of merchant bankers, their responsibilities as lead managers in public issues, due diligence, restrictions on associates, the code of conduct and disclosure obligations. It also covers the role of underwriters, underwriting agreements and the obligations of bankers to an issue in collecting application money and making refunds. When revising, focus on due diligence duties, conflicts of interest and the division of responsibilities among issue intermediaries.
questions: Before an offer document is filed, the lead manager must submit to SEBI a:
Tax clearance certificate
No objection certificate from the stock exchange
Certificate of incorporation
Due diligence certificate
The lead merchant banker certifies that it has exercised due diligence and that disclosures in the offer document are true, fair and adequate.
A merchant banker's responsibility for the accuracy of disclosures in an offer document is:
Not reduced by the issuer's own responsibility for the contents
Limited to errors in the price band and the basis of issue price only
Fully transferred to the issuer once the document is filed
Applicable only if the issue is undersubscribed
Lead managers must independently verify disclosures. The issuer's responsibility does not absolve the merchant banker of its due diligence obligations.
Which intermediary collects application money from investors in a public issue and handles refunds?
Custodian
Banker to an issue
Debenture trustee
Credit rating agency
Bankers to an issue accept applications and money, maintain escrow and public issue accounts, and handle refunds in coordination with the registrar.
An underwriter has agreed to underwrite part of an issue. If the issue is undersubscribed and the underwriting is called on, the underwriter must:
Ask SEBI to extend the issue indefinitely
Subscribe for the shortfall in its share within the time stated in the agreement
Refund all investors' money and ask the issuer to reopen the issue at a lower price
Withdraw from the agreement without consequences
An underwriter's commitment becomes binding when devolvement occurs, and it must subscribe to the unsubscribed portion as per the underwriting agreement.
Which of the following is a typical activity of a merchant banker?
Settling trades as a clearing corporation
Issuing insurance policies to investors
Managing public issues, including drafting the offer document and coordinating intermediaries
Accepting public deposits like a bank
Merchant bankers manage issues, advise on capital structure, conduct due diligence and coordinate other intermediaries. Accepting deposits and settlement are not their functions.
A merchant banker learns price sensitive information about an issuer client during due diligence. It must:
Use it to advise its other clients on trading
Publish it on its website for transparency so that all investors have equal access
Not use the information for its own trading or share it except as permitted
Trade quickly before the issue closes
Merchant bankers are bound by confidentiality and insider trading rules and must not misuse information obtained from clients. Misuse could breach both PIT and PFUTP rules.
Under the merchant banker framework, a lead manager must ensure that the advertisements for a public issue:
Are released before SEBI's observations to build demand
Highlight only positive aspects without risk factors
Promise a guaranteed listing gain to attract retail investors
Are consistent with the offer document and not misleading
Issue advertisements must be truthful, fair and consistent with the offer document, and must not contain misleading statements or promises of returns.
Following the post-issue period, the lead merchant banker is responsible for:
Acting as the issuer's statutory auditor
Running the company's day-to-day operations
Monitoring allotment, refunds, listing and other post-issue activities until completion
Nothing, as its role ends on the issue closing date

Post-issue, the lead manager coordinates with the registrar, bankers and exchanges to ensure timely allotment, refunds, unblocking and listing. Its responsibility ends only after these steps are complete.

SEBI (ICDR) Regulations, 2018.overview: The SEBI (Issue of Capital and Disclosure Requirements) Regulations, 2018 govern public issues, rights issues, preferential issues, qualified institutions placements, bonus issues and SME issues. The chapter covers eligibility for an IPO under Regulations 6(1) and 6(2), offer document filing, price discovery through book building, allocation to investor categories, anchor investors, minimum promoter contribution and lock-in, pricing of preferential allotments, and timelines for listing. When revising, focus on eligibility conditions, allocation percentages, lock-in rules and the differences among issue types, and keep track of the reduced listing timeline after issue closure.
questions: A company that does not meet the profitability track record under Regulation 6(1) can still make an IPO under Regulation 6(2) if:
At least 75% of the net offer is allotted to qualified institutional buyers
At least 75% of the net offer is allotted to retail investors
The issue is priced below face value
Promoters guarantee a minimum listing price to all applicants in the public issue
Under Regulation 6(2), a company not meeting 6(1) criteria must allot at least 75% of the net offer to QIBs, with retail allocation capped at 10%.
In a book-built IPO, anchor investors are:
Retail investors applying for less than ₹2 lakh
Qualified institutional buyers who are allocated shares a day before the issue opens
Employees applying under the employee reservation portion at a discount to the issue price
Promoters contributing to the minimum promoter contribution
Anchor investors are QIBs who bid one working day before the issue opens, receive allocation from the QIB portion and are subject to lock-in.
Under ICDR, equity shares held by persons other than promoters before an IPO are generally:
Locked in for ten years
Locked in for six months from the date of allotment in the IPO
Compulsorily sold in the offer for sale
Free from any lock-in
Pre-issue shareholding of non-promoters is generally locked in for six months from IPO allotment, subject to specified exemptions. Promoter shareholding is subject to separate, longer lock-in rules.
After a public issue closes, SEBI requires listing and commencement of trading within:
Six months of issue closure
Three working days of issue closure (T+3)
Thirty days of issue closure
Fifteen working days after the issue closure
SEBI reduced the listing timeline from T+6 to T+3 working days, made mandatory from December 2023, so investors get allotment and refunds faster.
A company issues equity shares to a select group of investors on a private basis that is not a rights or public issue. Under ICDR this is a:
Bonus issue
Rights issue
Offer for sale
Preferential issue
A preferential issue is an issue to selected persons on a private placement basis, governed by Chapter V of ICDR including pricing and lock-in rules.
In a bonus issue, shareholders receive additional shares:
At a discount to market price, payable in cash within thirty days
In exchange for surrendering their debentures
Without paying any consideration, by capitalising reserves
Only if they apply within the offer period
Bonus shares are issued free of cost by capitalising free reserves or securities premium, in proportion to existing holdings. No money is raised from shareholders in a bonus issue.
A listed company raises funds by issuing shares only to qualified institutional buyers through a placement document. This route is called:
Employee stock option scheme
Qualified Institutions Placement (QIP)
Rights issue
Initial Public Offer
A QIP allows listed companies to raise capital quickly from QIBs under Chapter VI of ICDR without filing a draft offer document with SEBI for observations.
In a rights issue, an existing shareholder who does not wish to subscribe can:
Transfer the rights only to the promoter group at the issue price
Renounce the rights entitlement in favour of another person
Demand cash compensation from the company
Convert the rights into bonus shares
Rights entitlements are credited in demat form and can be renounced or traded, so a shareholder who does not subscribe can still realise value.

Depositories Act, 1996.overview: The Depositories Act, 1996 provides the legal basis for holding and transferring securities in electronic form. This chapter covers the definitions of depository, participant, issuer and beneficial owner, the investor's option to hold securities in physical or demat form, the role of the depository as registered owner for transfer purposes, fungibility, register of beneficial owners, pledge and hypothecation, the rights of beneficial owners, opting out of a depository, liability of depositories for losses, and penalties. When revising, focus on the distinction between registered owner and beneficial owner and the legal effect of dematerialisation.
questions: For securities held in a depository, the depository is deemed to be the registered owner. This status allows it to:
Vote at company meetings on the shares on behalf of all its account holders
Receive dividends on the shares for itself
Effect transfer of ownership on behalf of the beneficial owner
