Sell the shares without the owner's instructions
Under Section 10, the depository is the registered owner only to effect transfers. It has no voting or other rights; those belong to the beneficial owner.
A beneficial owner wants to pledge his demat shares as security for a loan. Under the Depositories Act, he:
Needs prior approval from SEBI for each pledge
Cannot pledge demat shares at all
Must first convert the shares into physical form
Can create the pledge through the depository, following prescribed procedures
Section 12 allows beneficial owners to pledge or hypothecate securities held in a depository, with the pledge recorded by the depository.
A beneficial owner wishes to opt out of the depository system for some securities. The process is called:
Dematerialisation
Consolidation
Sub-division
Rematerialisation
Under Section 14, an investor can opt out of a depository, and the issuer then issues physical certificates. This reverse process is rematerialisation.
If a beneficial owner suffers a loss due to the negligence of a depository or its participant, under the Act:
The depository must indemnify the beneficial owner
The issuer company must make good the investor's loss
The investor bears the loss entirely
SEBI compensates the investor from its own funds
Section 16 makes the depository liable to indemnify beneficial owners for losses caused by its own or its participant's negligence.
Under the Depositories Act, a depository must be:
A department of the Reserve Bank of India that is constituted under the Banking Regulation Act, 1949
A trust registered with the Charity Commissioner
A partnership firm owned by brokers
A company registered under the Companies Act and holding a SEBI certificate of registration
A depository is defined as a company formed and registered under the Companies Act that has been granted a certificate of registration by SEBI.
Which document does an issuer maintain for securities held in demat form, based on details provided by the depository?
Register of charges
Minutes book of board meetings
Register of contracts with related parties
Register and index of beneficial owners
Section 11 requires the depository to maintain a register of beneficial owners, which is deemed to be the issuer's register of members for demat holdings.
An investor holds physical shares and wants to hold them electronically. Under the Act, he must:
Destroy the certificates and inform the company
Send the certificates directly to SEBI
Surrender the certificates to the issuer through a depository participant for dematerialisation
Sell the shares and buy them again in demat form
The investor surrenders physical certificates via the DP, the issuer verifies and cancels them, and the depository credits the securities to the beneficial owner's account.
Which right does a beneficial owner have for securities held through a depository?
Only voting rights, while the dividends are paid to the depository participant
All rights and benefits, such as voting and dividends, and all liabilities
No rights until the shares are rematerialised
Only the right to sell, with dividends going to the depository
Section 10(3) gives the beneficial owner all rights, benefits and liabilities attached to the securities held by a depository. The depository itself holds no such rights.

SEBI (Depositories and Participants) Reg.overview: These regulations govern the registration, governance and operations of depositories and their participants. The chapter covers eligibility and net worth for depositories and DPs, ownership limits and governance norms, bye-laws, the agreement between DP and client, account opening, transfer and pledge operations, nomination and transmission, statements of account, internal controls, audits, record keeping, inspection and grievance redressal. Focus on the operational duties of DPs towards clients, safeguards such as freezing and authentication of instructions, and the role of the depository in supervising its participants.
questions: Which of the following entities is eligible to apply for registration as a depository participant?
A listed manufacturing company
A proprietary concern with no financial business
A scheduled commercial bank
An individual retail investor
Banks, financial institutions, custodians, clearing corporations, stock brokers and NBFCs meeting criteria can become DPs. Ordinary companies and individuals are not eligible.
Depositories send investors a Consolidated Account Statement (CAS) mainly to:
Show only the balance in the investor's linked savings bank account along with interest credited
Calculate the investor's income-tax payable
Give a single view of the investor's securities holdings and transactions across accounts
Replace the need for contract notes from brokers
CAS consolidates holdings and transactions across demat accounts and mutual fund folios linked by PAN, helping investors detect unauthorised activity.
A client wants to prevent any debit from his demat account while he is abroad. He can request his DP to:
Transfer all shares to the DP's account
Convert all holdings into physical form
Close the account permanently
Freeze the account for debits
Clients can freeze their demat accounts for debits, credits or both, which protects against unauthorised transfers during the period. The client can revoke the freeze when he returns.
When a sole holder of a demat account dies and has registered a nominee, the securities are:
Frozen permanently until a court order is obtained
Transmitted to the nominee's account after the DP verifies the required documents
Forfeited to the depository
Sold and the proceeds paid to the DP
On death of a sole holder, securities are transmitted to the registered nominee on submission of the death certificate and transmission request.
Before executing a delivery instruction slip (DIS) submitted in paper form, a DP should:
Verify the client's signature and that the slip was issued to that client
Execute it immediately without any verification
Accept it only if signed by the stock broker
Ask SEBI to approve the transfer before it is processed in the depository system
DPs must verify signatures and DIS serial numbers to prevent misuse of slips, and must keep records of instructions received.
A Basic Services Demat Account (BSDA) is designed for:
Companies holding treasury shares
Small investors with low holdings, offering reduced or nil annual maintenance charges
Foreign portfolio investors only, who need a low-cost account for their custodial holdings
Clearing members holding pool securities
BSDA aims to reduce the cost of holding securities for small investors, with lower or zero annual maintenance charges up to specified holding values.
Under the D&P Regulations, a depository is required to:
Leave supervision of DPs entirely to SEBI
Allow DPs to operate without any agreement
Guarantee all trades executed on stock exchanges
Conduct periodic inspection of its participants and act on deficiencies found
Depositories act as first-level regulators of DPs, inspecting them, monitoring compliance and taking action under their bye-laws. SEBI also inspects depositories and DPs directly.
A DP's books show a client holding of 500 shares, while the depository's records show 450. The DP should:
Identify and resolve the difference through reconciliation immediately
Treat its own books as correct and ignore the depository
Credit 50 shares from another client's account
Wait until the client complains and only then check the depository's records
Daily reconciliation between DP records and depository records ensures accuracy, and any difference must be investigated and corrected promptly. Unresolved differences can put client assets at risk.

SEBI (RTA) Regulations, 1993.overview: This chapter covers the SEBI (Registrars to an Issue and Share Transfer Agents) Regulations, 1993. It explains the two categories of RTAs, registration and capital requirements, and the functions of registrars to an issue, such as processing applications and finalising allotment, and of share transfer agents, such as maintaining registers of members and handling investor service requests. It also covers the code of conduct, record keeping, inspection, grievance handling and the shift to dematerialised transfers. Focus on the difference between the two roles, the RTA's duties in issue processes and its obligations in investor servicing.
questions: Which of the following is a function of a registrar to an issue?
Finalising the basis of allotment along with the lead manager and stock exchange
Acting as the custodian of FPI investments
Rating the debt instruments issued by the company and publishing the rating rationale
Underwriting the unsubscribed portion of the issue
The registrar processes applications, finalises the basis of allotment with the lead manager and exchange, and handles allotment and refund instructions.
An RTA registered under Category I can:
Act both as a registrar to an issue and as a share transfer agent
Act only as a registrar to an issue
Act as a stock broker and depository
Act only as a share transfer agent
Category I RTAs may carry on both activities, while Category II RTAs may act as either a registrar to an issue or a share transfer agent.
An investor holding physical shares of a listed company wants to transfer them to a buyer. Under current rules:
The company must issue new physical certificates to the buyer
The RTA will register the physical transfer in the same way as before
The buyer must apply to SEBI for permission
Transfers of listed securities can be effected only in demat form
Since April 2019, transfers of listed securities other than transmission or transposition are processed only in demat form, so physical holders must dematerialise first.
When an RTA processes a request for issue of duplicate securities, it now issues a:
Letter of confirmation, which the investor uses to get the securities dematerialised
Fresh offer document to the investor
New physical share certificate in all cases
Cash refund equal to the market value of the lost securities on the date of the request
For service requests like duplicates or transmission, RTAs issue a letter of confirmation, and the investor must submit it for dematerialisation within the validity period.
Which of the following best describes the RTA's role in investor grievance redressal?
Fixing the dividend rate for the company
Resolving complaints on transfers, transmission, dividends and records within set timelines
Deciding appeals against SEBI orders
Approving changes in the company's articles
RTAs handle investor service requests and complaints on behalf of issuers and must address them within set timelines, including those received via SCORES.
An RTA must maintain proper books and records for its clients and keep them:
Accessible to any member of the public on request
Only in the issuer's registered office and never at the RTA's own premises
Destroyed once the issue is complete
Available for inspection by SEBI and preserved for the specified period
RTAs must maintain records such as applications, allotment, transfers and grievances, preserve them for prescribed periods and produce them during SEBI inspections.
In a public issue, the registrar to the issue is appointed by:
The issuer company, usually in consultation with the lead manager
The stock exchange where the shares are proposed to be listed after the issue
SEBI, through a lottery among registered RTAs
The depository that will hold the shares
The issuer appoints the registrar to its issue, normally with input from the lead manager, and enters into an agreement setting out the registrar's duties.
Investor service requests such as change of address for physical holders are submitted to the RTA using:
Standardised forms prescribed by SEBI for investor service requests
A request to the depository participant only
An application to the Registrar of Companies
A plain letter to the stock exchange
SEBI has standardised ISR forms for physical holders to update PAN, KYC, nomination and other details with RTAs, simplifying the process.

SEBI (Research Analysts) Regulations, 20.overview: This chapter covers the SEBI (Research Analysts) Regulations, 2014, which regulate persons who prepare and publish research reports or make buy, sell or hold recommendations on securities. It explains who needs registration and who is exempt, qualification and certification requirements, the management of conflicts of interest, disclosures required in research reports and public appearances, restrictions on personal trading, separation of research from investment banking and sales, record keeping, fee and client-facing obligations, and the role of the administration and supervisory body. Focus on disclosure requirements, independence from business pressures and limits on trading by analysts.
questions: A research entity also has an investment banking division. To protect the independence of research, it must:
Maintain an effective separation (Chinese wall) between research and investment banking
Publish research only on companies that are its banking clients
Link each analyst's pay to the revenue earned from specific investment banking deals it covers
Allow investment bankers to approve research reports before release
The regulations require separation of research from investment banking and sales, and bar analysts' compensation from depending on specific banking transactions.
In a research report, an analyst must disclose whether the analyst or associates had actual or beneficial ownership of 1% or more of the subject company's securities. The purpose of this is to:
Let readers judge possible conflicts of interest
Advertise the analyst's personal portfolio
Inform tax authorities of the analyst's income
Help the company calculate its public shareholding
Disclosure of financial interests and holdings in the subject company helps readers assess whether the recommendation may be biased. Material conflicts must also be disclosed.
A research analyst is asked to take part in a roadshow to market an IPO for which his firm is the lead manager. Under the regulations he should:
Participate and present a buy recommendation
Participate only if paid separately by the issuer
Participate after informing the stock exchange and the issuer
Not participate in the marketing or roadshow of the issue
Analysts must not take part in business solicitation or marketing activities such as roadshows for issues handled by their firm, as this compromises independence.
Which of the following persons generally needs registration as a research analyst?
A person who publishes research reports with buy or sell recommendations for consideration
A company publishing its own audited results
A journalist writing a general market news report
An investor discussing his own trades with family
Registration is needed by persons preparing research reports or making recommendations on securities as a business. General news and personal discussions are outside the scope.
A research analyst appears on a television channel and recommends a stock. He must:
Guarantee a target price to viewers
Ask viewers to trade only through his firm so that the trades can be tracked
Disclose any financial interest or conflict of interest he has in that stock
Avoid mentioning that he is registered with SEBI
Disclosure requirements apply to public appearances too, so viewers know of any holdings or conflicts that may affect the recommendation.
A research analyst uses an AI tool to generate parts of research reports for clients. Under SEBI's framework, the analyst is:
Prohibited from using any software in research
Required to get SEBI's prior approval for every report that is prepared with such tools
Fully responsible for the output and must disclose the use of such tools to clients
Not responsible for errors made by the AI tool
SEBI's amended framework makes analysts solely responsible for data security, confidentiality and accuracy of output generated using AI tools, with disclosure to clients.
A research analyst's compensation should NOT be:
Paid as a fixed salary
Reviewed periodically by a committee
Based on specific investment banking or brokerage transactions
Linked to the quality and accuracy of research
To maintain objectivity, analysts' pay cannot be tied to specific investment banking or brokerage transactions, though it can reflect research quality.
Under the RA Regulations, a research analyst must maintain records of research reports and the basis of recommendations so that:
The analyst can claim tax deductions
The analyst can avoid giving disclosures in reports
The rationale for each recommendation can be verified during inspection
Clients can resell the reports to other investors for a fee at a later date
Analysts must keep records of research, the data used and the rationale, and make them available to SEBI or the supervisory body during inspections.

SEBI (Investment Advisers) Regulations,.overview: This chapter covers the SEBI (Investment Advisers) Regulations, 2013, which regulate persons giving investment advice for a fee. It explains registration and exemptions, qualification and certification, net worth, the separation of advice from distribution, the investment advisory agreement, risk profiling and suitability, fee modes and limits, implementation services, disclosure of conflicts, record keeping, annual compliance audit and grievance redressal. It also covers the administration and supervisory body for advisers. Revise who must register, the duties owed to clients, rules on fees and agreements and the restrictions on earning commissions from products recommended.
questions: An investment adviser wants to help a client invest in mutual funds recommended in its advice. Under the regulations, the adviser may provide implementation services:
Through regular plans to earn trail commission
Only in schemes of the adviser's associate AMC
Only through direct plans, without earning any commission
Only if the client separately pays an extra commission to the adviser
Investment advisers may offer implementation through direct plans of mutual funds, and cannot receive commission or consideration from product providers.
Before providing investment advice, a registered investment adviser must:
Enter into an investment advisory agreement with the client
Collect fees for five years in advance
Obtain the client's demat account password
Get the client's employer to approve the advice
The regulations require an advisory agreement setting out terms, fees and the scope of services before advice is given. The agreement also covers fees and termination terms.
A mutual fund distributor describes himself as an 'independent financial adviser' on his visiting card. This is:
Permitted as long as he holds a valid ARN and has passed the relevant NISM distributor exam
Permitted after informing his AMC
Permitted if he advises fewer than 100 clients
Not permitted, as the term 'adviser' is restricted to registered investment advisers
SEBI prohibits distributors who are not registered as investment advisers from using terms like 'adviser' or 'IFA', to avoid misleading investors.
Who among the following is generally exempt from registration as an investment adviser?
An individual charging fees for stock-specific advice via an app
A firm giving portfolio advice to the public for a fixed fee
A person giving advice exclusively on insurance products regulated by IRDAI
A company providing comprehensive financial planning services to families for a fee
Persons advising only on products regulated by another regulator, like insurance agents on IRDAI products, are exempt. Paid securities advice generally needs registration.
A registered investment adviser must get an annual compliance audit conducted. The audit is meant to:
Certify the adviser's investment returns for marketing
Approve the adviser's personal investments
Check the adviser's compliance with the IA Regulations and SEBI circulars
Calculate the adviser's income-tax liability
The annual audit, conducted by a qualified auditor, verifies adherence to the regulations and circulars, and its findings must be acted upon.
An investment adviser recommends a high-risk small-cap fund to a retired client whose risk profile shows low risk tolerance. This is a breach of:
No rule at all, since the client was always free to refuse the advice given
Only the client's own responsibility to read documents
The suitability obligation, as advice must match the client's risk profile
The adviser's duty to maximise returns at any cost
Advisers must ensure that advice is suitable for the client based on risk profiling, and must not recommend products beyond the client's risk capacity.
The administration and supervisory body for investment advisers, recognised by SEBI, is responsible for:
Fixing the fees that advisers can charge
Registering new mutual fund schemes before they are launched to investors
Paying compensation to all clients of advisers
Supervising registered advisers, including inspection and monitoring
SEBI recognised a stock exchange subsidiary as the administration and supervisory body for IAs, which handles supervision, inspection and related functions.
A registered investment adviser should disclose to clients:
Any conflict of interest, including any consideration received from associates
Its competitors' fee structures
The names of its other clients
Only the positive outcomes of past advice
Advisers must disclose material conflicts, such as associate relationships or interests in recommended products, so clients can evaluate the advice.

SEBI (Debenture Trustees) Regulations, 1.overview: This chapter covers the SEBI (Debenture Trustees) Regulations, 1993, which regulate entities that act as trustees for debenture holders. It covers eligibility and capital requirements, restrictions arising from conflicts of interest, the debenture trust deed, due diligence on security and assets before issue, monitoring of covenants and asset cover, calling meetings of debenture holders, actions on default including enforcement of security, the recovery expense fund, disclosures and reporting to exchanges, and the code of conduct. When revising, focus on the trustee's duties before, during and after the issue and the steps taken when an issuer defaults.
questions: Before a secured debt issue opens, the debenture trustee must:
Underwrite the issue to ensure full subscription
Fix the coupon rate of the debentures
Allot the debentures to investors and dispatch the allotment advice to each successful applicant
Carry out due diligence on the assets proposed to be charged and the adequacy of security
Debenture trustees must exercise independent due diligence to confirm that assets are free and adequate to create the stated security before the issue.
The document setting out the terms on which the debenture trustee holds security for the benefit of debenture holders is the:
Underwriting agreement
Debenture trust deed
Memorandum of association
Red herring prospectus
The debenture trust deed, executed between the issuer and the trustee, records the security, covenants, and rights and duties of the trustee.
Issuers of listed debt securities must create a Recovery Expense Fund. This fund is used to:
Pay the debenture trustee's annual fees
Meet expenses incurred by the debenture trustee for enforcement and recovery on default
Buy back the debentures at a premium from holders who want to exit well before maturity
Pay interest to debenture holders every quarter
The Recovery Expense Fund, kept with the stock exchange, finances legal and enforcement action by the trustee if the issuer defaults.
If an issuer defaults on interest payments, the debenture trustee should:
Wait until maturity before taking any action
Reduce the interest rate on behalf of holders
Resign immediately and appoint a new trustee
Inform debenture holders, seek their consent and take steps to enforce the security
On default, the trustee must notify holders, convene meetings, follow their decisions and take action, such as enforcing security or entering inter-creditor arrangements.
Which of these would create a conflict of interest that bars an entity from acting as debenture trustee for an issue?
Being a scheduled commercial bank
Being an associate of the issuer company
Having long experience in debenture trusteeship
Having its registered office in Mumbai
An entity cannot be a debenture trustee for an issuer it is associated with, since it must act independently for the debenture holders.
A debenture trustee should periodically verify the issuer's asset cover. Asset cover refers to:
The number of debenture holders in the issue
The credit rating assigned to the issuer's parent or holding company by a CRA
The value of secured assets in relation to the outstanding debentures
The share price of the issuer company
Asset cover shows whether the charged assets are adequate to cover the outstanding principal and interest, and trustees must monitor and report it.
Debenture holders want the trustee to convene a meeting to discuss a breach of covenant. The trustee must call a meeting when requested by holders representing at least:
Every single debenture holder
One-tenth of the outstanding amount of debentures
Half of the outstanding amount of debentures
Three-fourths of the outstanding amount of debentures
The regulations require the trustee to call a meeting of debenture holders on a requisition by holders of at least one-tenth in value of the outstanding debentures.
A debenture trustee must disclose information such as defaults and breach of covenants to:
No one, as such information is confidential
Only the Registrar of Companies
Only the issuer's statutory auditor
The stock exchanges and debenture holders, as required
Trustees must report defaults, breaches and actions taken to the stock exchanges and keep debenture holders informed, as part of their transparency obligations.

SEBI (Credit Rating Agencies) Regulation.overview: This chapter covers the SEBI (Credit Rating Agencies) Regulations, 1999, which regulate entities that rate debt instruments and other securities. It covers eligibility of promoters, net worth, the rating process, rating committees, surveillance and review, rating symbols, disclosures such as rating rationales, non-cooperation by issuers and default recognition, restrictions on rating related entities, separation of non-rating businesses and the code of conduct. Revise the nature of a credit rating, the safeguards against conflicts of interest, the obligation to keep ratings under continuous surveillance and the disclosures a CRA must make to investors and the market.
questions: A credit rating agency must keep a rating under surveillance during the life of the instrument. This means it must:
Review the rating at least once a year and whenever significant developments occur
Review the rating only when the issuer requests it and pays a separate additional review fee
Withdraw the rating after the first interest payment
Never change a rating once assigned
CRAs must continuously monitor ratings, conduct at least annual reviews and act promptly on material events that may affect creditworthiness.
An issuer stops giving information to its credit rating agency. The CRA should:
Upgrade the rating to encourage cooperation
Delete the rating from its records without disclosure
Keep the rating unchanged indefinitely until the issuer resumes sharing information with it
Flag the issuer as 'not cooperating' and review the rating based on available information
Where an issuer is non-cooperative, the CRA must disclose this, flag the rating as 'issuer not cooperating' and rate based on available information.
To discourage 'rating shopping', CRAs must disclose:
Ratings that were not accepted by the issuer
The names of their own shareholders' clients
The personal holdings of the issuer's directors
The fees charged to each issuer
Disclosure of non-accepted ratings prevents issuers from seeking multiple ratings and publishing only the most favourable one. Investors can then see the full rating history of the issuer.
A credit rating decision at a CRA is taken by:
The issuer's board of directors
A rating committee, based on analysis by the rating team
The stock exchange where the debt is listed
The marketing team that obtained the mandate
Ratings are decided by a rating committee to ensure objectivity, separating rating decisions from business development and commercial considerations. Business teams cannot influence rating outcomes.
A CRA publishes a press release explaining the key factors behind a rating. This is called a:
Rating mandate
Rating agreement
Rating symbol
Rating rationale
CRAs must publish rating rationales covering the key drivers, strengths, weaknesses and outlook, so investors understand the basis of the rating.
Under SEBI norms, an issuer's failure to pay principal or interest even by one day beyond the due date is generally recognised by CRAs as:
A reason to upgrade the rating
A default
A minor delay with no rating impact
A technical error that can be ignored
CRAs follow a uniform default recognition policy in which even a one-day delay in servicing debt is treated as a default unless specific conditions apply.
Which of the following is a correct statement about a credit rating?
It reflects the market price of the security
It is not a recommendation to buy, sell or hold the instrument
It is binding on the issuer's lenders when they price their loans
It guarantees repayment of the debt
A rating is an opinion on credit risk only. It is not investment advice, it does not cover market price risk and it is not a guarantee.
A CRA also offers non-rating services such as consulting. Under the regulations, it must:
Rate only companies that also buy its consulting services
Let consultants sit on rating committees
Offer discounted rating fees to all those issuers that also take its consulting services
Keep these activities separate from rating activities to avoid conflicts of interest
CRAs must segregate non-rating activities and manage conflicts so that commercial relationships do not influence ratings. Such separation protects the credibility of ratings.

SEBI (Custodian) Regulations, 1996.overview: This chapter covers the SEBI (Custodian) Regulations, 1996, which govern entities that provide custodial services for securities and other assets. It explains what custodial services are, eligibility and net worth, separation of custodial business, obligations such as safekeeping, segregation, reconciliation and collection of corporate benefits, internal controls and audit, record keeping, and the code of conduct. It also covers custodians' roles for mutual funds and FPIs. Focus on the core services, the duty to keep client assets separate and reconciled, and restrictions on custodians that are associated with the entities they serve.
questions: A custodian must reconcile client holdings with depository records regularly in order to:
Increase its fee income from clients
Reduce the net worth it needs to maintain
Avoid informing clients of corporate actions
Detect and correct any mismatch in clients' securities promptly
Regular reconciliation ensures that the custodian's books match depository records and that client assets are accounted for correctly. Breaks must be investigated and reported promptly.
Which client typically must appoint a SEBI-registered custodian before investing in India?
A salaried employee investing via SIP
A resident individual buying shares through a broker
A foreign portfolio investor
A retail investor applying in an IPO
FPIs are required to appoint a custodian for safekeeping, settlement and regulatory reporting. Retail investors use DPs instead. DPs serve resident retail investors instead.
Under the Custodian Regulations, a custodian must have adequate internal controls. A key reason is to:
Allow the custodian to lend client securities without consent
Prevent loss, misuse or unauthorised use of client assets
Enable the custodian to trade on clients' behalf
Replace the need for audits
Internal controls, audits and checks protect client assets from errors, fraud and misuse, which is the custodian's core responsibility. Internal and external audits test these controls regularly.
A custodian receives notice of a rights issue by a company whose shares it holds for a client. It should:
Sell the client's shares to avoid the rights issue
Ignore the notice, as rights issues are optional
Inform the client promptly and act on the client's instructions
Subscribe to the rights on its own without asking, using the client's cash
Custodians must keep clients informed of corporate actions and act on their instructions, while collecting benefits such as dividends and rights.
For a mutual fund, SEBI rules restrict the appointment of a custodian that is:
Registered with SEBI for over five years
An associate in which the sponsor or its associates hold a controlling stake
Based in a different city from the asset management company's registered head office
A scheduled commercial bank
To protect independence, a custodian in which the sponsor or its associates hold 50% or more of voting rights generally cannot be the fund's custodian.
A custodian provides custodial services for gold held by a gold ETF. This is:
Prohibited, as custodians can hold only shares
Allowed only if the gold is held abroad
Permitted, as custodial services can extend to goods such as gold held by mutual funds
Allowed only for foreign investors
Custodians may provide safekeeping for goods such as gold or silver held by mutual fund schemes, in addition to securities.
Under the Custodian Regulations, a custodian must maintain records of its clients' securities and transactions so that:
Only the custodian's directors can see them, and not even SEBI inspectors
SEBI can inspect them and clients can be given accurate statements
The records can be deleted after each quarter
The custodian can sell the records to data vendors
Custodians must keep accurate and complete records for the prescribed period and make them available to SEBI and clients as required.
Which of the following is NOT ordinarily a custodial service?
Safekeeping of securities
Deciding which securities the client should buy
Informing clients of corporate actions
Collecting dividends and interest for the client
Custodians safeguard assets, settle trades and collect benefits. Investment decisions are made by the client or its fund manager, not the custodian.

Proxy Advisors.overview: This chapter covers proxy advisors, who advise institutional investors and shareholders on how to vote at company meetings. Proxy advisors register with SEBI as research analysts and follow additional norms set by SEBI. The chapter covers their role in corporate governance, the code of conduct, disclosure of voting recommendation policies and methodology, management of conflicts of interest, sharing of reports with clients and the company, procedures for company comments and grievance redressal, and the link with stewardship responsibilities of institutional investors. Revise the transparency obligations and conflict-management rules, since these are the main focus of SEBI's framework for proxy advisors.
questions: A proxy advisor must share its voting recommendation report with the company concerned:
At the same time as it shares the report with its clients
Only after the shareholder meeting is over
Never, as the report is confidential to clients
Only if the company agrees to pay a fee for receiving the report
SEBI requires proxy advisors to share reports with the company at the same time as with clients, and to include the company's comments, if any, as an addendum.
To ensure transparency, a proxy advisor must publicly disclose:
The final votes cast by each client
Its voting recommendation policies and methodology
The salaries of its analysts
The personal portfolios of its clients

Proxy advisors must disclose their policies, procedures and methodologies for voting recommendations and review them periodically. This lets clients and companies understand how recommendations are reached.
A proxy advisor provides consulting services to a company and also issues voting recommendations on that company's resolutions. This raises a concern of:
Failure to file an offer document with SEBI before advising
Insider trading by the company's shareholders
Conflict of interest, which must be disclosed and managed
Market manipulation under PFUTP
Providing consulting to a company while advising investors on its resolutions can bias recommendations, so such conflicts must be disclosed and managed.
Institutional investors such as mutual funds use proxy advisors mainly to help them:
Analyse resolutions and decide their votes as part of stewardship responsibilities
Fix the company's dividend policy and recommend the payout ratio to its board each year
Execute trades in the shares of the company
Prepare the company's annual accounts
Proxy advisors support institutional investors in meeting stewardship obligations by analysing resolutions, though the final voting decision rests with the investor.
A company disagrees with a proxy advisor's recommendation and sends its comments. The proxy advisor should:
Report the company to SEBI for interference
Withdraw its recommendation automatically
Share the company's comments with its clients along with the report
Delete the comments to avoid confusing clients
Proxy advisors must have a process to receive company comments and communicate them to clients, so that investors see both views.
A proxy advisor's voting recommendation is:
A legal opinion approved by SEBI
Advisory in nature, and the institutional investor decides how to vote
Binding on the institutional investor that subscribes to the proxy advisory service
Binding on the company's board of directors
Recommendations help investors decide but are not binding. Institutional investors remain responsible for their own voting decisions and must disclose them.
If a proxy advisor finds a factual error in a report already sent to clients, it should:
Ignore the error, since the report has already been sent and is final
Delete the report without informing clients
Issue a correction or clarification to clients promptly
Wait for the company to point it out publicly
Proxy advisors are expected to have procedures for correcting errors and informing clients promptly, maintaining the reliability of their recommendations.
Which of the following best explains why SEBI regulates proxy advisors?
They act as stock exchanges for voting rights
They hold investors' money in escrow
Their recommendations can significantly influence voting outcomes and corporate governance
They decide the listing of companies
Because institutional investors often follow proxy advice, proxy advisors affect governance outcomes, which is why SEBI requires transparency and conflict management.

Introduction to the Financial System.overview: This chapter explains how the Indian financial system moves savings from surplus units (households) to deficit units (businesses and government). It covers financial markets (money and capital, primary and secondary), financial instruments (debt, equity, hybrids), financial intermediaries and market infrastructure institutions such as stock exchanges, clearing corporations and depositories. When revising, be clear on the difference between direct and intermediated finance, the role of the secondary market in liquidity and price discovery, the maturity boundary between money and capital markets, and the priority of claims of creditors over shareholders.
questions: A company raises fresh capital by offering its shares to the public for the first time through an IPO. In which market does this transaction take place?
Over-the-counter derivatives market
Secondary market
Primary market
Money market

An IPO is a fresh issue of securities by the company itself, so the money flows to the issuer. That is the primary market. The secondary market only involves trading of already-issued securities between investors.
Which of the following is a money market instrument?
Ten-year government dated security
Equity share of a listed company
Unit of an open-ended equity mutual fund scheme
Certificate of deposit issued by a bank

Money market instruments have original maturities of up to one year and include treasury bills, commercial paper and certificates of deposit. A ten-year G-sec and equity shares are capital market instruments.
What is the core economic function of a financial system?
Collecting direct and indirect taxes for the government
Printing currency notes as required by businesses
Channelling savings from surplus units to deficit units
Fixing the prices of goods and services in the economy

A financial system mobilises savings from those with surplus funds and allocates them to those who need funds for investment or consumption. Price-setting, taxation and currency issue are not its core function.
A bank accepts one-year fixed deposits from households and uses them to give five-year term loans to small businesses. This is best described as:
Maturity transformation by a financial intermediary
Direct finance raised through the capital market by issuers
Price discovery in the secondary market
Disinvestment of public sector holdings

The bank converts short-term deposits into longer-term loans, which is maturity transformation, a key service of intermediaries. Direct finance would involve the business raising money from investors without the bank in between.
A large company sells non-convertible debentures directly to investors through a public issue instead of taking a bank loan. This is an example of:
Direct (market-based) finance
Financial repression by the regulator
Money market borrowing by the issuer
Indirect finance through a bank

When the borrower raises funds straight from investors by issuing securities, it is direct or market-based finance. A bank loan would be indirect finance because the bank stands between saver and borrower.
Which of the following is the most important benefit that an active secondary market gives to investors?
Protection from all market price risk
Fresh capital for the issuing company
A guaranteed minimum return on every investment made
Liquidity and continuous price discovery

A secondary market lets investors exit by selling to other investors and reveals fair prices through trading. It does not raise new capital for the issuer, nor does it guarantee returns or remove price risk.
Which of the following is NOT a market infrastructure institution (MII) in the Indian securities market?
A recognised clearing corporation
An asset management company
A depository
A recognised stock exchange

Stock exchanges, clearing corporations and depositories are MIIs because they provide the core trading, settlement and holding infrastructure. An asset management company is a market intermediary that manages mutual fund schemes, not an MII.
A company is being wound up. In what order are the following generally paid out of its assets?
Preference and equity shareholders share equally
Secured creditors first, equity shareholders last
All claimants are paid in proportion to holdings
Equity shareholders first, debenture holders last

Debt holders have a contractual, prior claim, with secured creditors ranking ahead of unsecured ones. Equity shareholders are residual claimants and receive only what remains after all creditors and preference holders are paid.

Regulatory Framework – General View.overview: This chapter maps India's financial regulators and the laws they administer. Learn which body regulates which segment: SEBI for securities and commodity derivatives markets, RBI for banks, NBFCs, money, government securities and foreign exchange markets, IRDAI for insurance, PFRDA for pensions and the NPS, IFSCA for GIFT City, and the Ministry of Corporate Affairs for company law. Also note coordinating bodies such as the Financial Stability and Development Council and appellate routes such as the Securities Appellate Tribunal. Focus on matching activities to the correct regulator in scenario questions.
questions: Which regulator supervises insurance companies operating in India?
IRDAI
PFRDA
NABARD
SEBI

The Insurance Regulatory and Development Authority of India (IRDAI) regulates insurers and insurance intermediaries. PFRDA regulates pension funds and the NPS, and NABARD is a development finance institution for agriculture and rural areas.
The National Pension System (NPS) and pension fund managers are regulated by:
RBI
IRDAI
PFRDA
Ministry of Corporate Affairs

The Pension Fund Regulatory and Development Authority (PFRDA) administers the NPS and registers pension fund managers. IRDAI covers insurance and RBI covers banking, so they are not the primary regulator for the NPS.
Trading in commodity futures on a national commodity derivatives exchange is currently regulated by:
RBI
Forward Markets Commission
Ministry of Consumer Affairs
SEBI
The Forward Markets Commission was merged with SEBI in 2015, and since then SEBI regulates commodity derivatives exchanges and brokers. The FMC no longer exists as a separate regulator.
The Companies Act, 2013 is administered primarily by:
Securities Appellate Tribunal
Ministry of Corporate Affairs
Department of Economic Affairs
Reserve Bank of India

The Ministry of Corporate Affairs administers the Companies Act, 2013, along with bodies such as the Registrar of Companies. SEBI administers securities-specific provisions for listed companies, but company law as a whole sits with MCA.
Which body, chaired by the Union Finance Minister, coordinates among financial sector regulators on financial stability matters?
Board for Financial Supervision of the Reserve Bank
Securities Appellate Tribunal
Monetary Policy Committee
Financial Stability and Development Council

The Financial Stability and Development Council (FSDC) is chaired by the Finance Minister and includes heads of the financial regulators. The Monetary Policy Committee sets the policy rate and is headed by the RBI Governor.
A fund manager wants to set up a fund in GIFT City, Gujarat. Which regulator will register and supervise this activity in the International Financial Services Centre?
RBI
IFSCA
SEBI
Gujarat State Government

The International Financial Services Centres Authority (IFSCA) is the unified regulator for financial services in IFSCs, including GIFT City. Fund management entities there register with IFSCA, not with SEBI.
An insurance company is aggrieved by an order passed by IRDAI. Where does its appeal lie?
Securities Appellate Tribunal
Debt Recovery Tribunal
National Company Law Tribunal
Directly to the Supreme Court

The Securities Appellate Tribunal hears appeals against orders of SEBI, and its jurisdiction has been extended to orders of IRDAI and PFRDA. NCLT handles company law and insolvency matters, not insurance regulatory orders.
Which of the following markets is primarily regulated by RBI rather than SEBI?
Units of mutual fund schemes
Listed equity shares on stock exchanges
Government securities and money market
Units of REITs and InvITs
RBI regulates the government securities, money and foreign exchange markets. Listed equities, mutual funds, REITs and InvITs all fall under SEBI's jurisdiction as part of the securities market.

Introduction to Compliance.overview: This chapter introduces compliance as a function that helps a regulated entity follow laws, regulations, internal policies and codes of conduct. Understand compliance risk (the risk of legal or regulatory sanctions, financial loss or loss of reputation), the importance of an independent compliance function with direct access to the board, the 'tone at the top', and the three lines of defence model. Revise how compliance policies, training, monitoring, testing and escalation work together, and the difference between preventive and detective controls. Expect scenario questions on what a compliance officer should do when a breach is found.
questions: Compliance risk is best described as the risk of:
Legal or regulatory sanctions, financial loss or reputational damage from not following rules
Loss due to changes in the market price of securities held in a portfolio
Loss caused by a sudden lack of buyers for an asset being sold
Default by a borrower or counterparty on its contractual obligations

Compliance risk arises from failing to comply with laws, regulations, codes and internal standards, leading to sanctions, financial loss or reputational harm. Market, credit and liquidity risk are separate risk types.
Why should the compliance function of a fund intermediary be independent of its business teams?
So that compliance staff can earn incentives linked to sales volumes
So that compliance does not need to report to the board at all
So it can assess and report breaches objectively without pressure from revenue targets
So that business heads can review and approve all compliance reports before they are submitted

Independence lets compliance staff challenge business decisions and escalate breaches without conflict. Linking compliance pay to sales or routing reports through business heads would undermine that objectivity.
In the 'three lines of defence' model, which function is generally regarded as the third line?
Compliance and risk management
Internal audit
Business and operations teams
External statutory auditors

Business units are the first line, compliance and risk management form the second line, and internal audit provides independent assurance as the third line. Statutory auditors are external to the model.
Ultimate responsibility for ensuring that an asset management company complies with regulations rests with:
The registrar and transfer agent
The mutual fund distributors empanelled by the AMC
Its board of directors and senior management
Only the compliance officer personally

The compliance officer monitors and advises, but accountability for compliance lies with the board and senior management, who set the 'tone at the top'. Distributors and RTAs have their own obligations but do not bear the AMC's overall responsibility.
A compliance officer finds that a scheme breached an investment limit. The business head asks her not to record it because the position has since been corrected. What should she do?
Delete the record since the position is now within the limit
Wait until the next audit to see if the auditor notices it
Ask the fund manager to sign an undertaking and then quietly close the matter without any report
Document the breach and escalate it as per policy and regulatory reporting requirements

Even corrected breaches must be recorded, reported to the board or trustees and to the regulator where required. Hiding a breach is itself a serious compliance failure and damages the integrity of the function.
Which of the following is a preventive compliance control rather than a detective one?
Training employees on new SEBI circulars before they take effect
Reviewing trade logs after month-end to find exceptions
Investigating a complaint received through SCORES
Conducting an internal audit of all of last year's completed transactions
Preventive controls stop breaches before they occur, such as training, approvals and system checks. Post-facto reviews, audits and complaint investigations detect problems that have already happened.
What does the phrase 'tone at the top' mean in the context of compliance?
Top-performing sales staff being exempt from compliance checks
Senior leadership visibly committing to ethical conduct and regulatory compliance
Compliance officers being seated on the top floor of the head office building
Regulators issuing directions only to large listed entities

'Tone at the top' refers to the ethical climate set by the board and senior managers. When leaders prioritise compliance, staff follow; exempting top performers from checks would send the opposite message.
An AMC's compliance team checks a sample of completed transactions each quarter against internal policies and regulatory limits. This activity is called:
Valuation of the scheme's assets
Credit rating of the scheme portfolio
Statutory audit of financial statements
Compliance testing and monitoring

Periodic sample checks against rules are compliance monitoring and testing, which help confirm that controls work. A statutory audit focuses on financial statements, while rating and valuation are different processes.

SEBI Act, 1992.overview: This chapter covers the SEBI Act, 1992, which gave SEBI statutory status to protect investors and to develop and regulate the securities market. Revise SEBI's composition, its functions and powers under Sections 11, 11B and 11C, the requirement for intermediaries to register under Section 12, and the penalty framework under Chapter VI-A imposed by adjudicating officers. Also learn the settlement mechanism, the appellate route to the Securities Appellate Tribunal and then the Supreme Court, and where penalty amounts are credited. Questions often test who exercises a power and the appeal time limits.
questions: SEBI was set up in 1988 as a non-statutory body. In which year did it get statutory powers through an Act of Parliament?

SEBI was constituted in 1988 by a government resolution and acquired statutory status under the SEBI Act, 1992. 1996 is the year of the Depositories Act, and 2002 saw major amendments to the SEBI Act.
A firm wants to start business as a portfolio manager. Under the SEBI Act, what must it do before commencing activity?
Obtain a certificate of registration from SEBI
Register only with the Registrar of Companies
Obtain a licence from the Reserve Bank of India
Seek approval from a recognised stock exchange

Section 12 of the SEBI Act prohibits any intermediary such as a portfolio manager, broker or investment adviser from dealing in securities without a certificate of registration from SEBI. ROC incorporation alone is not sufficient.
One member of the SEBI board is nominated from which of the following institutions?
Reserve Bank of India
Insurance Regulatory and Development Authority of India
Comptroller and Auditor General of India
National Stock Exchange
The SEBI board includes a Chairman, two members from the Central Government ministries, one member from RBI and five other members. No member is nominated from IRDAI, a stock exchange or the CAG.
SEBI wants to direct a mutual fund to refund money to investors to protect their interests. Under which provision does SEBI generally issue such directions?
Section 12 of the SEBI Act
Section 15Z of the SEBI Act
Section 26 of the SEBI Act
Section 11B of the SEBI Act

Section 11B empowers SEBI to issue directions to any person or intermediary in the interest of investors or orderly development of the market. Section 12 deals with registration and Section 15Z with appeals to the Supreme Court.
A broker is aggrieved by an order of the Securities Appellate Tribunal. Within how many days of communication of the order may it appeal to the Supreme Court?
30 days
60 days
45 days
90 days

Under Section 15Z, an appeal against a SAT decision lies to the Supreme Court within 60 days, extendable by up to another 60 days for sufficient cause. The 45-day limit applies to appeals from SEBI orders to SAT.
A registered intermediary facing SEBI proceedings wants to resolve the matter without admitting or denying the findings. Which route can it use?
Request the stock exchange to withdraw the case
Surrender its registration to end the proceedings
File a writ petition before the Securities Appellate Tribunal immediately
Apply for settlement under the SEBI settlement proceedings framework

SEBI's settlement framework allows a noticee to settle administrative and civil proceedings by paying a settlement amount, without admission or denial of guilt. Surrendering registration does not automatically end proceedings already initiated.
Under Chapter VI-A of the SEBI Act, monetary penalties for specified defaults are imposed by:
The Securities Appellate Tribunal on its own
The Central Government through a notification
An adjudicating officer appointed by SEBI
The stock exchange where the default occurred
SEBI appoints adjudicating officers to hold inquiries and impose penalties under Chapter VI-A. SAT is an appellate body, and stock exchanges act under their own bye-laws, not Chapter VI-A.
Penalty amounts realised by SEBI under the SEBI Act are credited to:
The investor's demat account directly
SEBI's own General Fund for salaries
The Consolidated Fund of India
The Settlement Guarantee Fund of the exchange

Section 15JA requires sums realised by way of penalties to be credited to the Consolidated Fund of India. Disgorged amounts are handled separately, for example through the Investor Protection and Education Fund.

SCRA, 1956 and SCRR, 1957.overview: This chapter covers the Securities Contracts (Regulation) Act, 1956 and the Securities Contracts (Regulation) Rules, 1957, which regulate stock exchanges, securities contracts and listing. Revise the wide definition of 'securities', recognition of stock exchanges, corporatisation and demutualisation, the legality of spot delivery and derivative contracts, delisting and the right of appeal to SAT, and the minimum public shareholding requirement under the SCRR. Focus on what is and is not a security and on the powers to recognise and supervise exchanges and clearing corporations.
questions: Which of the following is NOT a 'security' as defined under the SCRA, 1956?
Units issued by a mutual fund scheme to investors
A government security
An equity derivative contract
A fixed deposit placed with a commercial bank

The SCRA definition includes shares, bonds, derivatives, units of mutual funds and collective investment schemes, government securities and similar instruments. A bank fixed deposit is a deposit, not a marketable security.
Under the SCRR, 1957, a listed company must generally maintain public shareholding of at least:

Rule 19A of the SCRR requires every listed company (other than certain exempted public sector or specified cases) to maintain minimum public shareholding of 25%. If it falls below, the company must restore it within the specified time.
Under the SCRA, a 'spot delivery contract' is one that provides for:
Delivery on a fixed date one year after the trade date
Delivery and payment on the same day or the next day
Delivery within one month of the trade date
Settlement by paying only the price difference

Spot delivery contracts involve actual delivery of securities and payment of price on the same day or the next day. Contracts settled only by price differences or for future dates are forward or derivative contracts.
What does 'demutualisation' of a stock exchange under the SCRA mean?
Merger of two or more stock exchanges into one
Conversion of the exchange into a department of the Ministry of Finance
Closure of the exchange and transfer of its members
Segregation of ownership and management from trading rights of members

Demutualisation separates ownership and management of the exchange from the trading rights of its members, reducing conflicts of interest. Under a mutual structure, broker-members owned and ran the exchange.
A recognised stock exchange delists the securities of a company. Where can the company appeal against this decision?
Reserve Bank of India
National Consumer Disputes Redressal Commission
Securities Appellate Tribunal
Registrar of Companies

Section 21A of the SCRA permits a listed company or an aggrieved investor to appeal to SAT against a delisting decision of a recognised stock exchange. Consumer forums and the ROC have no role in delisting appeals.
A recognised stock exchange is granted recognition under the SCRA. In practice, this power is exercised by:
The exchange's own board of directors
The Reserve Bank of India for all exchanges
SEBI, to which the Central Government has delegated the power
The Ministry of Corporate Affairs through the Registrar of Companies
Recognition of stock exchanges under Section 4 is a Central Government power that has been delegated to SEBI. SEBI therefore grants, renews and can withdraw recognition of stock exchanges.

Two parties enter into a derivative contract on a stock outside any recognised exchange and without any clearing arrangement. Under Section 18A of the SCRA, derivative contracts are legal and valid when they are:
Approved individually by the Central Government in advance
Traded on a recognised exchange and settled through its clearing house or corporation
Registered with the Registrar of Companies within 30 days
Signed by both parties on stamp paper before a notary public

Section 18A makes derivative contracts legal and valid if they are traded on a recognised stock exchange and settled on its clearing house or a recognised clearing corporation, as per its rules and bye-laws. Notarisation or ROC filing does not validate them.
Under the SCRA, which body may make or amend the bye-laws of a recognised stock exchange, subject to approval?
The recognised stock exchange itself, with SEBI's previous approval
Any group of investors holding its shares, through a resolution passed at a meeting
The listed companies through a joint resolution
The Comptroller and Auditor General of India

A recognised stock exchange may make bye-laws for regulating contracts, subject to SEBI's previous approval, and SEBI can also make or amend bye-laws itself. Investors, listed companies or the CAG cannot do so.

SEBI (Intermediaries) Regulations, 2008.overview: These regulations give a common framework for registration and supervision of SEBI intermediaries such as brokers, depository participants, merchant bankers and portfolio managers. Revise the registration process and validity of the certificate, the 'fit and proper person' criteria and who must satisfy them, the general obligations and code of conduct, appointment of a compliance officer, investor grievance redressal through SCORES, and the procedure for action in case of default, including the designated authority, show cause notices, suspension and cancellation. Learn what an intermediary must do for its clients when registration is cancelled.
questions: Under the Intermediaries Regulations, the 'fit and proper person' criteria apply to:
Only employees in the sales and marketing team
Only the statutory auditor appointed by the intermediary
The applicant and its principal officer, directors, promoters and key managerial persons
Only the individual clients who open trading or demat accounts with the intermediary

Fit and proper criteria apply to the applicant or intermediary as well as its principal officer, directors, promoters, persons in control and key managerial persons. Clients, auditors or sales staff are not the subject of these criteria.
At what stage must an intermediary satisfy the 'fit and proper person' criteria?
Only at the time of applying for initial registration
At the time of registration and on a continuous basis thereafter
Only when SEBI conducts a periodic inspection of the intermediary
Only when the intermediary renews its office lease
Being fit and proper is a continuing requirement, not a one-time check. If a person later ceases to meet the criteria, SEBI can take action against the intermediary.
Which online platform does SEBI use for receiving and tracking investor complaints against registered intermediaries?
MCA21
CERSAI
SCORES
e-FRRO

SCORES (SEBI Complaints Redress System) lets investors lodge complaints online, and intermediaries must respond within the timelines prescribed. MCA21 is the corporate affairs portal and CERSAI maintains CKYC and security interest records.
In proceedings for action in case of default, which officer examines the matter and submits a report with recommendations to SEBI?
The designated authority
The statutory auditor
The intermediary's compliance officer
The Securities Appellate Tribunal

The Intermediaries Regulations provide for a designated authority to issue a show cause notice, consider replies and submit a report recommending action such as suspension or cancellation. SAT only hears appeals after an order is passed.
SEBI has cancelled the registration of a stock broker. What is the broker required to do in respect of its clients?
Transfer client securities to its promoters for safe custody
Keep client money until the appeal period is over, without exception
Continue trading for existing clients until their contracts expire
Stop the activity and allow clients to withdraw or transfer their funds and securities

On cancellation, the intermediary must cease the activity, allow clients to withdraw or transfer their securities and funds, and hand over records as directed. Continuing to trade or moving assets to promoters would be a violation.
Under the Intermediaries Regulations, a certificate of registration once granted is generally:
Valid only until the intermediary changes its auditor
Permanent, unless suspended or cancelled, subject to payment of fees
Valid for five years and automatically lapses after that period ends
Valid for one year and renewable every financial year

The regulations provide for a permanent certificate of registration, subject to payment of applicable fees and continued compliance. It remains valid unless SEBI suspends or cancels it or the intermediary surrenders it.
An intermediary wishes to give up its registration voluntarily. What should it ensure before SEBI accepts the surrender?
Pending client obligations and complaints are settled or suitably provided for
Its employees are transferred to another SEBI intermediary
Its shares are listed on a recognised stock exchange first
Its competitors and industry associations are informed about the surrender in writing

SEBI accepts surrender after it is satisfied that client interests are protected, for example that pending obligations, assets and complaints are dealt with. Informing competitors or listing shares has no bearing on surrender.
Who is generally responsible within an intermediary for monitoring adherence to securities laws and for redressal of investor grievances?
The SEBI regional office in that city
The statutory auditor appointed by the intermediary's shareholders
The largest client of the intermediary
The compliance officer appointed by the intermediary

Intermediaries must appoint a compliance officer who monitors compliance with the Act, rules, regulations and circulars and handles investor grievances. The auditor reviews accounts, and SEBI's regional office is the regulator, not an internal officer.

SEBI (Prohibition of Insider Trading) Re.overview: This chapter covers the SEBI (Prohibition of Insider Trading) Regulations, 2015. Revise the definitions of insider, connected person, generally available information and UPSI, the restrictions on communicating or procuring UPSI and the 'legitimate purposes' exception, trading plans and their approval and disclosure, the trading window, and the code of conduct for designated persons including pre-clearance and the contra trade restriction. Also learn the disclosure regime (initial and continual disclosures), the structured digital database, the Chief Investor Relations Officer under the fair disclosure code, and the consequences of violations.
questions: A person is treated as a 'connected person' if, in the company's context, he was associated with it during what period before the concerned act?
Three years
One year
Six months
One month

The PIT Regulations treat a person as connected if, during the six months prior to the concerned act, he was associated with the company in a way that gives or may reasonably be expected to give access to UPSI.
Which of the following is 'generally available information' under the PIT Regulations?
Draft results shared with the statutory auditor for review
Board discussions on a proposed acquisition that is not yet announced
A merger proposal circulated among the deal team only
Quarterly results disseminated through the stock exchange platform

Generally available information is information accessible to the public on a non-discriminatory basis, such as results published through the exchange. Draft results and unannounced deal discussions are still UPSI.
A company plans to share UPSI with a merchant banker for due diligence on a proposed acquisition. Under the regulations, this sharing is permitted only if it is:
Approved verbally by any director of the company
For legitimate purposes, performance of duties or discharge of legal obligations
Communicated only through a private messaging app
Paid for by the merchant banker at a fair price

UPSI may be communicated only in furtherance of legitimate purposes, performance of duties or discharge of legal obligations, and recipients must be bound by confidentiality. Approval by any director or the mode of communication does not make it lawful.
An insider wants to trade under a trading plan. Under the PIT Regulations, the trading plan must be:
Approved by the auditor and published in newspapers
Registered with the depository and kept with the DP
Approved by the compliance officer and disclosed to the stock exchanges
Approved by SEBI and kept strictly confidential by the company until expiry

A trading plan is presented to the compliance officer for approval and, once approved, is notified to the stock exchanges where the securities are listed. SEBI, the auditor and the DP do not approve trading plans.
A designated person buys shares of his company. Under the code of conduct, he generally cannot sell them (enter a contra trade) within the next:
One month
Six months
One year
Three months

Designated persons must not execute a contra trade within six months of a trade. If one is executed in violation, the profits are liable to be disgorged and remitted to the Investor Protection and Education Fund.
A director of a listed company trades its shares worth a total of ₹12 lakh during a calendar quarter. Under continual disclosure, he must inform the company because the value exceeds:
₹10 lakh in a calendar quarter
₹5 lakh in a single day
₹1 crore in a calendar quarter
₹25 lakh in a financial year

Promoters, directors, KMP and designated persons must disclose trades whose aggregate value exceeds ₹10 lakh in a calendar quarter within two trading days. The company then informs the stock exchanges within two trading days.
The board of a listed company must ensure maintenance of which record of persons with whom UPSI is shared?
A newspaper notice listing all such recipients
A physical register signed only by the Chairman
A list of names handed over to the statutory auditor once every financial year
A structured digital database with names and PAN or other identifiers

The PIT Regulations require a structured digital database containing the nature of UPSI shared and names and PAN (or other identifiers) of persons with whom it is shared, with adequate internal controls such as time-stamping and audit trails.
Under the Code of Practices and Procedures for Fair Disclosure, which official deals with universal dissemination and disclosure of UPSI?
Chief Investor Relations Officer
Chief Risk Officer
Registrar and transfer agent
Company's statutory auditor

Listed companies must designate a senior officer as Chief Investor Relations Officer to deal with dissemination of information and disclosure of UPSI. The RTA and auditor have no role in fair disclosure of UPSI.

SEBI (PFUTP) Regulations, 2003.overview: This chapter covers the SEBI (Prohibition of Fraudulent and Unfair Trade Practices relating to Securities Market) Regulations, 2003. Learn the broad definition of 'fraud' and the list of prohibited practices: creating a false appearance of trading, price manipulation, circular and wash trades, front running, spreading false or misleading information, mis-selling of securities or services, and misuse of client funds or securities. Note that the prohibitions apply to any person, not only intermediaries, and revise the penalty and enforcement powers available to SEBI. Expect scenario questions where you must identify the specific prohibited practice.
questions: A dealer at a broking firm learns of a large buy order from an institutional client and buys the same stock in his own account just before placing the client's order. This practice is called:
Front running
Bear raiding
Insider trading
Circular trading

Trading ahead of a substantial client order using knowledge of that order is front running, specifically prohibited under PFUTP. Insider trading involves UPSI about the company, which is a different offence.
A group of connected entities repeatedly buy and sell the same shares among themselves to create an impression of heavy trading interest. This is:
A legitimate block deal executed through the separate trading window
Hedging of an existing portfolio position
Circular trading to create a false appearance of volume
Arbitrage between two stock exchanges

Trades among a closed group that create artificial volumes or prices are circular trades, a manipulative practice. Arbitrage and hedging are legitimate strategies, and block deals follow a separate disclosed mechanism.
Trades in which the buyer and seller are the same person, so there is no real change in beneficial ownership, are known as:
Odd-lot trades
Wash trades
Spot trades
Bulk deals

Wash trades do not transfer beneficial ownership and only create a misleading appearance of trading. PFUTP prohibits any act that creates a false or misleading appearance of trading in the securities market.
A person posts fabricated 'insider tips' about a small company on social media and sells his holdings after the price jumps. This is best described as:
An offer for sale through the stock exchange
A permitted expression of personal investment opinion
A buy-back of shares by the company
A 'pump and dump' scheme using false information

Spreading false or misleading information to inflate a price and then selling is a fraudulent and manipulative practice under PFUTP. Genuine, honest opinion is different from knowingly circulating false tips.

A distributor sells a high-risk credit risk debt scheme to an 80-year-old retired investor seeking capital safety, without checking suitability or explaining risks. Under PFUTP, this is an example of:
Legitimate portfolio rebalancing
A permitted execution-only transaction by the distributor
Mis-selling of units of a mutual fund scheme
Market making in mutual fund units

PFUTP treats mis-selling to include selling without reasonable regard to the investor's suitability and without disclosing risk factors. Ignoring the investor's risk profile and needs amounts to mis-selling.
To whom do the prohibitions under the PFUTP Regulations apply?
Only listed companies, their promoters and the directors on their boards
Only foreign portfolio investors
Only stock brokers registered with SEBI
Any person dealing in securities, whether or not a SEBI intermediary

PFUTP prohibitions are framed as 'no person shall', so they cover any person dealing in securities, including investors, companies and intermediaries. Restricting them to brokers or listed companies is incorrect.
Under Section 15HA of the SEBI Act, the penalty for fraudulent and unfair trade practices can extend to:
₹1 lakh or the amount of profit made by the person, whichever is lower
₹25 crore or three times the profits made, whichever is higher
₹10 lakh only, irrespective of profit made
Twice the brokerage earned on the trades

Section 15HA provides a penalty of not less than ₹5 lakh, which may extend to ₹25 crore or three times the profits made, whichever is higher. The fixed lower amounts in the other options are not correct.
A broker uses securities lying in Client A's account to meet the pay-in obligation of Client B without authorisation. Under PFUTP, this is:
Misuse of client securities, a prohibited fraudulent practice
An approved securities lending transaction
Permitted if Client B repays within a week
A normal netting practice allowed for all brokers under exchange bye-laws

Using one client's funds or securities for another client or for the broker's own purpose without authority is a fraudulent practice. Securities lending is permitted only through the approved SLB mechanism with consent.

Prevention of Money Laundering Act, 2002.overview: This chapter explains the PMLA, 2002, the PML Rules and SEBI's AML/CFT guidelines applicable to intermediaries such as AMCs, brokers and depository participants. Learn the stages of money laundering (placement, layering, integration), the role of FIU-IND, client due diligence including beneficial ownership thresholds and enhanced due diligence for high-risk clients such as politically exposed persons, the duties of the Principal Officer and Designated Director, reporting obligations (CTR, STR) and their timelines, record retention, and the ban on tipping off. Scenario questions usually ask how to treat an unusual transaction pattern.
questions: In the money laundering process, moving illegal funds through a series of complex transactions to hide their source is known as:
Placement
Structuring
Integration
Layering

Placement introduces illicit cash into the financial system, layering obscures its trail through multiple transactions, and integration brings it back as apparently legitimate money. Structuring is breaking amounts to avoid reporting thresholds.
Once a reporting entity is satisfied that a transaction is suspicious, within what time must it file a Suspicious Transaction Report with FIU-IND?
24 hours
7 working days
30 days
15 days

Under the PML Rules, an STR must be furnished within seven working days of the Principal Officer arriving at a conclusion that the transaction is suspicious. Delay in reaching that conclusion should also be avoided.
Under the PMLA, records of transactions and client identification must generally be maintained for at least:
Three years
Ten years
Five years
One year

Section 12 of the PMLA requires reporting entities to maintain transaction records and identity records for five years from the date of transaction or end of the business relationship, as applicable. Longer retention may apply if investigations are pending.
Under the PML Rules, for a client that is a company, a natural person is a beneficial owner if he has a controlling ownership interest of more than:
10% of shares, capital or profits
5% of shares, capital or profits
51% of shares, capital or profits
25% of shares, capital or profits

Following the 2023 amendment to the PML Rules, the threshold for a company is ownership or entitlement of more than 10% of shares, capital or profits, or control through other means. The earlier threshold was 25%.
FIU-IND, the central agency for receiving and analysing financial intelligence, functions under:
Securities and Exchange Board of India
Ministry of Home Affairs
Reserve Bank of India
Department of Revenue, Ministry of Finance

The Financial Intelligence Unit – India is an independent body reporting to the Economic Intelligence Council and functions under the Department of Revenue, Ministry of Finance. It is not part of SEBI or RBI.
An AMC has filed an STR on a client. The client calls the AMC asking whether any report has been made about him. What should the staff do?
Withdraw the STR if the client gives an explanation
Confirm the report so the client can explain the transactions
Not disclose the STR, as tipping off the client is prohibited
Send the client a copy of the STR for his records
Reporting entities and their staff must keep STRs strictly confidential and must not tip off the client. The STR, once filed, is not withdrawn because the client offers an explanation.
