A wealthy client who is a serving senior government official abroad wants to open a mutual fund folio. Under SEBI's AML guidelines, the intermediary should:
Apply enhanced due diligence and obtain senior management approval
Refuse to open the account automatically, whatever the source of funds or documents
Open the account immediately without additional checks
Accept the account only if the investment is in cash

Politically exposed persons are high-risk clients; intermediaries must apply enhanced due diligence, verify source of funds and obtain senior management approval. An automatic refusal is not required.
Under the PML Rules, the person designated by a reporting entity to ensure overall compliance with PMLA obligations, usually a whole-time director, is the:
Nodal Investor Officer
Designated Director
Compliance Auditor
Principal Officer

The Designated Director ensures overall compliance with PMLA obligations and is typically the managing or a whole-time director. The Principal Officer is responsible for furnishing information and reports to FIU-IND.

SEBI (KYC Registration Agency) Regulatio.overview: This chapter covers the SEBI (KYC Registration Agency) Regulations, 2011 and the KYC framework for the securities market. Understand why KRAs were created (one-time KYC that can be used across intermediaries), the obligations of intermediaries to perform KYC and upload records, the obligations of KRAs to maintain, validate and protect data, interoperability between KRAs, and the link with the Central KYC Records Registry maintained by CERSAI. Revise the newer requirement for KRAs to validate key KYC attributes and the treatment of records whose details cannot be verified.
questions: What is the main purpose of setting up KYC Registration Agencies in the securities market?
To collect brokerage and other charges on behalf of all stock brokers
To let a client complete KYC once and use it across intermediaries
To issue PAN cards to new investors
To settle trades between clearing members
KRAs centralise KYC records so that an investor who has completed KYC with one SEBI intermediary need not repeat the full process with others. Issuing PAN or settling trades is not their function.
After completing the KYC of a new client, who is responsible for uploading the KYC details to the KRA system?
The client himself through the stock exchange
The depository with which the client later opens a demat account
The SEBI-registered intermediary that performed the KYC
SEBI's regional office in the client's state

The intermediary that performs initial KYC, including verification, must upload the details and documents to the KRA within the prescribed time. The client and SEBI do not upload KYC records themselves.
An investor who is already KYC-compliant on a KRA opens an account with a new broker. What can the broker generally do?
Open the account without seeing any KYC record at all
Refuse the account because KYC was done by another intermediary
Insist on fresh in-person verification and a full set of new documents in all cases
Fetch and rely on the KRA record, doing additional checks only where needed

The KRA framework allows a new intermediary to download and rely on the existing KYC record, carrying out additional due diligence if its own risk policy requires. Repeating full KYC every time defeats the purpose of KRAs.
Under the KRA framework, what happens when key attributes of a client's KYC record (such as PAN, address, mobile number or email) cannot be validated?
The intermediary is fined automatically by the stock exchange for the error
The record is permanently deleted without any notice
The client's securities are automatically sold by the KRA
The record may be placed 'on hold' until the attributes are verified

KRAs now validate key KYC attributes against official sources. Records that fail validation may be marked 'on hold', and the client must update or re-verify details before transacting. No automatic sale or deletion takes place.
Which statement about interoperability among KRAs is correct?
An intermediary can access a client's KYC record through any KRA
A client must complete KYC with each KRA separately
Each intermediary must register with every KRA separately for each client
Only the KRA that first stored the record can ever view it
KRAs are required to be interoperable, so a KYC record uploaded to one KRA can be accessed by intermediaries connected to another KRA. The client does not need separate KYC for each KRA.
A KRA wants to use the KYC data in its system to sell targeted marketing lists to a third party. Under the KRA Regulations, this is:
Not permitted, as KRAs must maintain confidentiality of KYC data
Permitted after informing the stock exchanges
Permitted if the third party buying the data is a SEBI-registered intermediary
Permitted if the data is more than five years old
KRAs must keep KYC records confidential and use them only for the purposes permitted under the regulations. Selling client data for marketing breaches these obligations, regardless of the buyer.
The Central KYC Records Registry (CKYCR) assigns each customer a KYC Identification Number (KIN) of how many digits?
CKYCR, maintained by CERSAI, issues a 14-digit KYC Identification Number that the customer can quote to other regulated entities. A 10-character code is a PAN and a 12-digit number is Aadhaar.
Which of the following is a duty of an intermediary under the KRA Regulations?
Prescribe the KYC forms and formats to be used across the entire securities market
Approve the registration of other KRAs
Carry out initial KYC and in-person verification before uploading
Audit the KRA's systems every month

The intermediary performs initial KYC, including in-person verification where required, and uploads the record. SEBI registers KRAs and prescribes KYC formats, while system audits of KRAs are not the intermediary's job.

SEBI (Foreign Portfolio Investors) Regul.overview: This chapter covers the SEBI (Foreign Portfolio Investors) Regulations, 2019, which govern portfolio investment in India by foreign entities. Revise the two categories of FPIs and their eligibility, who cannot register as an FPI, the role of Designated Depository Participants, jurisdictional requirements relating to IOSCO and FATF, the investment limit for a single FPI or investor group and the consequences of breaching it, and the rules on issue of offshore derivative instruments (ODIs). Focus on classification scenarios and the 10% investment limit.
questions: Under the SEBI (FPI) Regulations, 2019, foreign portfolio investors are classified into how many categories?
Three
Five
Two
Four

The 2019 regulations simplified the earlier three-category system into two categories, Category I and Category II, based on the nature and regulation of the investor. Categorisation affects KYC and some investment conditions.
A single FPI, together with its investor group, must hold less than what share of the total paid-up equity capital of an Indian company on a fully diluted basis?

Investment by a single FPI including its investor group must be below 10% of the company's total paid-up equity capital on a fully diluted basis. If this is breached, the FPI must divest within the permitted time or the holding is reclassified as FDI.
An FPI's holding in a listed company crosses the individual investment limit. What are its options under the regulations?
Keep the excess holding indefinitely if the investee company's board does not object
Divest the excess within five trading days or have it reclassified as FDI
Convert the excess shares into a bank fixed deposit
Transfer the excess shares to a resident Indian relative

If the limit is breached, the FPI may divest the excess holding within five trading days of the settlement of the trades or the investment is treated as FDI, subject to FDI conditions. Other options listed are not permitted.
Who among the following CANNOT register as a foreign portfolio investor?
A non-resident Indian investing in his individual capacity
A regulated foreign mutual fund
A foreign pension fund that is appropriately regulated in its home country
A foreign central bank

NRIs and OCIs investing as individuals have their own investment routes and cannot register as FPIs, though they may be constituents of an FPI within limits. Foreign pension funds, central banks and regulated funds can register.
Offshore derivative instruments (such as participatory notes) with Indian securities as underlying can be issued only by:
Indian stock brokers to foreign clients
Indian mutual funds through their overseas offices
Category I FPIs, subject to SEBI conditions
Any Category II FPI without restriction

ODIs can be issued only by Category I FPIs (other than certain excluded types), subject to KYC, reporting and other conditions. Category II FPIs, Indian brokers and mutual funds are not allowed to issue them.
To be eligible for FPI registration, an applicant should generally be a resident of a country whose securities market regulator:
Has been in existence for at least 50 years
Is a member of the Indian Banks' Association and has an office in India
Has a permanent office located in Mumbai
Is a signatory to the IOSCO MMoU or has a bilateral MoU with SEBI

An FPI applicant must be from a jurisdiction whose securities regulator is a signatory to the IOSCO Multilateral MoU or has a bilateral MoU with SEBI, and it must not be from a jurisdiction identified by FATF as high-risk.
A Designated Depository Participant (DDP) under the FPI framework is generally:
A custodian or bank that is a depository participant approved by SEBI
A credit rating agency registered with SEBI
A stock exchange or clearing house located in the investor's home country
Any individual chartered accountant in India
DDPs are SEBI-approved entities, typically custodians that are also authorised dealer banks and depository participants. They grant FPI registration on SEBI's behalf and carry out KYC and monitoring.
A sovereign wealth fund and an unregulated family office both apply for FPI registration. Which is the correct classification?
Sovereign wealth fund as Category II; family office as Category I
Both as Category II
Both as Category I
Sovereign wealth fund as Category I; family office as Category II

Government and government-related investors such as sovereign wealth funds fall in Category I. Unregulated family offices and individuals fall in Category II, which carries different KYC requirements.

Foreign Exchange Management Act.overview: This chapter covers the Foreign Exchange Management Act, 1999, which aims to facilitate external trade and payments and promote orderly development of India's foreign exchange market. Revise the definitions of 'person resident in India', current account and capital account transactions, the role of RBI and authorised persons, the Liberalised Remittance Scheme, FDI under automatic and approval routes, and the civil nature of contraventions with penalties, compounding and investigation by the Directorate of Enforcement. Practise classifying transactions and identifying the correct authority for each action.
questions: Which of the following is a current account transaction under FEMA?
A long-term loan raised from a foreign lender
Payment for imported goods in the ordinary course of business
Purchase of a residential flat abroad by a resident
Acquisition of shares of a foreign company by a resident individual

Current account transactions do not alter assets or liabilities outside India; payments for imports, travel and services are typical examples. Buying foreign property or shares and raising foreign loans are capital account transactions.
Under FEMA, a person is generally a 'person resident in India' if he has resided in India for more than how many days in the preceding financial year?
365 days
90 days
182 days
120 days

FEMA treats a person as resident if he resided in India for more than 182 days during the preceding financial year, subject to conditions about the purpose of stay. Leaving India for employment or business can change this status.
Under the Liberalised Remittance Scheme, a resident individual can currently remit up to what amount per financial year for permitted transactions?
The LRS allows resident individuals to remit up to US$ 250,000 per financial year for permitted current and capital account transactions, such as education, travel and overseas investment.
Which agency investigates contraventions of FEMA?
FIU-IND
Serious Fraud Investigation Office
Central Bureau of Investigation
Directorate of Enforcement

The Directorate of Enforcement is empowered to investigate contraventions under FEMA and also enforces the PMLA. SFIO deals with corporate frauds under the Companies Act, and FIU-IND collects and analyses financial intelligence.
Where the amount involved in a FEMA contravention is quantifiable, the maximum penalty is up to:
Twice the sum involved
₹2 lakh irrespective of the amount
Three times the sum involved
The sum involved plus interest
Section 13 of FEMA provides a penalty of up to three times the sum involved where quantifiable, or up to ₹2 lakh where it is not, plus a further daily penalty for continuing contraventions.
A bank authorised by RBI to deal in foreign exchange is known under FEMA as an:
Approved intermediary
Authorised person (authorised dealer)
Designated depository participant
Accredited investor

Under Section 10 of FEMA, RBI can authorise persons such as banks to deal in foreign exchange; banks so authorised are authorised dealers. DDPs and accredited investors are SEBI concepts, not FEMA terms.
A foreign company invests in an Indian company in a sector open to 100% FDI under the automatic route. What approval is needed before the investment?
Prior approval of SEBI's board
Prior approval of the Union Cabinet in every case, irrespective of the amount invested
Prior approval of the State Government
No prior government approval; only post-investment reporting is required

Under the automatic route, no prior approval of the Government or RBI is needed; the investee company must report the investment within the prescribed timelines. The approval route applies only to specified sectors or limits.
A resident realises he has made an inadvertent technical contravention of FEMA. Which mechanism lets him settle it by paying a sum instead of facing adjudication?
Compounding of the contravention
Applying under the SEBI settlement framework
Registering as a foreign portfolio investor
Filing a Suspicious Transaction Report

FEMA contraventions can be compounded by RBI or the Directorate of Enforcement on payment of a compounding amount, closing the matter without adjudication. The SEBI settlement framework applies to securities-law proceedings.

Depositories Act, 1996.overview: This chapter covers the Depositories Act, 1996, which enabled holding and transfer of securities in electronic (dematerialised) form. Revise the roles of the depository, depository participant and issuer, the distinction between registered owner and beneficial owner, the investor's option to hold securities in physical or demat form, rematerialisation, pledge and hypothecation of demat securities, and the depository's liability to indemnify investors for losses due to negligence. Also note SEBI's requirement that transfers of listed securities be done only in demat form and the two depositories in India.
questions: Which are the two depositories currently operating in India?
NSE and BSE
NSCCL and ICCL
CERSAI and CKYCR
NSDL and CDSL

National Securities Depository Ltd and Central Depository Services (India) Ltd are India's two depositories. NSE and BSE are stock exchanges, NSCCL and ICCL are clearing corporations, and CERSAI maintains CKYCR.
In the depository system, a depository participant (DP) acts as:
The issuer of the securities held by investors
An agent of the depository providing services to investors
A regulator of the depository on behalf of SEBI
The registered owner of all the securities held in the depository system
A DP is an agent of the depository through which investors open demat accounts and access depository services. The depository is the registered owner, and SEBI, not the DP, regulates depositories.
In the books of the issuer, the depository is shown as the registered owner of demat securities. Which rights does the depository have in this capacity?
The right to receive dividends on the securities
The right to sell the securities to recover fees
Only the right to effect transfers, without voting or economic rights
Full voting rights at all general meetings and the right to appoint directors
Under the Act, the depository is deemed registered owner only for effecting transfer of ownership. It has no voting or other rights; all rights and benefits belong to the beneficial owner.
An investor wishes to convert securities held in his demat account back into physical certificates. This process is called:
Transmission
Dematerialisation
Rematerialisation
Transposition

Converting electronic holdings back to physical form is rematerialisation, the opposite of dematerialisation. Transmission is transfer on death, and transposition is a change in the order of joint holders' names.
An investor wants to pledge shares held in demat form as security for a loan. How must the pledge be created?
By signing a transfer deed in favour of the lender
By handing over the delivery instruction slip book to the lender
By informing the company's auditor in writing
Through the depository system, with an entry recorded by the depository

Section 12 of the Depositories Act requires a pledge or hypothecation of demat securities to be recorded with the depository on intimation through the participant. Handing over slips or signing a transfer deed does not create a valid pledge.
An investor suffers a loss because of negligence by his depository participant. Under the Depositories Act, who must indemnify him?
The depository, which may then recover from the participant
SEBI out of its own funds
The issuer company whose shares were affected
The stock exchange where the shares are listed

Section 16 makes the depository liable to indemnify the beneficial owner for losses caused by negligence of the depository or its participant. The depository can in turn seek recovery from the participant at fault.
Since April 2019, SEBI requires transfers of securities of listed companies to be done:
In either form at the investor's choice without restriction
Only in demat form, except transmission or transposition
Only through the company's registered office
Only in physical form with a signed transfer deed
SEBI amended listing norms so that, from 1 April 2019, transfer of listed securities can be effected only in dematerialised form. Requests for transmission or transposition are an exception.
Under the Depositories Act, an investor subscribing to securities of an issuer has the option to:
Receive them in physical form or hold them through a depository
Hold them only in the name of the depository participant chosen by the issuer
Hold them only in physical form in all cases
Hold them only with the registrar and transfer agent

Section 8 of the Act gives the investor the option to hold securities either in physical form or with a depository. However, separate SEBI rules now mandate demat for certain issues and for transfers of listed securities.

SEBI (Mutual Funds) Regulations.overview: This chapter covers the SEBI (Mutual Funds) Regulations, 1996 and key circulars. Revise the structure of a mutual fund (sponsor, trust, trustees, AMC, custodian, RTA), eligibility and obligations of each party, scheme launch and documents, investment and borrowing restrictions, valuation and NAV, expense rules, unitholder rights including winding up and exit options, and recent reforms such as 'skin in the game', swing pricing, IDCW nomenclature and redemption timelines. Focus on the role and duties of trustees and AMCs, as compliance questions frequently test who is responsible for what.
questions: In a mutual fund structure, which entity holds the scheme's securities in safe custody?
The custodian
The registrar and transfer agent
The mutual fund distributor
The sponsor

A SEBI-registered custodian holds and safeguards the scheme's securities and handles related settlement and corporate actions. The RTA maintains investor records, and the sponsor sets up the fund but does not hold its assets.
Since April 2021, the dividend option in mutual fund schemes is required to be named:
Guaranteed Income Payout Option (GIPO)
Bonus Reinvestment Option (BRO)
Systematic Profit Distribution (SPD)
Income Distribution cum Capital Withdrawal (IDCW)
SEBI required dividend options to be renamed IDCW so that investors understand that distributions may be paid partly out of their own capital. The other names do not exist in the regulations.
Under the MF Regulations, a scheme may be wound up if unitholders pass a resolution to that effect. What proportion of unitholders is required?
51% of the unitholders
75% of the unitholders
90% of the unitholders
66% of the unitholders
A close-ended or open-ended scheme can be wound up if 75% of its unitholders pass a resolution to that effect, among other grounds such as the trustees' opinion or a SEBI direction.
All schemes of a mutual fund together cannot own more than what percentage of the paid-up capital carrying voting rights of any single company?

The Seventh Schedule of the MF Regulations prohibits a mutual fund, across all its schemes, from owning more than 10% of any company's paid-up capital carrying voting rights. This prevents mutual funds from gaining control of companies.
Under the 'skin in the game' framework, what must AMCs do with part of the compensation of their key employees?
Pay it entirely in cash in advance every year
Pay it into a fixed deposit with the sponsor's bank for three years
Pay it in units of the schemes they manage, subject to a lock-in
Pay it into the trustees' personal accounts

SEBI requires a portion of the compensation of designated AMC employees to be paid in units of the schemes they oversee, locked in for a specified period. This aligns their interests with unitholders.
During severe market stress, a debt scheme applies an adjustment that lowers the NAV for redeeming investors so that they bear part of the liquidity cost. This mechanism is called:
Exit load
Swing pricing
Side pocketing
NAV smoothing

Swing pricing adjusts NAV to pass on the cost of large redemptions to the investors causing them, protecting remaining unitholders. Side pocketing segregates a stressed security, and an exit load is a fixed charge on redemption.
Within how many working days of a valid redemption request must an AMC generally transfer redemption proceeds to the investor?
Fifteen working days
Ten working days
Seven working days
Three working days

SEBI has shortened the redemption timeline so that proceeds must generally be paid within three working days, with limited exceptions for schemes investing significantly overseas or in other specified situations.
A mutual fund scheme wants to borrow money. Under the MF Regulations, it may borrow only:
To meet temporary liquidity needs for redemptions or dividend payouts, within limits
To fund the AMC's office expenses
To take leveraged positions to boost returns
To lend money at attractive interest rates to the sponsor's group companies

Schemes may borrow only to meet temporary liquidity needs for repurchase, redemption or payout, capped at 20% of net assets and for a maximum of six months. Borrowing for leverage or for the AMC or sponsor is not allowed.

SEBI (AIF) Regulations.overview: This chapter covers the SEBI (Alternative Investment Funds) Regulations, 2012. Revise the three categories of AIFs and their sub-types, minimum corpus and investment amounts, limits on number of investors, continuing interest of the sponsor or manager, tenure and close-ended structure, leverage rules, investment concentration limits, accredited investors, filing of the private placement memorandum through a merchant banker, and restrictions on investing in associates. Practise classification of different fund strategies and calculations of the sponsor's continuing interest.
questions: A private equity fund that does not use leverage except for day-to-day operational needs and does not receive government incentives is usually registered as a:
Category I AIF
Category II AIF
Venture capital undertaking
Category III AIF

Category II covers AIFs such as private equity and debt funds that are not in Category I or III and do not use leverage other than for operational requirements. Category I is for funds with positive spillovers, and Category III for complex trading strategies.
A Category II AIF scheme has a corpus of ₹300 crore. What is the minimum continuing interest the manager or sponsor must hold in the scheme?
₹5 crore
₹15 crore
₹10 crore
₹7.5 crore
For Category I and II AIFs, the continuing interest is 2.5% of the corpus or ₹5 crore, whichever is lower. Here 2.5% of ₹300 crore is ₹7.5 crore, so the lower figure of ₹5 crore applies.
Which of the following statements about the structure of AIFs is correct?
Category I AIFs may be open-ended with daily NAV, but Category III AIFs must always be close-ended
Only Category II AIFs may be close-ended
All AIFs must be open-ended with daily NAV
Category I and II AIFs must be close-ended; Category III may be open-ended or close-ended
Category I and II AIFs must be close-ended with a minimum tenure of three years. Category III AIFs, which use trading strategies, can be either open-ended or close-ended.
What is the minimum corpus required for each scheme of an AIF (other than an angel fund)?
₹20 crore
₹100 crore
₹5 crore
₹50 crore
Each AIF scheme, other than an angel fund, must have a corpus of at least ₹20 crore. This is different from the minimum investment per investor, which is generally ₹1 crore.
A Special Situation Fund that invests in stressed loans and other special situation assets falls in which AIF category?
It is not an AIF
Category III
Category II
Category I
SEBI introduced Special Situation Funds in 2022 as a sub-category of Category I AIFs to invest in stressed assets, including loans acquired under the relevant frameworks.
Under the AIF Regulations, the private placement memorandum of an AIF scheme must be filed with SEBI through:
The fund's statutory auditor
A stock broker registered with an exchange
A SEBI-registered merchant banker
A credit rating agency
SEBI requires the PPM of AIF schemes to be filed through a merchant banker, who carries out due diligence on the disclosures. Brokers, auditors and rating agencies do not perform this role.
Under the AIF framework, which body issues the certificate that allows an investor to be treated as an 'accredited investor'?
The Income Tax Department
An accreditation agency recognised by SEBI
The branch of the bank where the investor holds a savings account
The AIF manager itself

Accreditation is granted by accreditation agencies, which are subsidiaries of depositories or stock exchanges recognised for this purpose, after verifying income or net worth. The fund manager cannot certify its own investors.
A Category II AIF wants to invest in a company that is an associate of its manager. Under the AIF Regulations, such investment generally requires:
Approval of the stock exchange where the units of the AIF scheme are listed
Approval only of the manager's board of directors
Approval of at least 75% of the investors by value of their investment
No approval, since associates are always permitted

Category I and II AIFs may invest in associates only with the approval of 75% of investors by value of their investment in the scheme, to address conflicts of interest. Manager approval alone is not sufficient.

SEBI (InvIT) Regulations.overview: This chapter covers the SEBI (Infrastructure Investment Trusts) Regulations, 2014. Understand the InvIT structure as a trust holding infrastructure assets directly or through holding companies and SPVs, and the roles of the sponsor, investment manager, project manager and trustee. Revise investment conditions, holding requirements in SPVs, borrowing limits and the conditions for higher leverage, distribution of cash flows, listing of units, valuation, sponsor holding and lock-in, and unitholder rights. Questions often test which party is responsible for a function and what conditions apply before an action can be taken.
questions: Under the InvIT Regulations, an InvIT is set up as:
A private limited company incorporated under the Companies Act, 2013
A trust registered under the Indian Trusts Act, 1882 and with SEBI
A limited liability partnership under the LLP Act
A cooperative society under State law
An InvIT is created as a trust under the Indian Trusts Act, 1882, with a registered trust deed, and must be registered with SEBI. It is not a company, LLP or cooperative.
In an InvIT, which party is responsible for executing and operating the infrastructure project as per the agreement?
The project manager
The valuer
The trustee
The unitholders

The project manager executes and operates the infrastructure projects or achieves their completion as per the project implementation agreement. The trustee oversees the InvIT for unitholders, and the investment manager handles investment decisions.
Units of an InvIT offered to the public are required to be:
Transferred only with the trustee's prior approval
Held only in physical form by unitholders
Listed on a recognised stock exchange
Redeemable on demand at NAV like an open-ended fund
Units of publicly offered InvITs must be listed on a recognised stock exchange so investors can trade them. InvIT units are not redeemable on demand like open-ended mutual fund units.
Where an InvIT invests in an SPV through a holding company, the InvIT (directly or through the holdco) must generally hold at least what share of the SPV's equity?

The InvIT Regulations require the InvIT, directly or through a holdco, to hold a controlling interest and at least 51% of the equity share capital or interest in the SPV, except where restricted by law or concession terms.
An InvIT wants its aggregate consolidated borrowings to exceed 25% of the value of its assets. Which conditions apply?
No conditions apply, as InvITs can borrow without any limit
Obtain a credit rating and approval of unitholders
Approval of only the project manager
Prior approval of RBI for every borrowing

Borrowings beyond 25% of asset value require a credit rating and approval of unitholders, and higher levels are subject to additional conditions such as a strong rating and distribution track record. Borrowing is not unlimited.
What is the main purpose of the requirement that the sponsor of an InvIT holds a minimum unitholding for a lock-in period after listing?
To exempt the InvIT from distribution requirements
To prevent unitholders from ever selling their units
To allow the sponsor to control all of the trustee's decisions on distributions
To keep the sponsor's 'skin in the game' and align it with investors

The sponsor's minimum holding and lock-in ensure that it remains committed to the assets it transferred, aligning its interests with unitholders. It does not restrict trading by other unitholders or override distribution norms.
Which entity in an InvIT structure makes investment decisions and oversees the activities of the project manager?
The stock exchange
The sponsor
The registrar to the issue
The investment manager

The investment manager takes investment decisions for the InvIT and is responsible for overseeing the project manager's performance. The sponsor sets up the InvIT, but day-to-day management sits with the investment manager.
The trustee of an InvIT is primarily responsible for:
Overseeing that the InvIT and its manager act in unitholders' interest
Providing the bulk of the InvIT's borrowing
Operating and maintaining the toll roads or power lines
Setting the daily trading price of the InvIT's units on the stock exchange

The trustee holds the InvIT assets in trust for unitholders and oversees the activities of the investment manager and others to ensure compliance and protect unitholders. Operations are with the project manager.

SEBI (REIT) Regulations.overview: This chapter covers the SEBI (Real Estate Investment Trusts) Regulations, 2014, including the 2024 framework for Small and Medium REITs. Learn the parties to a REIT (sponsor, manager, trustee, valuer), the trust structure, investment conditions focused on completed rent-generating properties in India, listing of units, related party transactions, valuation and independence of the valuer, distributions, and unitholder rights such as nominating a director on the manager's board. Revise what makes REITs attractive to retail investors and the safeguards that protect them.
questions: Which party is responsible for managing a REIT's assets and investments and for day-to-day operations?
The manager
The auditor
The valuer
The trustee

The manager of a REIT makes investment decisions and manages the real estate assets, either directly or through property managers. The trustee oversees on behalf of unitholders, and the valuer only values assets.
For a retail investor, which is a key benefit of investing in a listed REIT?
Freedom from all market and interest rate risks
Direct ownership of a specific office floor in the building that the investor can occupy personally
A guaranteed fixed return set by SEBI each year
Exposure to income-generating commercial real estate with small amounts and exchange liquidity

REITs let investors own a share of a diversified portfolio of rent-generating properties with small ticket sizes and the ability to trade on exchanges. Returns are not guaranteed, and unitholders do not own specific floors.
Under the REIT Regulations, a REIT may invest in real estate assets located:
Anywhere in the world without restriction
Only in Special Economic Zones abroad
Only in India
In India and any FATF member country
REITs registered with SEBI can invest only in real estate and related assets located in India. Overseas property investment is not permitted under the regulations.
Under the framework introduced in 2024, a Small and Medium REIT (SM REIT) is meant for assets of value in the range of:
₹5 crore to ₹25 crore
₹50 crore to less than ₹500 crore
Above ₹5,000 crore only
₹500 crore to below ₹1,000 crore

SEBI created SM REITs in 2024 for asset sizes from ₹50 crore up to less than ₹500 crore, bringing fractional ownership platforms under regulation. Larger portfolios continue under the main REIT framework.
A REIT plans to buy a property from its sponsor. How should this related party transaction be handled?
At arm's length, with valuation and disclosure, and unitholder approval where required
Only with the oral consent of the sponsor's chairman
Only after delisting the REIT units from the exchange and seeking approval of the sponsor's lenders
Without any valuation since the sponsor is trusted

Related party transactions must be on an arm's length basis, in the unitholders' best interest, consistent with REIT strategy, supported by valuation reports and disclosed, with unitholder approval above specified thresholds.
Under the REIT Regulations, a valuer cannot value the same property for more than how many consecutive years?
Ten years
Six years
Four years
Two years

To preserve independence, a valuer may not undertake valuation of the same property for more than four consecutive years, and can be reappointed only after a gap. The valuer also must not be an associate of the sponsor, manager or trustee.
Unitholders holding at least what percentage of a REIT's units have the right to nominate one director on the board of the manager?
SEBI's 2023 amendment gave eligible unitholders holding 10% or more of the total outstanding units the right to nominate one non-independent director on the manager's board, improving governance.
Units of a REIT that are offered to the public must be:
Held by only one institutional investor
Issued only in physical certificate form
Redeemable daily at NAV by the manager
Listed on a recognised stock exchange

Publicly offered REIT units are mandatorily listed on a recognised stock exchange, which provides trading liquidity. REIT units are not redeemed daily like open-ended mutual fund units and are held in demat form.
